3.2.2.10 	
Conclusions
The France-Spain AC interconnection lines trips are 
aligned with the protection system design. The 
­disconnection of these lines enabled the isolation of 
the disturbance, preventing it from affecting the French 
system. This, in turn, allowed for a faster re-energisation 
of part of the Spanish system from France.
The Morocco – Spain interconnection lines trips are 
aligned with the protection system design in the 
Moroccan side. The disconnection of these lines enabled 
the isolation of the disturbance, preventing it from 
affecting the Moroccan system. Given the size of the 
Moroccan power system and the weak Spain – Morocco 
interconnection, with only two transmission lines, 
­maintaining both systems interconnected would not 
have prevented the blackout and would likely have 
caused a voltage collapse in the Moroccan system. This 
isolation, in turn, allowed for a faster re-energisation of 
part of the Spanish system from Morocco.
One of the internal trips in the Spanish transmission 
network occurred before reaching, in the primary meas­
urement, the voltage level at which the overvoltage 
protection function is expected to operate according to 
its settings (264 kV), due to an error in the voltage meas­
urement. However, given the security margin applied 
with respect to the voltage level at which generator 
disconnections may begin even for units with the highest 
voltage requirements (253 kV), the trip took place once 
the voltage threshold required for generation had 
already been exceeded. 
Therefore, this trip did not worsen the incident, both 
because of the voltage level at which it occurred and 
because of the limited operational significance of the 
line that tripped.
Once the system was no longer recoverable, with 
very low voltage and low frequency levels, trips of 
­transmission network elements occurred that are 
­considered unavoidable, as system conditions were 
already highly degraded and the protection equipment 
cannot deal with these conditions. These trips are also 
deemed to have had no impact on the development 
of the ­incident, since at the moment they occurred the 
system was already unrecoverable.
No trips occurred on the Portugal side of the Portugal –
Spain interconnections. The protection functions on the 
Portuguese side remained stable under low‑voltage 
and low‑frequency dynamic conditions and correctly 
refrained from operating, as no faults were detected on 
the interconnection circuits. This behaviour is consistent 
with the design of the Portuguese protection system.
In Portugal, two internal transmission lines tripped due 
to the operation of zone 1 of the distance protection 
function. These trips were triggered by highly unstable 
voltage conditions after the system had already reached 
the point of no return, preventing the distance protection 
algorithm from maintaining a valid voltage reference.

===== PAGE 197 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  197 
The France-Spain interconnection AC lines trips are 
aligned with the protection system except for the Argia – 
Hernani, the Argia – Arkalé lines and the Argia busbar 
coupler in 225 kV. This problem is currently identified by 
RTE and has been addressed for the other protection. 
The disconnection of the AC interconnection enabled 
the isolation of the disturbance, preventing it from 
affecting the French system. This, in turn, allowed for a 
faster re-energisation of part of the Spanish system from 
France.
Concerning the French 63 kV lines. Many out of step 
protection tripped before the interconnection lines. This 
is considered appropriate by RTE. 
Concerning the only distance protection that tripped in 
the South-west, the situation is known by RTE and have 
been addressed.
3.3	
System Defence Plan
Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/2196 of 24 November 
2017 established the Network Code on Electricity 
­Emergency and Restoration (NC ER). This regulation 
outlines the rules for (i) safeguarding operational 
­security, (ii) preventing the propagation and deteriora­
tion of an incident, (iii) avoiding widespread disturbance 
and the blackout state, and (iv) allowing the efficient 
and rapid restoration of the electricity system from 
­emergency and/or blackout states.
Section 2 of the regulation establishes the ­requirements 
for the design and implementation of the System Defence 
Plan. In particular, Article 15 sets out the ­requirements for 
the automatic underfrequency control scheme.
3.3.1	
Spanish System Defence Plan
The Spanish defence plan for a situation involving a 
sudden drop in system frequency due to an imbalance 
between production and consumption includes the 
following two strategies, in accordance with Article 15 
of the NC ER:
»	1.	 Automatic low frequency pump-storage 
disconnection plan
»	2.	 Automatic low frequency demand 
­disconnection strategy.
The first strategy consists of two steps, with activation 
thresholds of 49.5 Hz and 49.3 Hz. The second strategy 
defines six frequency thresholds, beginning at 49 Hz 
and decreasing in 0.2 Hz intervals down to 48 Hz. At 
each threshold, portions of demand are progressively 
­disconnected, as shown in Table 3-8 and Figure 3-69.

Figure 3-69: Activation of the Low Frequency Demand Disconnection Plan for RE.
The Spanish defence plan has incorporated demand 
across different frequency steps, taking into account its 
geographical location to ensure a balanced impact on 
both congestion and voltage levels. The plan does not 
have specific measures related to voltage; it is primarily 
designed to maintain the balance between ­generation 
and demand, which is reflected in the change of 
frequency.
Per the Spanish defence plan, the LFDD demand 
­disconnected at each frequency level is, in some 
cases, physically disconnected at the connection point 
of specific load units, while in others, it is physically 
disconnected at the distribution connection points. This 
means that a specific section of the distribution system 
is ­disconnected in its entirety, regardless of whether 
active/reactive power is being injected or absorbed by 
that section.
3.3.1.1	
Automatic Low Frequency Disconnection of Pump Storage
Before the incident, the total power from pumping units 
was 3,031 MW, of which 2,365 MW came from pumping 
associated with the first frequency threshold (49.5 Hz) 
and 666 MW with the second frequency threshold 
(49.3 Hz).
At 12:33:20.180, the system frequency fell below 
49.5 Hz, triggering the first step of the automatic low 
frequency disconnection of pump-storage units. The 
disconnection associated with this initial threshold was 
effective between 12:33:20.133 and 12:33:20.800. At 
that time, 24 pumping units were available, 20 of which 
were tripped. However, two of these were disconnected 
due to unrelated causes, before the operation of the 
underfrequency relay. Of the remaining four units, 
one was disconnected at 12:33:23.888 due to loss of 
synchronism. No information is available for the discon­
nection of the remaining three. The total pump-storage 
power disconnected at this frequency threshold amounts 
to 2,168 MW out of 2,365 MW (91 %).
At 12:33:20.500, the frequency fell below 49.3 Hz, 
­triggering the activation of the second step. At this 
stage, six pump units were available. However, one 
pump-storage unit disconnected at 12:33:24.000 due 
to undervoltage issues. At this frequency threshold, the 
total power disconnected amounts to 588 MW.
Considering both frequency thresholds, the pump 
storage disconnection amounts to 2,756 MW.

3.3.1.2	
Low Frequency Automatic Demand Disconnection
On 28 April 2025 at 12:30:00, the total consumption in 
Spain reached 29,631 MW, representing the total load 
estimate closest to the instant of LFDD activation. From 
12:33:20.600 onwards, the six frequency steps of the 
low frequency automatic demand disconnection plan 
were activated as follows: 
»	At 12:33:20.600, the system frequency dropped 
below 49.0 Hz, triggering the activation of the 
first step of load shedding. During this step, a 
total of 1,175.9 MW of load was disconnected.
»	At 12:33:20.760, the system frequency dropped 
below 48.8 Hz, triggering the activation of the 
second step of load shedding. The total load 
shed in this step was 1,669.1 MW.
»	At 12:33:21.000, the system frequency dropped 
below 48.6 Hz, triggering the activation of 
the third stage of load shedding. The total 
amount of load disconnected in this stage was 
1,574.6 MW.
»	At 12:33:21.380, the system frequency dropped 
below 48.4 Hz, triggering the activation of the 
fourth step of load shedding. The total load 
shed in this step was 1,523.9 MW.
»	At 12:33:21.820, the system frequency dropped 
below 48.2 Hz, triggering the activation of the 
fifth step of load shedding. The total load shed 
in this step was 1,294.3 MW.
»	At 12:33:22.040, the system frequency dropped 
below 48.0 Hz, triggering the activation of the 
sixth step of load shedding. The total load shed 
in this step was 1,267.1 MW.
Notably, two DSOs reported that a few underfrequency 
relays had not yet been adapted to the agreed low 
frequency demand disconnection scheme. As a result, 
71.03 MW were disconnected at 48.7 Hz, although they 
are currently programmed to activate at 48.6 Hz. There­
fore, the 71.03 MW at 48.7 Hz were added to the 48.6 Hz 
frequency threshold.
The total disconnected demand was 8,504.9 MW, 
­representing approximately 29 % of the prior total 
consumption. This value falls short of the theoretical 
target set by the defence plan, which establishes a range 
with a minimum of 38 %. This includes the load from 
consumers connected at the transmission grid and at the 
distribution grid. Table 3-10 presents the net demand 
disconnected during the six steps.

3.3.2	
Portuguese System Defence Plan 
The frequency drop activated the underfrequency 
defence plan of the Portuguese electrical system, in 
accordance with Article 15 of Regulation (EU) 2017/2196 
issued by the Commission on Emergency and ­Restoration. 
The plan foresees progressive load shedding based on 
frequency thresholds, described as follows:
»	From 49.8 Hz to 49.3 Hz, the defence plan 
automatically shed the hydroelectric units in 
pumping mode.
»	At 49.2 Hz, the defence plan shed the electro-in­
tensive industrial load at the TSO and DSO level.
»	From 49.0 Hz to 48.0 Hz, the defence plan shed 
distribution-connected consumers.
According to REN and E-REDES data, the total shed active 
power was:
»	Hydroelectric units in pumping mode:
2,098 MW
»	Electro-intensive industrial consumers:
218 MW
»	Distribution network consumers:
1,955 MW.
On 28 April 2025 at 12:33:00, the total consumption in 
Portugal amounted to 5,865 MW.
The preliminary estimation of the total demand discon­
nected as part of LFDD, between 49.0 Hz and 48.0 Hz, 
amounted to 1,955 MW, representing 33.3 % of the prior 
total consumption. Considering the 218 MW of electro-­
intensive industrial consumers disconnected at 49.2 Hz, 
the total disconnected demand represents 37.1 % of prior 
total consumption. This value falls short of the ­theoretical 
target set by the defence plan, which establishes a range 
with a minimum of 38 %. Details can be found in Table 
3-11, Table 3-12, Table 3-13, and Figure 3-70.
The Portuguese defence plan is designed to shed 
consumption in different frequency steps. ­Geographical 
dispersion of the consumption to be shed in each 
frequency step is assured, mitigating the impacts of 
congestions and voltages in the grids.
Per the Portuguese defence plan, the LFDD demand 
disconnected at each frequency level is, in some 
cases, physically disconnected at the connection point 
of specific load units, while in others, it is physically 
disconnected at the distribution grid and at ­transmission 
connection points with the distribution grid. This 
means that a specific section of the distribution system 
is ­disconnected in its entirety, regardless of whether 
active/reactive power is being injected or absorbed by 
that section.

3.4	
Impact of the Blackout on System Users 
on the French Network
The incident of 28 April 2025 resulted in a full blackout in 
Spain and Portugal, interrupting the power supply of all 
consumers in both countries. The impact of the incident 
was much more limited in France, as described in this 
section. 
This impact was mainly concentrated in the southwest 
area of France. 
Regarding the load, two substations at the ­distribution 
level in the Basque Country were impacted by the 
dynamic phenomena during the collapse phase. 
The first substation was shed due to the frequency load 
shedding defence plan.
The second substation lost supply due to the activation of 
the loss of synchronism protection. 
The total unsupplied power amounted to 7 MW. System 
users were restored within 15 – 20 minutes. 
Regarding the impact on industrial system users, 
­approximately 15 experienced total or partial process 
interruptions due to the activation of their own 
­protections (related to voltage or oscillations).
Some suffered equipment damage, while others 
­experienced a slow restart following necessary cleaning 
procedures. Additional users experienced voltage dips. 
On the generation side, one nuclear power plant 
­experienced an automatic interruption of the reactor, 
and around 20 other generation facilities connected to 
the transmission grid, as well as additional power plants 
on the distribution grid, tripped.
This was related either to:
»	Low transient frequency
»	High current level on the stator side 
»	Loss of synchronism
Other generation facilities tripped due to high voltage 
levels. This was the case for two hydraulic power units, as 
well as some PV and wind turbines. The two hydropower 
pumps were consuming around 200 MW.
Generation facilities connected to networks below 45 kV 
were disconnected due to the activation of protections, 
primarily related to overvoltages.
Finally, a few batteries that were connected before the 
event were disconnected very briefly. The total loss 
of supplied power was minor (around 5 MW), and the 
restart took between one and three minutes.

4	
ANALYSIS OF RELEVANT FACTORS
This chapter presents detailed technical analyses of the various phenomena and 
actions that preceded the blackout, with the purpose of understanding precisely the 
causes of the incident. All these analyses are based on the factual data collected and 
presented essentially in Chapters 2 and 3. 
Based on the results of these technical analyses, the 
Expert Panel established the root cause tree describing 
the key factors that eventually led to blackout. The root 
cause tree is presented in the last section of this chapter.
It should be noted that these technical analyses focus 
on the Spanish system, as the facts described in chapters 
2 and 3 indicate that the origin of the blackout lies in 
Spain, not in Portugal. 
The chapter is structured according to the following sections :
4.1 	Voltage control
4.2 	Oscillations
4.3 	Analysis of TSO-DSO flows
4.4 	System Defence Plans
4.5 	Alarm handling 
4.6 	Root Cause Tree
4.1	
Voltage control
4.1.1	
Structure of the section
This section discusses voltage control.
»	The first subsection (4.1.2) discusses the reac­
tive power resources that collectively were 
unable to respond to the voltage increase. It 
addresses technical and regulatory aspects and 
suggests future improvements. 
»	The second subsection (4.1.3) describes voltage 
management aspects that contributed to the 
loss of voltage control.
»	The third subsection (4.1.4) describes voltage 
trends on 28 April, explains the voltage increase 
in more detail, and considers the conditions in 
the morning and on a previous day.
»	The fourth subsection (4.1.5) presents the 
static-­model voltage sensitivity analyses that 
were performed. 
»	The recommendations regarding voltage 
control referenced throughout this chapter 
are, like other recommendations, located in 
Chapter 9.
»	The additional areas for attention/improve­
ment identified during the investigation are 
listed in the conclusions of Chapters 4.1.2 
and 4.1.3.
This section complements the data already included in 
Chapter 2.

4.1.2	
Reactive power contribution by various assets
This section describes the capabilities of various assets to provide reactive power to the system on 28 April. 
4.1.2.1	
Integrated network components (shunt reactors, STATCOMs) 
30	
The chronology of voltage control actions is provided in Table 2-2 in Section 2.1.2, and the status of shunt reactors is summarised in Section 2.6.4.1.
31	
The Expert Panel has not comprehensively assessed the approach across all TSOs. Nevertheless, several TSOs participating in the Panel indicated that they only 
have manual control of shunt reactors, while RTE indicated they have a hybrid approach combining manual and automatic control. 
32	
Furthermore, as described in Section 4.1.3.2 (Alarm handling), voltage remedial actions were not included in the operator’s handbook.
On the day of the incident, only one STATCOM was in 
operation. Another was undergoing final testing before 
commissioning, while others were planned for the 
future and were not yet operational at the time of the 
incident. Only the available STATCOM was considered in 
the security analysis.
There are around 90 shunt reactors installed in the 
Spanish grid, corresponding to a reactive power capacity 
of 13,300 MVAr. Of these, 43 shunt reactors (with a total 
of 6,000 MVAr) were manoeuvred for voltage control in 
the period 09:00 – 12:30 on 28 April (84 switching oper­
ations in total, 40 in the south).30 In Spain, shunt reactors 
are operated by RE manually.31 
Some shunt reactors were disconnected and reconnected 
during or around oscillation episodes due to the low and 
high voltages experienced during voltage swings, espe­
cially during the low voltages during the oscillations.
Following the oscillation episodes, between 12:20 
and 12:25, three shunt reactors were disconnected 
and four transmission lines were connected, increasing 
the grid’s reactive power production. To address the 
resulting voltage rise, five shunt reactors were connected 
between 12:25 and 12:28. As a result of these switching 
manoeuvres, the voltage returned to within allowed 
limits by 12:30.
No additional shunt reactors were connected from 
12:28 until the incident. Throughout the voltage rise 
from 12:32:00 to 12:33:16 and the blackout, 7,700 MVAr 
of shunt reactors remained connected and 5,600 MVAr 
remained disconnected. The share of connected reactors 
was particularly low in southern Spain, where voltages 
had been particularly low after the oscillations, as shown 
in Table 4-1.
The following chart summarises the status of shunt 
reactors.
As the actions to connect shunt reactors were manual, 
given the short lead time, the shunt reactors were not 
manually connected during the minute-long voltage 
rise (see Figure 4-8).32 RE considered, both on 28 April 
and previously, that the assets intended to absorb fast 
voltage variations were conventional generators, 
STATCOM, and the HVDC link, rather than shunt reactors. 
The Expert Panel issued related recommendations in 
Chapter 9.

4.1.2.2	
Generators in Spain
This section focuses on the reactive power provisions by generators connected to the transmission network in Spain.33
4.1.2.2.1	
Introduction
33	
CNMC indicated that in Spain, the regulatory framework is complex, as regulatory technical operational details are proposed by the TSO and must be approved 
by the relevant regulatory authorities before entering into force. CNMC is responsible for markets and system services, while the Ministry is responsible for 
security criteria and grid connection requirements.
34	
The utilisation of the requirements in Spain is discussed in Section 4.1.2.3.
35	
Royal Decree 413/2014 of 6 June, which regulates the activity of producing electrical energy from renewable energy sources, cogeneration, and waste. 
36	
This means that the fixed power setpoint was explicitly sent from the system operator to each unit, in this case via email. While the communication is direct, 
there is nevertheless no direct data link – i. e. there is no direct setpoint in the sense of the system operator’s instruction automatically applying to the genera­
tor’s control system. In Portugal, voltage control is implemented via setpoints sent through the SCADA systems of the TSO and the generator. Generators should 
be capable of operating in three modes (reactive power control setpoint, voltage control setpoint, power factor control). After receiving a voltage setpoint, 
it is up to the power plant control (PPC) to manage the plant’s resources to deliver the desired output at the grid interconnection point. Older wind power plants 
function on a fixed tan fi mode (between −0.2 and 0.2), according to a fixed setpoint determined by the TSO. These setpoints were communicated via email and 
are not changed regularly. 
37	
Resolution of 10 March 2000, of the Secretary of State for Industry and Energy, which approves the operating procedure of the system (P.O. 7.4) “Complementary 
service for tension control of the transmission network”.
In terms of how power system users provide reactive 
power, this report distinguishes three reactive power 
control modes (generally, not limited to Spain):
»	Reactive power control mode (where the 
unit assumes a reactive power setpoint and 
provides a set value (in MVAr) of reactive power 
injection or absorption); 
»	Voltage control mode (where the unit assumes 
a voltage setpoint that can be defined either 
at the connection point or at the generator’s 
low-voltage side and injects or absorbs reactive 
power as needed to move the voltage towards 
that setpoint);
»	Fixed power factor (where the unit assumes 
a power factor setpoint and injects or absorbs 
reactive power proportional (i. e. capacitive 
power factor) or inversely proportional (i. e. 
inductive power factor) to its instantaneous 
active power output).
With regard to power park modules of Type C and above, 
Article 21 (3)(d) of the Commission Regulation 2016/631 
(NC RfG) provides that the power park module shall be 
capable of providing reactive power automatically by 
either of the three modes and that the relevant system 
operator may specify which of the three reactive power 
control mode options and setpoints to apply.34 Neverthe­
less, this requirement does not apply to the power park 
modules connected before the application of the NC RfG. 
4.1.2.2.2	
Implementation in Spain
On the day of the incident, the requirements concerning 
reactive power provision by generators in Spain varied 
by generator type:
»	A.	 RES generators (either connected to the transmission 
or the distribution grid) followed a fixed power 
factor range. The national regulation35 defined the 
power factor range, while for some RES generators 
above 5 MW, the TSO36 set a specific range for each 
power plant to reflect system needs, resulting in 
different values across plants. The power factor for 
facilities connected to the distribution network was 
agreed upon by the TSO in coordination with the 
relevant DSO.
»	B.	 Conventional/Synchronous generators above 30 MW 
–	 i.	 By default, they were mandated to provide 
reactive power according to a function 
Q(U-actual, P-installed, ­U-reference), 
where the non-real-time voltage refer­
ence (U-reference) was defined for the 
electrical point not shared with other 
generation units (usually corresponding 
to the ­connection point) – as detailed in 
Operational ­Procedure PO 7.4 (2000)37
–	 ii.	Some generators were also able to volun­
teer to receive direct voltage setpoints 
from the system operator.

===== PAGE 209 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  209 
A process to amend Operational Procedure PO 7.4 
(2000) was initiated by RE in 2021 and approved by 
the national regulatory authority (CNMC) in June 2025, 
after the ­incident.38 By 2023, the process had led to the 
­development of a pilot market-based voltage control 
project in two regions of Spain. After the pilot projects 
and regulatory sandboxes concluded, participating 
conventional generators were allowed, on a voluntary 
basis, to follow a direct voltage setpoint sent by the 
system operator to the participating unit in real time. 
38	
The amendment proposed in 2021 had to be approved by the national regulatory authority (CNMC), which in 2019 was granted the power to regulate non-­
frequency services, among others. The NRA’s assessment with stakeholders identified several difficulties, including a conflict with other national rules outside 
the competence of the NRA – specifically regarding the obligation for RES to provide dynamic (i. e. non fixed-power-factor-based) voltage control – and a lack 
of evidence to discard a market-based approach due to economic inefficiency, as required by Article 40 of Directive (EU) 2019/944. To continue developing the 
voltage control framework, two pilot projects were launched in 2022 and 2023: the first tested a market-based voltage control service in two regions of Spain, 
and the second explored the voltage control capabilities of consumers. Based on the findings of the pilot projects, the TSO proposed an amendment to the initial 
proposal in March 2024, which was subsequently consulted on, revised, and approved in June 2025.
39	
If the plant was connected to the distribution grid, the instruction was agreed upon with the DSO.
40	
The process related to paragraph iii had begun but had not reached agreement. A separate process related to paragraph ii never took place but there was a 
proposal of voltage control service provided by RES in 2011, under the scope of a different Royal Decree (RD661/2007) and which appears to have not been 
finalised.
41	
Pilot projects did take place.
42	
I.e. CNMC, the national regulatory authority designated according to Article 57 of Directive (EU) 944/2019.
This meant that some generators were able to transition, 
in real time, between the optional direct voltage setpoint 
control mode (pilot project, direct voltage setpoint) 
and the default non-real-time voltage reference mode 
(Operational Procedure PO 7.4).
The following subsections provide a more detailed 
description of reactive power provision in Spain by 
generators.
4.1.2.3	
Reactive power provision by RES generators in Spain
4.1.2.3.1	
Technical aspects
As indicated in point A in Section 4.1.2.2.2, RES genera­
tors were set to follow a fixed-power-control mode. This 
was a key factor in the incident for two reasons:
»	First, it meant that resources operating in fixed-
power-factor mode injected a proportional 
(fast) reactive power ramp, and thus a voltage 
ramp, into the system for every (fast) active 
power ramp (e. g. a schedule change).
»	Second, fixed-power-factor-mode resources 
provided no reactive power support that 
would compensate for voltage fluctuations, 
since their reactive power output did not 
respond to conditions in the grid. 
The Expert Panel has issued a related recommendation, 
which can be found in Chapter 9. Further takeaways are 
detailed in the summary of conclusions in Section 4.1.2.7.
4.1.2.3.2	
Applicable requirements
The operational requirements for certain aspects of RES 
power plants are based on the national Spanish Royal 
Decree in force since 2014 (RD 413/2014 on renew­
able energy sources). These requirements specify the 
power factor range for RES installations, set between 
0.98 inductive and 0.98 capacitive (see Article 7e 
of the Royal Decree). Based on provisions in Article 
7e, RE also instructed some power plants to operate 
within a narrower range (e. g. 0.98 – 0.99 inductive) 
deemed more in line with system needs.39 In effect, RES 
power plants followed a fixed power factor within 
the required range. Article 7e of the Royal Decree did 
not explicitly mandate any other approach to voltage 
control for RES. 
The decree also appears to provide for the option of a 
RES-specific voltage control service (see paragraph 
ii of Article 7e) or for RES participation in the regular 
voltage control service (see paragraph iii of Article 7e), 
but these regulatory developments had not been final­
ised.40, 41 The Royal Decree, as in force on the relevant 
date, does not appear to assign the TSO or the national 
regulatory authority42 any direct competence to modify 
its provisions, particularly regarding the voluntary 
nature of participation in these services. 
For the Expert Panel’s observations on the applicable 
requirements, please refer to Chapter 9.

===== PAGE 210 =====
210  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
4.1.2.4	
Reactive power provision by conventional generators in Spain
43	
As noted above, the generators that participated in the pilot project were able to alternate between a) providing reactive power considering the direct voltage 
setpoint in the pilot project and b) providing voltage control considering the Operational Procedure 7.4 (2000). 
44	
It was issued on 28 April for one generator outside the southern region.
As indicated in point B.i of Section 4.1.2.2.2, the default 
requirements for reactive power provision by conven­
tional generators at the time of the incident were 
defined by Operational Procedure PO 7.4 (2000).43 
At the same time, as indicated in point B.ii, some gener­
ators had the option to receive direct voltage setpoints 
from the TSO. 
4.1.2.4.1	
Technical aspects
The basic service described in Operational Procedure 
PO 7.4 requires each generator to set its reactive power 
output based on a function described in the Operational 
Procedure. The generator sets its reactive power output 
based on: 
»	The system voltage reference set by the TSO (set 
at 405 – 410 kV on 28 April, as it had been for 
several years beforehand). While the voltage 
reference for Operational Procedure PO 7.4 
was generally set for the whole system, it 
was temporarily set independently for some 
generators.
»	The actual voltage at the generator connection 
point
»	The installed active power of the generator
Thus, under the applicable requirements outlined in 
Operational Procedure PO 7.4, a generator was to deter­
mine its reactive power output itself, according to the 
formula set out in Operational Procedure PO 7.4, and 
considering the global voltage reference published by 
the TSO.
In some cases, a specific voltage reference for an indi­
vidual generator could be sent via telephone commu­
nication,44 but this was not the default approach. In 
contrast, if the generator participated in the pilot project, 
a direct voltage setpoint was sent to each participating 
generator each minute. 
Under the requirements of Operational Procedure PO 
7.4, the system operator was responsible for calculating 
the expected reactive power provision by generators. 
Unlike in the pilot project, this reference was not sent to 
generators in real time; instead, it was used ex post to 
determine remuneration, penalties, and monthly fulfil­
ment reports, which were shared with the respective 
generators. Generators were also expected to calculate 
the reference themselves, but the TSO did not conduct 
close-to-real-time monitoring of differences between 
its calculated reference (using the Operational Proce­
dure PO 7.4), and the generator’s actual reactive power 
output.
The Expert Panel issued related recommendations in 
Chapter 9.
4.1.2.4.2	
Applicable requirements
The Operational Procedure PO 7.4 was published in 
2000. On 28 April 2025, the process to amend the proce­
dure was ongoing, but the original version still applied. 
In June 2025, the new version was approved.
CNMC’s interpretation of the Operational Procedure 
PO 7.4 is included in Section 2.6.5.1. The Operational 
Procedure PO 7.4 (2000), as applicable on 28 April 2025, 
established the rights and responsibilities of generators 
for providing reactive power. It required generators 
to provide a minimum reactive power contribution 
(absorbing or injecting, depending on the voltage) 
whenever the voltage was outside a margin around the 
voltage reference set by the TSO. 
According to the Procedure, in order to determine penal­
ties or payments related to the voltage control service, 
the service is considered delivered if reactive power 
meeting these requirements is provided in at least 75 % 
of the samples (i. e. nine out of 12 measurement samples 
taken in an hour, according to the Procedure). 
The Procedure PO 7.4 prescribed penalties for generators 
not complying with the procedure. However, it appears 
that the penalties were not applicable in practice, since 
the economic scheme required by the Operating Proce­
dure PO 7.4 had not been developed.

4.1.2.4.3	
Assessment of reactive power provision
The scope of this investigation and the mandate of the 
Expert Panel do not grant it the authority, nor does it 
have any intention, of interpreting the applicable legis­
lation or determining liabilities for non-compliance with 
legal requirements. Within the limits of its mandate, and 
for the purposes of identifying the causes of the incident, 
the Expert Panel sought to understand the actual tech­
nical behaviour of relevant generators with respect to 
reactive power on 28 April.
As depicted in the relevant figures,46 on 28 April, the 
actual reactive power output of some conventional 
synchronous generators that were providing ­reactive 
power diverged from the TSO’s reference, which 
it ­established in accordance with the Operational 
­Procedure PO 7.4. It was also observed that for several 
generators, during the morning hours of 28 April (i. e. 
between 9 am until the incident), actual reactive power 
output (based on RE SCADA data) aligned with reference 
values (Q-reference, also calculated from RE SCADA data 
according to the formula in Article 10 and the associated 
graph in the Operational Procedure PO 7.4 47) in less than 
75 % of the samples.
It is noted that the number of conventional generators 
providing reactive power is set by the TSO according to 
its daily security assessments of system needs after the 
results of the market.48 
The Expert Panel’s in-depth examination focused on 
three thermal conventional generators connected in the 
south – the region where voltage conditions first deteri­
orated and the first overvoltage disconnections occurred.
RE provided records showing that the three thermal 
conventional generators in the south had, at least once 
in the year preceding the incident and under different 
grid conditions, delivered reactive power exceeding the 
TSO’s reference values.
In seeking to understand the discrepancies between the 
days, the Expert Panel reached out to the owners of two 
of the power plants. Due to time constraints, by the time 
the investigation was finalised, the Expert Panel was 
only able to request generator information for these two 
thermal power plants in the south, and not for any other 
plants in Spain.

According to the generator owner of one, the ­generator 
in question performs differently depending on the 
manual configuration, which includes changing the 
voltage setting at its terminal (i. e. the generator follows 
a different capability curve reflected in a different 
­function Q(U)). This change can be implemented 
­manually by the generator on its own initiative or after a 
suggestion by the TSO.
Based on information provided by owners for the 
assessed past day, RE sent the generator an advance 
instruction to increase reactive power absorption. 
However, it appears this instruction was not sent for 
this generator for 28 April. According to the owner, this 
explains why the provision of nominal reactive power 
was different (higher) in the past day compared to 
28 April.

of reactive power output of another conventional

trajectory that was slower than the faster changes in the 
TSO’s reactive power reference.50 After steep changes 
in the reference (driven by steep changes in voltage), 
the generator’s reactive power output began ramping 
towards the reference. However, given the ramp slope, 
reaching the new reactive power reference would have 
required a certain amount of time (several minutes). 
RE provided a record implying51 that the same thermal 
conventional generator did, on at least one other occa­

different grid conditions, provide a faster reactive power 
response than on 28 April. Conversely, the generator 
indicated that its response time on 28 April was similar to

4.1.2.4.4	
Findings
The Expert Panel found several potential unclarities 
and areas potentially requiring further specification 
in the applicable requirements for voltage control by 
conventional generators. These include the absence of 
an explicit requirement on response speed, the lack of 
reliable immediate reaction due to the 75 % hourly fulfil­
ment target, and the absence of economic consequences 
in case of underperformance. 
Furthermore, the actual reactive power output of several 
conventional power plants on the day reached the TSO’s 
expected reference according to the applicable require­
ments in the Operational Procedure PO 7.4 less than 75 % 
of the samples (hourly), and there was no close-to-real-
time monitoring of this divergence.
The combination of these factors resulted in the lack of 
effective voltage control support by the conventional 
generators. 
For the Expert Panel’s observations on the applicable 
requirements, please refer to Chapter 9.

4.1.2.6	
Loss of reactive power provision by disconnected elements
4.1.2.6.1	
Downstream networks
The Expert Panel found that the design of some down­
stream networks54 in Spain was not aligned with system 
needs, resulting, among other issues, in more chal­
lenging voltage control. In some cases, voltage control 
in these networks was insufficient due to a combination 
of factors, including generators operating in fixed power 
factor control mode, fast generation ramps, the physi­
cally slower changes of tap-changing transformers, and 
downstream element disconnection settings.
In particular, the Panel investigated a case in a substa­
tion in the south (400 kV TS 1 − Granada). The down­
stream network connected to the TSO grid at the 400 kV 
level. It is important to note that this network is neither 
transmission nor distribution: it is owned by the gener­
ators. A tap-changing transformer connected the 400 kV 
and 220 kV levels. Following a voltage rise across both 
sides of a tap-changing transformer (which remained 
at a given tap setting throughout the fast voltage rise), 
downstream system components disconnected due to 
overvoltage (the overvoltage disconnection setting at 
the disconnected element was 1.1 p.u., with no delay). At 
the time of disconnection, the voltage was not exceeded 
on the 400 kV side. This occurred because the tap posi­
tion, remaining unchanged during the voltage rise, 
resulted in a transmission ratio that produced a higher 
p.u. voltage value at the 220 kV side than at the 400 kV 
side. In this case, the tap position (despite the presence 
of an on-load automatic tap changer) worsened the 
situation, as it caused the voltage on the 220 kV side to 
be higher. 
The overvoltage trip led to the disconnection of all 
downstream generation, resulting in the loss of reactive 
power absorption from the disconnected units.55
The rise in voltage that led to the disconnection (partly 
due to fixed-power-factor generators changing 
setpoints) occurred faster than the physical or design 
constraints of tap-changing transformers, meaning that 
changing a single tap position could take longer. As a 
result, the combination of transformer tap changes and 
fixed-power-factor generators was insufficient to with­
stand fast voltage changes.
This points to the need for solutions regarding the 
design and coordination of the downstream networks. 
It appears that, due to the network design, the down­
stream network owner’s responsibility to ensure that 
generators remain connected while the voltage at the 
connection point is within limits was not fulfilled. 
Regarding protection coordination, it is worth noting 
that the protection setting (zero time delay at 1.1 p.u.) 
had not been reviewed by RE, since the coordination 
with transmission protection was not deemed necessary. 
(In contrast, such coordination is needed for protections 
that operate under short-circuit conditions, as these 
must be cleared by tripping the minimum number of 
elements.) In the original communication of structural 
information to RE, a 1-second delay for the activation of 
voltage protection was indicated. During the investiga­
tion of the incident, the Expert Panel received informa­
tion that the delay was actually zero seconds. However, 
RE indicated that this change had not been communi­
cated in advance.56

===== PAGE 214 =====
214  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
Regarding the operation of tap-changing transformers, 
the transformers between the transmission and distribu­
tion grids in Spain have been governed by an agreement 
between RE and DSOs since 2022. The agreement speci­
fies that taps are operated by distribution operators, and 
that the TSO may issue an order to block tap-changing 
transformers if voltages at certain reference points 
exceed set thresholds for 15 minutes. Since the voltage 
fluctuations on 28 April were faster than 15 minutes, and 
since the reference points only contained a subset of the 
nodes in the system, no order to block tap-changing 
transformers was issued.
Regarding protection settings in general, the investiga­
tion further revealed that under Spain’s national network 
codes, the upper limit of the allowed voltage operating 
range (435 kV) was reaching the threshold at which 
some pre-NC RfG generators were able to immediately 
disconnect (435 kV). This means that no margin existed. 
The margin could be restored by either reducing the 
allowed operating range or by raising the disconnection 
requirements for pre-RfG generators. For post-RfG gener­
ators in Spain, the threshold was 440 kV and the margin 
was 5 kV. The margin could be increased by reducing the 
allowed operating range.
The Expert Panel issued a related recommendation in 
Chapter 9.
4.1.2.6.2	
The HVDC
The behaviour of the 2 × 1000 MW VSC-type HVDC 
between Spain and France is discussed in Chapters 2 and 
3 of the report. 
The HVDC’s reactive power contribution is described in 
Chapter 2.7. Following the blackout in Iberia, the HVDC 
system between Spain and France disconnected and 
active power transfer was lost. At the same time, the VSC 
HVDC had also been providing voltage control at both 
converter stations independently. 
However, together with the loss of the DC connection, 
reactive power support (voltage control) was lost at both 
ends (including in the station at the French side, where 
the grid otherwise remained in operation). 
The Expert Panel issued a related recommendation in 
Chapter 9.

As discussed in this section, the operation of shunt 
reactors in Spain was manual. Given the large number 
of installed shunt reactors (around 90 across Spain), a 
fast utilisation of these assets using manual decisions is 
prohibitively difficult. Achieving a more effective utilisa­
tion of available shunt reactors to address system voltage 
needs (e. g. quickly connecting the most relevant58 assets 
when necessary) would thus require either automatic or 
semi-automatic systems.
During the investigation, the French TSO RTE indicated 
that in France, automatic utilisation of shunt reactors 
(and capacitors) is implemented for a large share of their 
reactors (around 50 % of the assets). These shunt reactors 
and capacitors can be operated either:
»	by manual remote control, or
»	automatically, whereby the assets connect/
disconnect automatically at preset voltage 
thresholds (at or close to the normal voltage 
limits), based on a local voltage measurement 
and with a response time of 5 – 10 seconds.
While not implying that this is a universal solution, RTE 
further explained that in its implementation, there are 
two operating modes on the automated assets: a regu­
lation mode and a safety mode. The regulation mode 
is activated from the control centre, while the safety 
mode is always active and cannot be deactivated. More 
specifically:
»	In regulation mode, the shunt reactor’s activa­
tion thresholds are within the normal voltage 
range, which for RTE is 200 – 245 kV (e. g., a 
shunt reactor would connect at 244 kV).
»	In safety mode, a shunt reactor would connect 
when the voltage is outside the normal range 
(e. g., a shunt reactor would connect at 248 kV). 
Furthermore, the settings are adapted to each case after 
dynamic studies. When there are several assets in the 
same electrical substation or nearby, the settings must 
prevent simultaneous switching on/off.
58

before disconnection was 434 kV. The analysis (subject to limits and caveats) indicated a voltage decrease of around 3 – 4 kV for each shunt reactor connected.

With regard to reactive power contribution by synchro­
nous conventional generators and RES generators, the 
Expert Panel observed that different approaches were 
implemented in other control areas. In Portugal,62 
synchronous generators by default receive a voltage or 
reactive power setpoint by phone directly from the TSO, 
and are required to deliver reactive power in accord­
ance with the setpoint, within restrictions defined by a 
P-Q area and a power factor range. Hydro power plants 
provide the service not only in generation mode but also 
in pumping/synchronous power mode. One hydro power 
plant is specifically contracted to provide voltage control 
even when not producing active power – it functions as 
a synchronous compensator, and the service uses a reac­
tive power setpoint. RES generators in Portugal (solar 
power plants with installed capacity above 1 MW, as well 
as newer wind power plants) receive real-time setpoints 
from the TSO’s SCADA, most commonly a voltage setpoint. 
Notably, solar PV generators provide voltage control 
service both during the day and at night (i. e. even in the 
absence of the primary energy source).
The relevance of providing comprehensive European 
cross-border guidance on voltage control practices is 
discussed in a recommendation in Chapter 9. 
62	
See Section 2.6.5.2.
Regarding the reactive power potential of invert­
er-based RES, the figures above assume operation 
within the constraints of a fixed-power-factor control 
mode. If a different voltage control mode is imple­
mented, a higher potential might be achieved, as the 
reactive power output would not be directly linked to 
the instantaneous active power output but rather to the 
capabilities of the inverter. Such technical decisions also 
enable further implementation options, such as e. g. the 
night use of solar PV for voltage control and/or the possi­
bility of inverter-based assets operating as STATCOMs, as 
described in a recommendation in Chapter 9.
Area of attention: The Expert Panel suggests assessing 
reactive power flows between the distribution and 
transmission grids, while also considering the control 
and design of the relevant tap-changing transformers.
Area of attention: The Expert Panel suggests that distri­
bution operators consider the most appropriate voltage 
control mode from distribution-connected generators. 
The relevance of this suggestion depends on local 
specifics and is relevant insofar as enabled by the appli­
cable requirements.

4.1.3.1	
Operational limits and disconnection thresholds
63	
While the allowed range was 435 kV, RE indicated that the preferred operation was below 420 kV.
64	
Resolution of 30 July 1998, of the Secretary of State for Energy and Mineral Resources, which approves a set of technical and instrumental procedures necessary 
to carry out the adequate technical management of the electrical system.

For example, at 12:33:11, one of the zero-to-phase voltages was around 5 kV higher than the positive sequence voltage (435 kV in Phase B-to-ground, 
vs 430 kV in positive sequence). At 12:33:11, the voltage measurement in PMU ARN4ALD (close to the node where disconnections occurred 5 seconds later) 
reached 430 kV in positive sequence voltage. However, at this time, one of the zero-to-phase voltages (Phase B) was already at 435 kV, as voltages in Phase B 
were notably higher than in the other two phases. The asymmetry was present throughout 12:00 – 12:33 (differences between two phases up to 9 kV).
The range of voltages expected in a power grid (the 
operating voltage range) generally considers the voltage 
withstand capabilities of system users and includes 
appropriate safety margins. 
As described in Section 3.2.1.1, the requirements appli­
cable in Spain enabled the generators connected to the 
400 kV network in Spain to disconnect when the voltage 
exceeded 435 kV (older connection dates) or 440 kV 
(newer connection dates).
On the day of the incident, the allowed upper limit of 
the operating voltage range in Spain was 435 kV.63 This 
meant that the safety margin between the allowed 
voltage operating range and the voltages at which 
generators could disconnect was low or non-existent.
The Spanish Operational Procedure P.O. 1.4 (1998)64 
and the exceptions introduced in European regulations 
specifically for Spain enabled the possibility for the 
Spanish TSO to operate the transmission grid at 435 kV 
(this is described in Section 2.6.1). In other EU Member 
States, the allowed operating range is up to 420 kV.
The Expert Panel identified the limited safety margin as a 
contributing factor to the incident. A related recommen­
dation is included in Chapter 9.
4.1.3.2	
Alarm handling
Detailed information on alarm handling at all levels of 
the system is included in Section 4.5.
The overvoltage alarm thresholds at 400 kV nodes in 
Spain were, depending on the node, at thresholds of 
420 kV, 430 kV, or 435 kV. For RE, voltage-related (curative 
or close-to-real-time preventive) remedial actions were 
not defined in an operator handbook.65 RE indicated that 
the actions are nevertheless known by all operators due 
to continuous training programs.
There are alarm thresholds defined for 220 kV nodes (at 
values of 240, 235, and 246 kV). However, for global 
monitoring of the system, only 400 kV pilot nodes are 
used (i. e. these actually generate specific voltage 
alarms). 
Between 12:00 and 12:30, 1,026 alarms below the 
low-voltage alarm thresholds (375 – 395 kV), 78 of which 
were not in RE’s transmission network, and 137 alarms 
above the high-voltage alarm thresholds (420 – 435 kV), 
eight of which were not in RE’s transmission network, 
were triggered in RE SCADA, in part due to voltage 
oscillations.
During the voltage rise between 12:25 and 12:29, 24 
430 kV alarms were triggered and five shunt reactors 
were connected, after which the voltage was mostly 
below 420 kV by 12:30.
After the 12:30 mark, the first 430 kV alarm was triggered 
at 12:33:01. This was only 15 seconds before the second 
disconnection (Event 4 in Table 3.1) and the overvoltage 
cascade, meaning that manual remedial actions such as 
disconnecting lines or connecting shunt reactors were 
not possible. 
There was one 435 kV alarm at 12:27:46. No other 435 kV 
alarm was triggered before the blackout. 
The SCADA alarm system usually does not distinguish 
voltage values in the three phases and therefore 
provided no input to operators regarding the voltage 
values of individual phases.66

===== PAGE 220 =====
220  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
4.1.3.3	
Managing reactive power capabilities to cope with expected reactive 
power fluctuations 
67	
Power system stabilisers in Spain have been declared and adjusted in cooperation with Red Eléctrica in most combined cycle units, in one nuclear power unit, 
and in a hydro-power plant in the Galician region.
A combination of factors affecting the voltage control 
capabilities of the power system occurred simultane­
ously on 28 April.
As discussed in Section 4.1.2.1, shunt reactors in Spain 
were operated manually, meaning that there was a 
decision-making lead time before they could be (re-)
connected. 
As discussed in Section 4.1.2.3, the RES generators 
followed a fixed-power-factor control mode and thus 
were unable to respond to voltage fluctuations.
As discussed in Section 4.1.2.4, the synchronous conven­
tional power plants were following the default Oper­
ational Procedure PO 7.4 framework, while one plant 
voluntarily (temporarily) took part in a direct voltage 
control set-point pilot project. 
At 12:30, the following conventional power plants were 
connected in the southwestern (Andalusia, Castilla-La 
Mancha, Extremadura) part of Spain:
»	One nuclear power unit with a total installed 
capacity of around 1,000 MW 
»	Two combined-cycle power units with a total 
installed capacity of around 800 MW
»	One hydro unit with a total installed capacity 
of around 70 MW
The rest of the generation mix in this region was 
inverter-based. 
After the incident, RE noted that some conventional 
power plants falling under the Operational Procedure 
PO 7.4 framework did not perform as expected. As per 
the design of the Operational Procedure PO 7.4 regime 
(generators follow Operational Procedure PO 7.4 voltage 
references), no real-time setpoint was sent directly to the 
generators. Hence, RE was unable to instruct conven­
tional generators to change their reactive power behav­
iour in real time. RE can instruct a change to the voltage 
reference in real time via a telephone call. One such call 
did take place on 28 April (for a unit outside the south­
west-centre region). 
On the other hand, for one generator investigated in 
more detail by the Expert Panel, the generator indicated 
that on the assessed past day, when its reactive power 
absorption was higher, it had received advanced instruc­
tions from RE to increase reactive power absorption. 
However, no such instruction was sent to this generator 
on 28 April.
Due to the oscillatory incidents in the power system 
(oscillations), the system operator dispatched an addi­
tional conventional unit in Andalucia in real time to 
increase the combined cycle generation equipped with 
power system stabilisers, aiming to increase damping of 
additional oscillations that could have appeared after 
these two oscillatory incidents. Although the connection 
order was issued at 12:26, the start-up time of the unit 
(and for combined-cycled units67 in general, ranging 
from 2 to 8 hours depending on the shutdown time) did 
not allow sufficient time to connect to the system, as the 
incident occurred before the start-up.
As discussed in Section 4.1.2.1, only one STATCOM was 
in operation in Spain that day, while another was 
performing its test before commissioning.
An additional factor regarding the voltage control 
management, as mentioned in Section 4.1.2.6.1, was 
that some renewable generation disconnections in Spain 
occurred faster than expected (while the voltage at the 
connection point was inside the limit). As these plants 
operated with a fixed power factor absorbing reactive 
power, these disconnections added to the increase in 
the power system voltage. Another factor involving 
voltage control management was that a certain amount 
of domestic PV disconnected after each oscillation 
and reconnected a few minutes later, causing some 
impact on voltages. This is discussed in more details in 
chapter 4.3.
The combination of these factors meant that the system’s 
reactive power capabilities on the day were unable to 
absorb the voltage rise after 12:32.
The Expert Panel issued a relevant recommendation in 
Chapter 9.

4.1.4.1.1	
Morning (09:00 – 12:00)
Voltages were fluctuating on the morning of 28 April. At

4.1.4.1.2	
Half-hour after 12:00
In the period 12:00:00 – 12:25:00, voltages oscillated 
with amplitudes of up to 30 kV peak-to-peak (at the 
400 kV level), during two notable periods of oscillation. 
No voltage values were outside the allowed range. 
From 12:00 to 12:20, six lines were connected to damp 
oscillations.
In the period 12:20:00 – 12:25:00, during one of the 
oscillation episodes, three shunt reactors (a total of 
400 MVAr) were disconnected due to low voltage swings. 
In addition, four 400 kV overhead lines in Spain, which 
were open for voltage control, were connected to 
increase damping and reduce the oscillations, according 
to the bilateral “oscillation and low damping” mitigation 
protocol.
In the period 12:25 – 12:29, after the second oscilla­
tion, a rise in voltage occurred, and five shunt reactors 
(total 700 MVAr) were connected, two of which were in 
­Andalucia. No voltage out of range was reached.

At 12:30, there was a 0.4 – 0.5 GW change in generation 
schedules expected, reflected in a scheduled reduction 
of export from Spain to Portugal of around 0.4 – 0.5 GW.69

As described in Section 4.1.2.3, RES units in Spain 
followed a fixed power factor. Therefore, each change of 
active power setpoint meant a change in reactive power 
injection, either proportionally (capacitive power factor) 
or negatively proportionally (inductive power factor).71 
As most RES units followed an inductive power factor, 
downwards changes in active power injection meant an 
decrease in their reactive power absorption.

generators also changed patterns of flows within the 
bidding zone, and hence additionally affected reactive 
power conditions through a changed loading of various 
transmission lines.

4.1.4.1.3.5	 After event “B”
78	
A lesson from the event was that a longer overlap is needed, meaning that the ramping time of conventional units should be taken into account, so that 
connecting these resources is considered earlier in operational planning.
The voltage control section did not investigate the 
voltage conditions after Event B (in the 2.5 seconds from 
Event B until 12:32:19, 12 further overvoltage discon­
nections occurred). The details of the disconnections are 
described in the Disconnections section 3.2.1.3.
A cascade of overvoltage disconnections led to frequency 
phenomena described in other chapters and, eventually, 
a blackout occurred.
4.1.4.2	
Voltage control in the days preceding 28 April
To better understand the circumstances of the inci­
dent, particularly the presence and impact of some of 
the factors related to the event on 28 April, the Expert 
Panel also assessed voltage fluctuations that occurred 
on certain previous days. In particular, the Expert Panel 
assessed 22 April, when an overvoltage event occurred, 
alongside changes in generation schedules, cross-border 
flows, and the connection of conventional power plants 
and shunt reactors. However, different circumstances 
meant that an incident of the same scale did not occur 
and no ICS investigation took place.
On 22 April, overvoltage disconnections of some gener­
ation and demand facilities occurred in Spain. At 19:00, 
the commercial net position of Spain decreased by 
1.6 GW, reflecting changes in generation schedules and 
also manifesting as changes in cross-border flows. There 
was a co-occurrence of a decrease in solar power (due 
to the sun going down) and conventional power plants 
connecting. 
At around 18:58, concurrent with the change in sched­
ules, voltages started rising in some nodes of the grid. 
The voltages rose for around 3 minutes, until 440 kV was 
reached in Phase B at PMU ARN4ALD at 19:01:30. After 
that, in some seconds, voltages rose above 450 kV and 
continued climbing for around half a minute. At the peak 
(19:02:27), a value of 452 kV (up to 455 kV in Phase B) 
was registered in PMU ARN4ALD. Around 3 minutes after 
19:00, the conventional power plants reached tech­
nical minimum power and became able to control the 
voltage.78 By 19:05, the situation was remedied, as RE 
connected 22 shunt reactors. 
It is worth noting that on 22 April, no significant oscilla­
tion and no low-voltage situation was observed before 
the voltage rise (as it was on 28 April).
Figure 4-14 shows the positive symmetrical component 
voltages in a set of PMUs.

4.2	
Oscillations
4.2.1	
Scope of the Chapter 
This chapter aims to analyse in detail, using various 
methodologies and data sources, the oscillatory 
phenomena that occurred from around 12:00 until the 
cascading events that led to the blackout. Summarising 
the main physical concepts allows us to understand, to 
the greatest extent possible, oscillatory phenomena. 
Oscillatory phenomena were also observed in the system 
on 28 April before 12:00, as well as on other days in April 
2025, but with a very low amplitude that did not pose 
a significant risk to the system. This section, however, 
focuses on 12:00 – 12:30, when two very prominent 
oscillation episodes occurred.
Setting aside the rigorous scientific definition already 
reported in Chapter 2, we will focus on the physics of the 
oscillations observed, which involved both phenomena 
particularly active in a specific area of the Iberian grid, 
yet involving a vast geographical area, as well as inter-
area oscillations involving the entire Continental Europe 
(CE) grid.
There is a common denominator in all oscillatory 
phenomena, which allows us to classify the scenario 
as more prone to triggering an oscillation; however, it 
does not guarantee their occurrence, as oscillations can 
arise from mechanisms associated with chaotic system 
behaviour.
The following factors can contribute to potential 
oscillations:
»	Generator reactance relative to the electrical 
system to which they are connected: This 
can be compared to the “electrical distance” 
from the system. If particularly high, it causes 
generators to operate at suboptimal points for 
controlling oscillations. Reactance depends on 
the short-circuit power at the connection point, 
which is influenced by network topology (e. g. it 
increases when more transmission lines are out 
of service, or when the ratio of conventional 
rotating generators delivering short-circuit 
power to static generators is low).
»	The transmission angle between the genera­
tors and the grid, which is influenced by system 
topology
»	Operating points (when a large area is under 
export conditions, the angle spreads) and 
voltage profiles (which induce under-­excitation 
operation of generators)
»	The presence of static and dynamic compen­
sation elements (e. g. reactors, STATCOMs, 
condensers)
»	Dynamic stabilisation features and their tuning 
(power system stabilisers on rotating machines, 
HVDC POD, STATCOM POD, static generators POD)
»	Eventual IBR converter-driven instability
We will analyse the dynamics of the oscillations in detail, 
assessing their extent and identifying the most active 
areas, and confirming the hypotheses and findings 
through root-mean-square (RMS) simulations, short-­
circuit power evaluation, and small-signal analysis. 
These results will inform actions and recommendations 
aimed at mitigating the occurrence of such phenomena 
in the future.

===== PAGE 232 =====
232  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
4.2.2	
Construction of Analytical Framework for Oscillatory Analysis
30	
The procedure for constructing the analytical framework for oscillatory analysis begins with a consistent snapshot, appropriately adapted to represent the grid 
configuration at the time of the oscillation.
To emulate the inter-area and 0.63 Hz phenomena, 
the full Continental Europe Synchronous Area (CE SA) 
transmission system was considered. A detailed model 
of the Spanish peninsular electric system (SPES) was 
used, based on a state estimator static case and supple­
mented with dynamic models of system generation, 
HVDC, and FACTS. For the inter-area oscillation study, data 
from 12:21 were used to represent SPES operating and 
topology conditions during the event, while the scenario 
at 12:0830 was employed to reproduce SPES operating 
conditions during the 0.63 Hz oscillation. The rest of 
the CE system was modelled with the “Dynamic model 
of continental Europe v2”. As this model represents a 
different time horizon and operating point than 28 April 
2025, it was adjusted to mimic the operating conditions 
(generation, load, system topology, etc.) at the time of 
interest. This adjustment was performed [7] using the 
data available at 12:00 in the ENTSO-E Transparency Plat­
form, which provides 1-hour resolution data. This hour 
was selected to reflect operating conditions immediately 
prior to the oscillations.
This model can represent the system’s oscillatory behav­
iour in terms of electromechanical modes, but the base 
damping must be properly adjusted. This was achieved 
by modifying variables outside the Spain and Portugal 
portions of the system, with the French and remaining CE 
SA regions calibrated to reproduce the system’s damping 
values at the two studied time stamps on 28 April 2025. 
The analyses in this chapter use two complementary 
methodologies: eigenvalue analysis, which operates in 
the frequency domain, and RMS simulation, which oper­
ates in the phasor domain. Eigenvalue analysis provides 
information on the existing electromechanical modes 
in the system and enables the extraction of quantitative 
information regarding the effect of different actions 
undertaken by Red Eléctrica to mitigate the oscillations. 
RMS simulation provides qualitative and illustrative 
information and helps analyse the 0.63 Hz oscillation, 
which does not appear in the model, supporting the 
hypothesis that this oscillation was not a natural mode 
of the system but rather the result of forced or induced 
generator behaviour.

===== PAGE 233 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  233 
4.2.3	
Validation of the Analytical Model
Once the electromechanical model of the network was created, a validation was performed to verify its adequacy in 
representing oscillatory phenomena.
4.2.3.1	
0.2 Hz Inter-Area Oscillation
Regarding the East–Centre–West inter-area oscillation, 
the validation process considered two different tests:
»	Stimulating the system with a perturbation 
(a “step” of imbalance between load and 
production)
»	Injecting stochastic noise on the loads to repro­
duce the natural ambient oscillation
The contingency involves simulating the loss of a large 
load in the CE power system, which triggers the inter-
area oscillation. It is relevant to mention that such event 
did not occur during the 28 April 2025 incident. However 
this report assumes a significant power deviation, such 
as a large load disconnection, to generate an RMS simu­
lation with appreciable inter-area oscillations.
With reference to the ambient oscillation mentioned 
before, a stochastic process associated with several 
loads – specifically, an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process – 
was used to begin fluctuations. In the literature, the OU 
process is used to emulate typical frequency variations 
under normal operating conditions [8]. It is characterised 
by a mean value, a standard deviation, and an autocor­
relation value. Typical standard deviations are around 
0.5 – 2 %, whereas the autocorrelation typically ranges 
between 0.01 Hz and 1 Hz, depending on the size of the 
network and the penetration of non-programmable 
generation [9]. In this case study, for implementation 
reasons, the process was applied to a small number 
of loads; thus, to trigger the inter-area oscillation, the 
standard deviation of the OU process associated with 
these loads was increased to 30 %. In future studies, a 
process with a more realistic standard deviation value 
(0.5 – 2 %) might be applied to all pertinent system 
loads to verify whether, under small damp conditions, 
the inter-area oscillations can be triggered without any 
contingency. The autocorrelation value used in this work 
is 0.1 Hz, which aligns with other studies.
The OU process is associated with some relevant loads (in 
terms of active power consumption) in several countries. 
Some are at the edges of the CE SA transmission system, 
such as Spain and Turkey, and others are in the central 
part of the system. In this manner, the inter-area oscilla­
tion is triggered quite naturally. 
All the loads in the SPES and the CE SA transmission 
system are assumed to follow an IZ model, with active 
power exhibiting the dynamic behaviour of a constant 
current model and reactive power following a constant 
impedance model. This is a common choice for transient 
stability analysis, as it captures the main characteristics of 
the average load dynamics while keeping computations 
simple due to the constant Z component [10].
The modal analysis of the CE model at 12.21 naturally 
provides information about the electromechanical 
modes of the system, including the East–Centre–West 
mode. The damping ratio of this mode, after adjusting 
the study model, is 0.28 %. This value is consistent with 
the initiation of an oscillation at that time. This case, 
which will be referred to as “A ₀”, represents the scenario 
at 12:21 pm, when the 0.2 Hz inter-area oscillation 
was observed. This case will be used as a reference 
throughout this document.

Figure 4-17 shows the inter-area oscillations obtained 
with the simulation model. Similar to the results reported 
in Figure 2-63 of [11], the frequencies in the Spanish 
system (Carmona, Vic, and Xove) show the most oscilla­

trigger inter-area oscillation. This process also excites 
other inter-area modes with higher frequency, as it 
occurs in real power systems. However, the general 
East–Centre–West mode is maintained, with the SPES 
frequency lagging central Europe by approximately 180º 
and Turkey by approximately 40 – 60º.
Thus, introducing the OU process enables the realistic 
reproduction of inter-area oscillations, supporting the 
idea that inter-area oscillations can occur even without 
a major incident.
Overall, the RMS simulations – both simulating a contin­
gency and incorporating an OU stochastic process – yield 
consistent results and can successfully capture the 
system’s oscillatory behaviour when the 0.2 Hz oscilla­
tion occurred.

4.2.3.2	
0.63 Hz Oscillation
This section outlines the assumptions used to reproduce 
the 0.63 Hz oscillations. Since this oscillation differs from 
an inter-area oscillation, validation focused on the HV 
active node during the oscillation, where an artificial 
signal was injected to observe system behaviour. The 
explanation and classification of the oscillation will 
be discussed in more detail, along with the techniques 
used to find the “most active” node, where the so-called 
“plant A” is located. The simulation is designed to verify 
that by injecting a forcing signal in the bay of plant A, it is 
possible to reproduce general system behaviour compa­
rable to the actual recordings.
As high-resolution data for the active and reactive 
power injected into the node under observation was 
unavailable, the adopted strategy was to reconstruct the 
injected signal using a PMU located in a nearby substa­
tion to capture the oscillatory trend, combined with 
SCADA data to obtain the average values of the active and 
reactive power injected by the plant.
Figure 4-19:  Synthetic signal used to trigger the 0.63 Hz oscillations (from 12:03.00 to 12:08:20).
The network model was adjusted to resemble the 
operating conditions during the 0.63 Hz oscillations, 
focusing on the connected lines, the control mode of 
the VSC–HVDC INELFE-1 when the oscillations occurred 
(angle difference control, ADC), and the active power 
interchange between Spain and France (≈1,350 MW).
Regarding the CE SA system, since the event occurred 
between 12:03 and 12:08, the closest available data 
from the Transparency Platform is at 12:00, which was 
therefore used for analysis.

4.2.4	
Analysis of Plausible Causes
4.2.4.1	
First Oscillation
The first oscillation at 0.63 Hz requires correct classifica­
tion. An analysis strategy was adopted to reach a logical 
and plausible conclusion. No high-resolution (with a 
sampling rate higher than 1 s) recordings were provided 
from the distribution grid level or main production sites. 
However, the extensive monitoring network of Red 
Eléctrica based on PMUs, along with the contribution of 
several locations across CE, enabled a detailed analysis 
of the oscillation. 
The following steps were investigated in detail to 
confirm the hypothesis of a “non-natural” 0.63 Hz oscil­
latory frequency. 
»	1.  Analyse all PMUs available measurands 
during the event and in the past (selected 
PMUs and selected time frames)
»	2.  Process historical data provided by Red 
Eléctrica’s modal analysis tool
»	3.  Examine any specific past event
»	4.  Check with the electromechanical model 
»	5.  Run an additional check with a different 
methodology using SCADA measurements
»	6.  Ask the more active power plants for any 
significant information
Following these steps, it is expected that the most plau­
sible explanation for the first oscillation will be identi­
fied. The topology of the grid before the first oscillation 
is depicted in the figure below.
Figure 4-25:  Grid topology before the first oscillation (in white the lines in open status)
4.2.4.1.1	
Analysis of Available Measurands
A complete set of CE PMU data was collected, comprising 
128 voltage and frequency measurands with a 100 ms 
sampling rate. 
The modal analysis was conducted using the Unscented 
Kalman Filter (UKF) algorithm, which is particularly effec­
tive for analysing nonlinear systems.
The algorithm calculates, for each time sample, the 
dominant modes, amplitudes, and damping ratios for 
the analysed measurand set. It can also display the mode 
shapes, showing the relative activity of each state vari­
able for a selected mode. The amplitude (normalised) 
provides the contribution of each single state variable to 
the mode, while the angle indicates the phase displace­
ment of each state variable active in the mode. Plotting 
these phase displacements on a geographical chart 
makes it possible to determine whether a location oscil­
lates in phase or in opposition to others.

===== PAGE 241 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  241 
Figure 4-26 shows the raw measurand analysed 
(frequencies), the modal dominant modes (Mode 1: 
0.63 Hz and Mode 2: 0.2 Hz), the mode amplitude, and 
the damping ratios. The figure clearly illustrates the 
dominance of Mode 1. Figure 4-27 shows the mode 
shapes of the two identified modes. The 0.2 Hz mode 
exhibits the well-known displacement where the Iberian 
grid and Turkey oscillate against central Europe, while 
the 0.63 Hz mode is primarily confined to the Iberian 
Peninsula, with only a very small amplitude in the CE 
system.

of rated value) again reveals the clear presence of the 
mode in the Iberian Peninsula.
The 0.2 Hz mode shape clearly shows the classical inter-

(180°) against central Europe. The 0.63 Hz mode is char­

»	A wide geographical analysis confirms that the

»	The mode shape does not follow the typical

shows pronounced activity in a specific area of

4.2.4.1.1.1	 Analysis of Historical Data
Once the specific local characteristics of the 0.63 Hz 
have been clarified, the next step is to examine a longer 
period to identify any evidence of a dominant mode that 
may normally be present.
To verify whether the 0.63 Hz mode is naturally present in 
the system, the results of the modal analysis of frequency 
between January and April 2025 were examined at 
different substations in the Spanish peninsular power 
system: Xove (northwest), La Cereal (centre), Cofrentes 
(east), and Carmona (south).
The algorithm used for the modal calculation processes 
20‑minute windows, and the analysis window is shifted 
every 20 s. Therefore, every 20 s it provides results based 
on the ambient modal analysis of the preceding 20 
minutes. 
The algorithm used for the modal calculation processes 
20‑minute windows, and the analysis window is shifted 
every 20 s. Therefore, every 20 s it provides results based 
on the ambient modal analysis of the preceding 20 
minutes. The algorithm is capable of detecting oscilla­
tion modes with frequencies between 0.04 and 4 Hz. 
The number of occurrences represents the number of 
those 20‑minute windows in which the mode is present 
(considering for each 20 minutes time frame all the 
modes that are present over a predefinied threshold 
2 mHz). The following figure shows the number of 
detected oscillations for each frequency range at those 
substations. All detected occurrences are shown, regard­

Since the algorithm relies on ambient measurements, 
the oscillation amplitude does not need to be large, nor 
does the damping need to be low, for the mode to be 
detected and characterised, making it well-suited for 
characterising the modes present in the system.

has been reduced to one-quarter of that in the previous 
figure to better highlight the number of occurrences.
Figure 4-30:  Number of occurrences of modes between 0.01 and 1.5 Hz with damping lower than 5 % detected between January and April 2025.
Analysis of the two previous figures indicates that the 
0.63 Hz oscillation mode is not naturally present (or, in 
other words, its low occurrence confirms the absence of 
a clear “dominance“) in the system. The inter-area East–
Centre–West oscillation mode, with a frequency around 
0.2 Hz, can be clearly observed, as well as another 
inter-area mode around 0.5 Hz, which corresponds to 
an oscillation mode between Morocco and the Iberian 
Peninsula. Additional local modes can then be observed 
between 0.8 Hz and 1.1 Hz.
In the 0.60 – 0.65 Hz interval, this modal analysis, 
performed using the frequency measurement from 
Carmona, found 48 occurrences between 10:00 and 
11:00 on 28 April 2025 (out of 180 possible), 140 occur­
rences between 11:00 and 12:00 (out of 180 possible), 
and 101 occurrences between 12:00 and 13:00 (out of 
101 possible), since from 12:33:33 on 28 April there are 
no data available to perform modal analysis.
An additional analysis was conducted using a different 
algorithm, Fast Stochastic Subspace Identification (FSSI), 
on data from four PMUs recorded in April 2025 before the 
incident.
