4.2.4.1.1.2	 Analysis of Event Data
There are several methods for locating the source of an 
oscillation based on measurement data. With the avail­
able data, no method can provide by itself definitive 
proof of the source. Therefore, multiple methods were 
applied in this analysis to check for coherent results. For 
the sake of brevity, these methods are not described 
here; the reader is referred to the bibliography for 
further details.
Dissipative Energy Flow Method
The dissipative energy flow (DEF) method [12] was applied to the Red Eléctrica PMU data between 12:00 and 12:15 
for the 0.63 Hz frequency.
Figure 4-36:  DEF against time.
DEF values are indicated in brackets in the legend. T = 0 corresponds to time = 12:00.

===== PAGE 247 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  247 
DEF values are plotted on the map in Figure 4-37.
Figure 4-37:  DEF calculated on Red Eléctrica PMUs.
The width of the black arrows is proportional to the 
computed DEF. Only |DEF| > 0.1 are shown. When PMUs 
are too close, the DEF are added: For example, the DEF 
on the east of the border between France and Spain is 
the sum of the DEFs from the 400 kV AC Baixax–Vic PMU 
and the PMUs from the HVDC between Spain and France. 
We can observe that the Iberian Peninsula as a whole is 
exporting oscillation energy to France (DEF: 2.39) and 
Morocco (DEF: 1.16). 
Focusing more closely, another area (DEF: 0.5) – circled in 
red on the map – is also exporting oscillation energy and 
could be the location of the oscillation source. Since this 
area is not fully covered by PMUs, it is difficult to compare 
the DEF of the likely source with the DEF exported from 
the Iberian Peninsula. However, it remains possible that 
the source in this area interacted with other sources in 
the Iberian Peninsula summing up with interaction with 
all generators a final total exported energy.

Presence of Harmonics
The presence of harmonics of the fundamental oscilla­
tion frequency (0.63 Hz) can be used to locate the source 
of forced oscillations [13]. As these harmonics propagate 
less far from the source, the PMU where they are highest 
is likely the closest to the source.
The FSSI [14] method was applied to the Red Eléctrica 
PMU data on active and reactive power between 12:00 
and 12:15 to analyse the modes and search harmonics. 
Figure 4-38:  Frequency of modes on P signal (Hz).
Figure 4-39:  Frequency of modes on Q signal (Hz).

P and Q measurements. However, the energy of these 
harmonics is quite low. Table 4-5 provides the ratio of 
the maximum energy of each harmonic to the maximum

SCADA Data Generation Analysis
31	
GitHub – rte-france/oscillation-analysis-with-scada-data: Python implementation of a method to locate the source of forced oscillations in a power system.
Another way to locate the source of forced oscillations 
is to use SCADA data. Several methods exist, but for this 
work, “SCADA-Based Detection and Analysis of Oscilla­
tions with Inferential Statistics” [15] was employed, for 
which open-source code is available.31 
The method was developed by the IEEE Forced Oscilla­
tion Task Force and is commonly used to identify a” more 
active generator. While this generator is not necessarily 
the main source of the oscillation, it is the most active 
plant identified during the oscillation.
The analysis was performed on all P and Q SCADA data 
from generators above 50 MW (144 in total). The plots 
below illustrate the measurands considered as probable 
sources of oscillations. The plots on the left show the 
raw data from measurements, while the plots on the 
right represent the data after a detrending stage. The 
detrending stage aims to remove long-term trends, such 
as the ramping up of a generator, which can obscure the 
detection of faster oscillations. The detrending method 
used here is the differencing method: the detrended 
value for sample n is calculated by subtracting the raw 
value of sample n-1 from the raw value of sample n.
Figure 4-42:  Source location software output.
 

===== PAGE 251 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  251 
In the first iteration, the tool identifies the generator 
located in the Coruna province – a combined cycled gas 
turbine (CCGT) in northern Spain – as the most active. 
However, this disappears in the next iteration. It is worth 
noting that, by design, the algorithm converges in several 
iterations. In this case, it detects a high energy value in 
the first iteration, which is subsequently surpassed by 
another node. This is confirmed by analysing the group 
recordings, where some energy is indeed detected 
during the oscillation, but with a lower amplitude than 
the node identified at the end of the procedure.
The amplitude of the active power is negligible but indi­
cates that the local oscillation in the Badajoz province 
triggers a “response” in the opposite side of the system.
The observed generator in Badajoz is the same as the 
one identified in Subsection 2.5.6.3 (Figure 2.59). An 
examination of the correlation between oscillations and 
the reactive power exchange reveals a clear correlation 
of reactive power at 0.63 Hz.
Figure 4-43:  Correlation between oscillations (FFT on sliding window) and reactive power (SCADA measurement 4 s).
Conclusion from Measurement Analysis
The DEF method, harmonic analysis (at least for 
the P signal), and SCADA data all point to consistent 
localisations.
The output of the specific analysis algorithms aimed at 
identifying a possible source of the oscillation converged 
on the same substation mentioned in Chapter 2.
4.2.4.1.2	
Summary of Causes and Possible Improvements
All the analyses carried out in this chapter confirm the 
plausible classification of the 0.63 Hz forced oscil­
lation within the family of converter-driven stability 
phenomena.
The oscillation has the maximum observability near a 
generator in the Badajoz province, as noted in Chapter 2. 
Based on the analysed historical data and simulations, 
no natural dominant mode is observed at this frequency. 
The analysis of the measurands (PMU and SCADA) using 
the oscillation source location method points to the 
same area.
In addition, the simulations were able to replicate the 
oscillatory effect.
On the one hand, according to the information provided 
to EP, no alarms or anomalies related to the oscillatory 
behaviour were found in the plant controller event 
list. In addition, the plant was classified as an “existing 
generator” under the RfG code. In contrast, the other 
generator connected to the same node, which exhibited 
a lower response to the oscillation, was commissioned in 
2021, meaning that the RfG provisions apply.
Instability phenomena in inverters due to the system 
reactance seen by the generator are well known [16] 
[17] [18] [19], and real events have also confirmed that 
old inverters can experience instability issues, especially 
when running at intermediate power levels. It was also 
observed that during the period 12:03 – 12:15:12, the 
inverter was not operating at maximum power, as the 
available RES energy was higher and the inverter was 
therefore limiting its electrical output. 

===== PAGE 252 =====
252  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
When the inverter increased its P setpoint at 12:16, its 
oscillatory behaviour became less pronounced. More­
over, given the large size of the generator, it can have a 
relevant impact on grid dynamics.
After collecting and evaluating all these elements, the 
most plausible conclusion is to classify this oscillation as 
forced/converter driven: the plant interacted with the 
other generators in the area, dominating the oscillation. 
Finally, the fact that a single generator was the most 
active during the oscillation at 0.63 Hz suggests that 
a converter-driven phenomenon plausibly induced a 
forced oscillation.
4.2.4.2	
Second Oscillation
In this section, the inter-area oscillation at 0.2 Hz will be 
analysed using PMU measurements. Subsection 4.2.5 
will investigate the effectiveness of the single damping 
countermeasure and explore possible improvements to 
oscillatory stability. Below the system topology before 
the second oscillation.
Figure 4-44:  Grid topology before the second oscillation (in white the lines in open status).
4.2.4.2.1	
Analysis of Available Measurands
The modal analysis of the frequency measurands shows 
a significant participation of the Iberian Peninsula oscil­
lation relative to central Europe and the eastern region. 
The northeast side of the system is observed to be in 
phase opposition. This behaviour is consistent with the 
characteristics of the ECW mode, especially when consid­
ering the recent interconnections with UC–MO and Baltic 
states.
Figure 4-45:  Mode shape of 0.2 Hz.

===== PAGE 253 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  253 
4.2.4.2.2	
Summary of Causes 
32	
It is worth recalling that the transmission angle is directly related to the active power flow, so any internal or external exchange ramp or deviation causes an 
angle deviation.
The East-Centre-West mode is the inter-area mode in CE 
SA with the lowest damping on average. It was triggered 
on several occasions, and strong oscillations occurred. 
The PMU and oscillation monitoring tools in place are 
sufficient to detect abnormal mode activity and initiate 
remedial actions.
This second oscillation arose from a combination of 
factors that together enabled the phenomenon, as 
described in the introduction to this chapter. The high 
transmission angle (around 80° between Carmona and S. 
Llogaia),32 some lines being out of service, and the insuf­
ficient action of a few power system stabilisers created 
the preconditions for the triggering of the oscillations. 
It must be emphasised that predicting the onset of an 
oscillation is very difficult, as it also depends on complex, 
sometimes chaotic interactions between generators, 
loads, and the grid.
However, managing this phenomenon solely in real 
time places significant pressure on the control room. 
Alleviating this burden requires the capability to antic­
ipate the damping of oscillations. Moreover, to avoid 
the existence of a low damping mode in the CE SA, it is 
necessary to study the evolution of inter-area modes 
over the coming years and make the right investment 
decisions to improve their damping. Lastly, the difficulty 
of reproducing the event, along with the need to inte­
grate a detailed model with a simplified one, with all the 
uncertainties it creates, must be addressed to improve 
the efficiency of post-mortem analysis. All of this can be 
achieved by maintaining an up-to-date CE SA dynamic 
model, allowing TSOs to conduct effective post-mortem 
analysis and planning studies.
4.2.5	
Effectiveness of Measures Against Oscillations 
The following section aims to assess the effectiveness 
of various measures against oscillations. First, Subsec­
tion 4.2.5.1 assesses the measures applied to the 
0.63 Hz forced oscillation. Subsection 4.2.5.2 details the 
impact of the applied measures on the 0.2 Hz inter-area 
oscillation. 
Subsection 4.2.5.3 then analyses how additional meas­
ures, which were not available during the incident, 
could impact the 0.2 Hz inter-area oscillation. Subsection 
4.2.5.4 summarises the findings and provides recom­
mendations to ensure proper damping of oscillations.
4.2.5.1	
Assessment of Measures Against Forced Oscillations
This section considers the oscillations characterised by 
a 0.63 Hz frequency that occurred between 12:03 and 
12:08. The calibration of the base case scenario used to 
reproduce this phenomenon, hereafter referred to as 
F0 for simplicity, is detailed in Subsection 4.2.3.2. This 
scenario reflects the actual network conditions at 12:03 
and is compared with other operating scenarios in the 
following subsections.
Since the eigenvalue analysis did not detect any poorly 
damped modes in the 0.4 – 0.8 Hz frequency range, 
the 0.63 Hz mode does not seem to be inherent to the 
system. In fact, these oscillations could not be repro­
duced by simulating a large active power deviation or 
introducing the aforementioned OU stochastic process. 
Thus, this section does not provide the eigenvalue 
results. Instead, RMS simulations are used during the 
sensitivity analysis to check the effectiveness of the 
actions taken by Red Eléctrica. A forced oscillation in 
the active and reactive power injections at 0.63 Hz was 
simulated at the most active node detected in Subsection 
4.2.4.1. The 0.63 Hz oscillation in P and Q injections were 
modelled based on PMU data from nearby lines. The 
average values of the P/Q injections were obtained from 
SCADA data. This study focuses on analysing the impact 
of forced oscillation introduced by a power park module 
on the overall oscillatory stability of the power system.

===== PAGE 254 =====
254  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
4.2.5.1.1	
Effectiveness of Actions Taken by Red Eléctrica
This subsection assesses the effectiveness of the actions 
taken by Red Eléctrica to mitigate 0.63 Hz oscillations – 
reducing the active power interchange between Spain 
and France, switching the VSC–HVDC INELFE-1 from an 
ADC to a CDC control strategy, increasing the active power 
flow from 180 MW to 500 MW per link (to reduce the 
flow through AC interconnection lines), and connecting 
several transmission lines [11]. The following cases are 
compared:
»	F₀: Base case: no corrective actions
»	FTOT: All corrective actions applied
Their joint effect is assessed by conducting an RMS simu­
lation, which is reported in Figure 4-46. As expected, 
although the protocol for addressing low damping is not 
designed for forced oscillations, the mitigation measures 
have a small but positive effect on the 0.63 Hz oscil­
lations, as FTOT exhibits smaller oscillation amplitudes 
compared to F0. However, compared to the inter-area 
oscillation study presented in Subsection 4.2.5.2, the 
effectiveness of these actions is relatively limited. This 
result is expected: if the source of the 0.63 Hz oscillation 
is not removed, these actions have limited effective­
ness, significantly influencing only the 0.2 Hz oscillation 
component of the oscillations, which is intrinsically 
present in the CE SA system. 
Figure 4-46:  Impact of actions taken by Red Eléctrica on the 0.63 Hz oscillations – F₀ vs FTOT.
Figure 4-47 shows the active and reactive power vari­
ations of VSC–HVDC INELFE-1 due to POD-P and POD-Q 
controls, respectively. The FTOT scenario exhibits higher ΔP 
and ΔQ because the frequencies at the AC terminals of 
the VSC–HVDC link are oscillating. 
Therefore, the POD-P and POD-Q controllers provoke P/Q 
modulation precisely to damp oscillations.

4.2.5.1.2	
0.63 Hz Oscillation Decay in 10 Seconds
In this case study, the artificially injected oscillation is 
supposed to stop at simulation time 30 s (approximately 
10 s after its amplitude became significant). The aim 
of this simulation is to determine whether the system 
continues oscillating at the same frequency – in other 
words, whether this oscillation mode is intrinsic to the 
electric network or purely related to the forced injection.
The results shown in Figure 4-50 suggest that this type of 
propagation cannot persist across the CE SA system once 
the source is shut down. In fact, immediately after 30 s in 
the simulation, the oscillations are almost immediately 
damped. This result aligns with the eigenvalue analysis, 
which did not identify any poorly damped modes near 
0.63 Hz.
Figure 4-50:  Trend of 0.63 Hz oscillations across the CE SA system if the injected signal is shut down.

===== PAGE 257 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  257 
4.2.5.1.3	
Inter-Area Resonance from the 0.63 Hz Oscillation
This case study analyses the potential resonant interac­
tions between forced oscillations and electromechanical 
inter-area modes. To achieve this, the damping ratio of 
the CE SA system is reduced (with respect to the one 
in scenario F₀) by acting on the calibration measures 
described in Subsection 4.2.2.
The simulation results reported in Figure 4-51 suggest 
that the inter-area oscillation can be triggered by the 
0.63 Hz oscillation if the damping ratio of the inter-area 
mode is sufficiently small.
Figure 4-51:  F₀ scenario with a small damping ratio of the inter-area mode.
In fact, by examining the leftmost magnified portion 
of the figure, both the 0.63 Hz and the inter-area oscil­
lations can be observed, whereas the same section in 
Figure 4-51 shows a more pronounced 0.63 Hz compo­
nent. In the rightmost magnified portion, representing 
the simulation time from 250 s to 280 s, the inter-area 
oscillation is clearly triggered, while the forced oscilla­
tion, still injecting the signal (see Figure 4-19), is less 
easily detectable.
This resonance between different oscillatory modes has 
been previously studied [20] [21], and the present work 
corroborates this concept in a very large model repre­
sentative of the CE SA system.
4.2.5.1.4	
Discussion
The results of the previous subsections allowed the following general conclusion to be drawn:
Forced oscillations can also excite natural electrome­
chanical modes in the power system if their damping 
ratio is low, with frequencies in a similar range. There­
fore, oscillations in different system variables might 
have two components: forced oscillations and electro­
mechanical oscillations. Measures designed to damp 
electromechanical oscillations (e. g. POD controllers in 
devices, power-exchange reductions, manoeuvres, etc.) 
can influence forced oscillations. 
As discussed previously, a forced oscillation cannot be 
completely mitigated unless the source of the oscilla­
tion is disconnected. However, since forced oscillations 
excite electromechanical modes in the power system, 
the corrective measures used to damp electromechanical 
oscillations can also help mitigate oscillatory behaviour 
in the presence of forced oscillations, as discussed in 
previous subsections.

===== PAGE 258 =====
258  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report

Assessment of Measures Against Inter-Area Oscillations
33

In the following section, the applied measures during 
this phase of the incident are analysed:
»	Performance of INELFE-1 VSC–HVDC link (2 x 1,000 MW)
»	Effect of manoeuvres taken by Red Eléctrica to dampen

4.2.5.2.1	
INELFE-1 VSC–HVDC Link
This subsection analyses the behaviour of the France–
Spain VSC–HVDC interconnection link INELFE-1 (2 x 
1,000 MW) during the incident on 28 April 2025 [22]. 
The analysis presented in this subsection focuses on the 
impact of INELFE-1 VSC–HVDC on damping inter-area 
oscillation.
The operating mode of the VSC–HVDC link at 12:19 was 
as follows:
»	The power order was distributed among the 
links according to their respective link capabil­
ities (MULTI-LINK control mode).
»	The Baixas converter station in France was set 
as the Master Station for Active Power Control 
(PCONMASTER).
»	There was active power flow from Spain to 
France, with power control proportional to 
the angle difference between both ends of 
the link (ADC).
»	The converter stations at Sta. Llogaia were 
operating in voltage control mode (V-mode), 
in which the HVDC link contributes to voltage 
control by providing reactive power exchange 
with the system through an AC voltage target 
setpoint.
»	Power oscillation controllers were activated by 
active power modulation (POD-P) and reactive 
power modulation (POD-Q).33

4.2.5.2.1.1	 Operation of the VSC–HVDC link (ADC to CPC and Psetpoint)
As described in [11] and [23], the VSC–HVDC INELFE-1 was 
operated with a transmitted active power of 1,000 MW 
(500 MW per link) and with the CPC control mode acti­
vated; the rationale behind this selection is as follows:
»	By increasing the transmitted active power 
through the VSC–HVDC link from approximately 
360 MW to 1,000 MW, the P flowing through 
the AC interconnection lines is decreased, thus 
increasing the damping ratio of the inter-area 
mode.
»	By switching from the ADC, which emulates 
an AC line and thus exacerbates the inter-area 
oscillations, to CPC control, the damp ratio is 
increased.
To confirm these statements, several simulations were 
conducted, using both the eigenvalue analysis and RMS 
simulations. 
The following cases were compared:
»	B₀: Base case + HVDC in ADC mode + 
180 MW/link + ES–FR 1,355 MW
»	B₁: Base case + HVDC in ADC mode + 
180 MW/link + ES–FR 875 MW
»	B₂: Base case + HVDC in CPC + 180 MW/link + 
ES–FR 875 MW
»	B₃: Base case + HVDC in ADC mode + 
ES–FR 875 MW
»	A ₀/B₄: Base case (HVDC in CPC mode + 
180 MW/link + ES–FR 875 MW). Notice that 
case B₄ corresponds to case A ₀: the base case 
considered for the scenario for the analysis of 
the 0.2 Hz inter-area oscillation.
The related damping ratios of the inter-area mode are 
reported in Table 4-6, providing the case in which the 
CPC and ADC are used and the P setpoint of the VSC–HVDC 
INFELFE-1 is changed. Additionally, a fourth case (B₀) 
is considered, where the operation point prior to the 
inter-area oscillation is analysed. This includes the ADC 
mode of the VSC–HVDC system, the interchanged power 
through the VSC–HVDC links of 180 MW (per link), and 
the overall interchanged P between Spain and France 
(approximately 1,350 MW). In this manner, the operation 
scenario of the VSC–HVDC system at 12:06 is replicated. 
This study enables the analysis of the combined effect 
of the actions taken by Red Eléctrica on the controls of 
the VSC–HVDC system and the active power interchanged 
between Spain and France.

4.2.5.2.1.2	 POD Controllers
This subsection provides the results of a sensitivity anal­

the effectiveness of the POD-P and POD-Q controllers 
in damping the 0.2 Hz inter-area oscillation observed 
during the incident. For the analysis, the VSC–HVDC link is 
in CPC mode and the converter stations in V-mode, as in 
the reference case A ₀.
The following cases were compared:
»	C₀: Base case A ₀ + HVDC POD-P off and 
POD-Q off
»	A ₀/C₁: Base case (with POD-P on and 
POD-Q off), corresponding to case A ₀
»	C₂: Base case + POD-P off and POD-Q on
»	C₃: Base case + POD-P on and POD-Q on
The results in Table 4-7 demonstrate that both the POD-P 
and POD-Q controllers of the INELFE-1 VSC–HVDC link are 
effective in damping the inter-area oscillations. In this 
scenario, the POD-Q controller is more effective than 
the POD-P controller. This is due to the 400 kV Vic–Baixas 
line (which runs parallel to the VSC–HVDC link) and the 
limited effectiveness of the POD-P controller, which uses 
as its input the difference between the two terminals 
of the link. These results were confirmed by the RMS 
time-domain simulation (Figure 4-55 and Figure 4-56).

4.2.5.2.2	
Effect of Topology Changes Taken by Red Eléctrica to Dampen the East-Centre-West Mode 0.2 Hz 
Inter-area Oscillation
As detailed in Table 2-2, Red Eléctrica took several 
topology actions between 12:02 and 12:25 to dampen 
the 0.6 Hz oscillation and the 0.2 Hz inter-area oscillation 
(connection of lines) and control voltage (disconnection 
of shunt reactors). In this section, a sensitivity analysis 
is conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of these 
manoeuvres in mitigating the inter-area oscillation 
at 0.2 Hz (connection of lines). The analysis considers 
each measure separately as well as their combined 
effect, and the total effect is also presented. As previ­
ously mentioned, to construct the model of the Spanish 
transmission system, this study relies on data from 
12:21 obtained via the state estimator. Consequently, 
all line switching operations occurring between 12:02 
and 12:21 are reverted. Lines were connected to damp 
oscillations in the power system. In this study, each line 
is then individually reconnected to evaluate its contribu­
tion to damping the 0.2 Hz inter-area oscillation. 
A reference case, L0, excluding these topology changes, 
serves as a benchmark case. It should be noted that L0 
does not match the calibrated base case A ₀, as seven lines 
differ in their connection status. In addition, because 
the active power control of the INFELFE-1 VSC–HVDC link 
employs the AC line emulation logic at the onset of the 
switching operations, this control mode is assumed for 
this sensitivity analysis. As this represents the normal 
operation of the HVDC link, this operation scenario seems 
more relevant for evaluating the impact of topology 
changes.
Table 4-9 provides the frequency of the inter-area mode 
fmode (Hz), its damping Ϛ (%), and the corresponding 
variation with respect to the L0 base case. As mentioned 
before, these results were obtained using the Modal/
Eigenvalue Analysis tool in a commercial software 
environment.

4.2.5.3	
Assessment of Additional Potential Measures Against Inter-Area Oscillations
In this subsection, several additional sensitivity analyses 
are reported. These studies cover different operating 
scenarios based on what occurred on the day of the 
incident. As before, particular attention is devoted to 
the influence of several factors on the damping ratio 
of the inter-area mode, including the effect of power 
system stabiliser (PSS) control systems in both CCGT and 
nuclear power plants (NPPs), the increased presence of 
synchronous generators (SGs) in the Spanish transmis­
sion system, the impact of the system’s equivalent inertia 
constant, the power flow through the AC Spain–France 
interconnection lines, and the potential role of synchro­
nous condensers (SCs) and STATCOMs in Spanish transmis­
sion system current plans in mitigating future inter-area 
oscillations.

the PSS and evaluating the damping ratio Ϛ relative to 
base case A₀. Additionally, for the sake of completeness, 
the combined effect of the PSS on all online CCGTs is 
computed. The results are reported in Table 4-12.

4.2.5.3.3	
Additional Synchronous Generators in the SPES System
This subsection assesses the effect of adding additional 
SGs to the Spanish transmission system on the damping 
ratio. For this purpose, 5 SGs – equipped with primary 
frequency control, AVR, and tuned PSS – are included in 
the calibrated model. An equivalent active power value 
is reduced in nearby CIG power plants. This allows the 
power flow through the interconnection AC lines to be 
maintained, avoiding any significant bias in this analysis, 
as power flow has a notable impact on the inter-area 
damping ratio.
The damping ratio provided by DIgSILENT ­PowerFactory’s 
Eigenvalue Analysis tool was used for quantitative 
­analysis. Table 4-14 reports the simulation results for 
their combined effect. The effect of connecting these 
additional generators with PSS is similar to that of acti­
vating and tuning the PSS in NPPs.
As expected, adding additional SG with correctly tuned 
PSSs to the Spanish transmission system helps mitigate 
the inter-area oscillation.

4.2.5.3.4	
Effect of Inertia
In this sensitivity study, the influence of the system’s 
equivalent inertia on the inter-area oscillation is 
assessed. For this purpose, the inertia of all SGs connected 
to the SPES is doubled and tripled. Obviously, increasing 
the inertia constant of each SG without changing any 
other parameter is not realistic. 
It would be more realistic to act on the number of SGs 
connected to the system. However, this would introduce 
other effects besides the inertia constant, such as the 
presence of additional control systems (PSS, AVR, and 
primary frequency control), whereas this sensitivity anal­
ysis is focused on isolating the effect of inertia alone on 
the damping ratio.

3.03

Table 4-15:  Sensitivity analysis – effect of inertia on damping ratio.
The results presented in Table 4-15 suggest that doubling 
the value of the equivalent inertia constant of the Spanish 
system increases the damping ratio of the inter-area 
mode by 0.93 %, while tripling the inertia value results in 
an increase of 2.76 %. These results are unsurprising, as it 
is well established in the literature that low inertia levels 
can promote inter-area oscillations. However, even with 
a tripled equivalent inertia of the Spanish system, the 
damping ratio remains relatively small, at around 3 %. It 
can be observed that this magnitude is comparable to 
that obtained by tuning and activating PSSs on synchro­
nous units or implementing other measures. 
Therefore, increasing inertia solely to damp inter-area 
oscillations is not a realistic option. These results indicate 
that while the role of inertia is non-negligible, it is not 
sufficient on its own to avoid the occurrence of inter-area 
oscillations.
Additionally, it can be observed that the frequency of 
the inter-area mode decreases as the system inertia 
increases. This can be explained by considering the 
equivalent mass of the Spanish system: as this mass 
increases, oscillations become slower.

4.2.5.3.5	
Effect of Power Flow Through AC Interconnection Lines Between Spain and France
This subsection assesses the effects of the power flow 
through the AC interconnection lines between Spain 
and France by changing the active power production of 
several CIGs. The results, considering four different inter­
change values, are reported in Table 4-16. These include 
decreases of approximately 200 MW and 400 MW, as well 
as increases of approximately 200 MW and 450 MW.
It should be noted that the interchange is considered 
positive when Spain is exporting towards France, and 
negative when importing power from France. The same 
convention is applied to active power variations ΔP.
As expected, reducing the power flow through the AC 
interconnections helps mitigate inter-area oscillations. 
Conversely, increasing the interchange power decreases 
the damping ratio. This result is expected and consistent 
with theoretical results reported in the literature [10].

4.2.5.3.8	
Impact of VSC Converters with POD Controllers (BESS, UCAP, E-STATCOMs, etc.) 
This subsection analyses the impact of generic voltage 
source converters (VSC) equipped with POD-P/POD-Q 
controllers on inter-area oscillation damping. These 
generic VSC converters could represent different tech­
nology enablers, such as:
»	An energy storage system (ESS) with a power 
converter, such as a battery energy storage 
system (BESS) or ultracapacitor (UCAP), 
equipped with POD-P/POD-Q controllers
»	E-STATCOMs: POD-P/POD-Q controllers
Two VSC converters with grid-following (GFL) control, 
located arbitrarily within the Iberian Peninsula power 
system, were analysed:
»	VSC-A (100 MVA): Located at Carmona 400 kV in 
the southern area of the Ibernia Peninsula
»	VSC-B (100 MVA): Located at La Cereal 400 kV in 
the central area of the Ibernia Peninsula power 
system
These two locations were selected for illustration 
purposes in this study. Generic dynamic models of the 
VSC converters and their controllers were used. Satura­
tion parameter of POD-P/POD-Q controllers is assumed to 
be ±10 % (% relative to the rating power base).
Table 4-19 shows the damping ratio of the East–Centre–
West inter-area oscillation in the CE power system. The 
results show that the POD-P and POD-Q controllers of 
both VSC converters are effective in damping the critical 
inter-area oscillation in the CE power system. In general, 
POD-P controllers are more effective than POD-Q control­
lers. In addition, VSC converters can have both POD-P/
POD-Q controllers activated simultaneously, producing 
significant improvements.
Therefore, technology enablers based on VSC converters, 
such as BESSs, UCAPs, or E-STATCOMs, could be an attrac­
tive solution to help damp inter-area oscillations in the 
CE power system through POD-P/POD-Q controllers.

4.2.5.3.9	
Impact of Several Devices to Be Included in the Future
This subsection assesses the joint effect of the devices 
scheduled for inclusion in the SPES over the next few 
years, i. e. the eight SCs (see Subsection 4.2.5.3.6), four 
STATCOMs (see Subsection 4.2.5.3.7), and two generic 
VSC systems equipped with POD controls (see Subsection 
4.2.5.3.8). Furthermore, for this analysis, the POD-Q of 
VSC–HVDC INELFE-1 is assumed to be in service. While the 
impact of these devices/controls on the inter-area modes 
is assessed individually in the previous subsections, this 
analysis aims to compare the scenario of the incident 
of 28 April 2025 at 12:21 against a hypothetical future 
scenario where these elements are in service.
The eigenvalue analysis results in Table 4-20 show a 
significant increase in damping ratio, around 2.6 %, indi­
cating that these devices would have a non-negligible 
positive effect in damping inter-area oscillations.
The time-domain simulation in Figure 4-65 confirms the 
previous observations, as the oscillations are damped 
more rapidly and therefore reach smaller amplitudes.
Of course, this analysis does not aim to provide a fully 
comprehensive representation of a future SPES scenario, 
as the network model is based on the state estimator of 
28 April 2025 at 12:21 (as detailed in Subsection 4.2.2), 
rather than on network planning assumptions. Never­
theless, these results provide a useful indication of the 
combined impact of the aforementioned devices.

4.2.5.4	
Conclusion 
This chapter aimed to analyse the oscillations, the effects 
of applied countermeasures on both forced and inter-
area oscillations during the event. 
In addition, potential measures for future implementa­
tion were assessed. Based on the simulations conducted 
and results obtained, it can be concluded that: 
Forced oscillations
»	The applied measures had a minor but positive impact 
on the observed forced oscillation of 0.63 Hz during 
the incident, even though these measures were not 
designed to dampen oscillations in this frequency 
range. This includes changing the control mode of 
INELFE-1, decreasing exports in the AC system, and 
topological changes (see Subsection 4.2.5.1.1). 
»	The most effective way to prevent forced oscillations 
is to localise their source and apply targeted 
countermeasures. This might include activating or 
deactivating controls, changing unit setpoints, or 
disconnecting the sources of forced oscillations. For 
this purpose, operational oscillation monitoring 
and detection must be improved,and effective 
countermeasures must be ready.Neither was available 
in the system during operation on 28 April.
Inter-area oscillations
»	The operational measures applied during the incident 
to mitigate inter-area oscillations can be confirmed 
as effective (see Subsection 4.2.5.2). This includes the 
control mode and POD control of INELFE-1, reduction of 
exports in the AC system, topological changes, and the 
performance of the Vitoria STATCOM.
»		The POD-P/POD-Q controllers of the INELFE-1 HVDC 
link have a positive impact on damping inter-area 
oscillations. The POD-Q controller was automatically 
disabled during the first 0.6 Hz oscillatory event due to 
a logic condition in the controller (repeated saturations 
in upper/lower POD-Q limits) to prevent it from 
malfunctioning. It would have been desirable to have 
the POD-Q controller enabled during the second 0.2 Hz 
inter-area oscillation. Thus, it should be ensured that 
the POD-Q is active during similar events, either through 
the use of alarms for POD-Q deactivation, automated 
reactivation of the controller, or by studying ways to 
avoid deactivation when limits are reached. 
»	Several additional measures to improve damping of 
inter-area oscillations have been identified, which 
have a significant impact. This includes installing and 
tuning of PSS on nuclear power plants, installation of 
SCs, installation of additional STATCOMs with POD-Q and 
VSC with POD-P/-Q. Activating additional synchronous 
machines or increasing the level of inertia also has 
a positive impact on the damping of inter-area 
oscillation, but cannot be considered as an efficient 
option taking into account the more efficient effect of 
planned synchous condensers and STATCOMs.

===== PAGE 277 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  277 
The analysis finally highlighted the following necessary actions at the system level: 
»	1.	 introduce TSO coordinated inspections and tests at 
the field level to verify and certify (eventually with 
the involvement of third party certification bodies) 
the stability and mandatory services required by 
the Grid Code of generators BESS and in the future 
of new types of loads (electrolyzers, data centers, 
etc.); 
»	2.	 intensify high-frequency and power quality 
monitoring tools at the level of individual 
relevant plants (generators, loads) and significant 
sub-transmission/distribution areas;
»	3.	 deepen the behavior of converter driven instability 
with system studies and laboratory tests, including 
laboratory and site acceptance tests to new 
generators and significant loads; 
»	4.	 evaluate, with ad hoc studies, the introduction of 
defense systems to manage automatic containment 
actions and improve oscillation damping; 
»	5.	 perform periodic tuning of power system stabilisers 
(PODs);
»	6.	 with reference to existing generators, evaluate 
any needed improvement of power quality 
monitoring system and needed intervention 
on plant control systems to improve stability;7.	
extend the mandatory requirement of Power System 
Stabiliser on new or existing power plants having 
a significant sensitivity on the system damping of 
oscillations;
»	8.	 to support system stability, it is needed to improve 
requirements for demand/generation/HVDC 
and FACTS to avoid converter driven instability 
phenomena.

4.3	
Analysis of Flows Between TSO and DSO Grids in Spain
4.3.1	
Scope of the Chapter and Data Basis
The scope of this chapter is to analyse the relevant factors 
that influenced the TSO–DSO flows in Spain, particularly 
after the oscillatory periods and during the 12:32 – 12:33 
timeframe on 28 April 2025.
To perform the analysis, the following data from Spain 
has been used:
»	TSO–DSO exchanges per region (P, Q) // 4 sec 
resolution
»	Load per region (P) // 4 sec resolution
»	aFRR activations (P) // 4 sec resolution
»	Datasets from two PV inverter manufacturers 
for each region of Spain
–	 Dataset manufacturer M#1, aggregated with 
5 min resolution
–	 Dataset manufacturer M#2, aggregated with 
10 sec resolution
»	DSO data from selected feeders // 
12 sec resolution
»	TSO data from selected feeders // 
8 sec resolution
Additionally, to analyse the effect on voltage depend­
ency, typical load parameters from the literature have 
been used.
4.3.2	
Relevant Factors Influencing TSO–DSO Flows 
The changes in TSO–DSO flows that occurred on 
28 April 2025 (particularly after the two oscillatory 
periods and between 12:32 and 12:33) are the result of 
complex interactions among various factors within the 
distribution and transmission grids.
Since no single factor can fully explain the deviating TSO–
DSO flow changes on 28 April 2025 (see Figure 2.13), it 
is important to provide an overview that summarises 
the relationships among the relevant factors influencing 
TSO–DSO flows (Figure 4-66). This chapter focuses on 
the description of the relevant factors in the distribution 
grids (bullet points in black-coloured box). However, it 
should be noted that these factors also apply to trans­
mission grids with directly connected grid users (bullet 
points in grey).

As shown in Figure 4-69, there is no clear correlation 
between aFRR activations and the sum of TSO–DSO flows 
in Spain during the 12:00 – 12:33 time period. The lack of

providers are on the transmission grid, with fewer than

regarding the correlation between mFRR activations and

12:30 shows that the share of mFRR in the distribution 
grids is around 10 – 20 %, while between 12:30 – 12:45 
the share is <10 %. Therefore, it is reasonable to apply the 
conclusions drawn from aFRR to mFRR (Table 4-21).

4.3.3.2	
Disconnection of Generation <1 MW (“Embedded Generation”)
4.3.3.2.1	
Description of data used and assumptions
In the course of preparing this Final Report, the Expert 
Panel received data from two PV inverter manufacturers, 
enabling the analysis of possible disconnections of 
embedded generation units <1 MW on 28 April 2025. 
Both datasets contain only information about inverters 
connected to low-voltage (LV) grids.
The dataset provided from PV inverter manufacturer 
#1 (M#1) includes the following information, which is 
aggregated per region in 5-minute intervals:
»	Number of reporting devices
»	Aggregated nominal active power capacity
»	Aggregated active and reactive power
»	Number of overvoltage warnings
»	Number of overvoltage trips
»	Number of undervoltage trips
»	Number of overfrequency trips
»	Number of underfrequency trips
The dataset provided from PV inverter manufacturer 
#2 (M#2) includes the following information, which is 
aggregated per region in 10-second intervals:
»	Number of reporting devices
»	Number of overvoltage trips
»	Number of undervoltage trips
»	Number of overfrequency trips
»	Number of underfrequency trips
The standard protection settings for overvoltage trips of 
inverters are the same for both manufacturers:
»	U>: 253 V/1.5 s
»	U>>: 264 V/0.2 s
The current Spanish grid code sets a minimum grid 
reconnection time of 180 seconds (3 minutes) after 
tripping. Furthermore, the PV inverter manufacturer M#2 
explained that an additional delay of approximately 60 
seconds is required before reconnection takes place, 
during which the inverter performs several technical 
tests. Therefore, in the context of this analysis (see in 
particular Section 4.3.3.2.2.3), it is considered that the 
total time between disconnection and reconnection of 
an inverter is 240 seconds (4 minutes).

===== PAGE 282 =====
282  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
The installed PV inverter capacity in Spain reported by the 
two manufacturers amounts to approximately 690 MW. 
Red Eléctrica estimates31 that the total installed PV 
capacity in Spain in April 2025 for facilities <1 MW was 
approximately 6,478 MW,of which approximately 75 % 
(4,860 MW) is connected to LV grids. Hence, the combined 
dataset provided by the two manufacturers represents 
approximately 14 %32 of the total installed PV inverter 
capacity connected to LV grids in Spain.

32	
The PV capacity reported by Red Eléctrica is the total peak capacity of PV panels, while the manufacturers report the aggregated peak capacity of their PV 
inverters. The capacities of PV panels and PV inverter for a given facility are usually different, but this difference can vary significantly from one facility to another. 
Therefore, in absence of information about the typical difference between the PV inverter and PV panel capacities, the Expert Panel considers them as being 
equivalent in the context of this analysis.
Red Eléctrica estimates that, on 28 April 2025, from 
10:00 onwards, the actual aggregated production from 
PV facilities <1 MW was approximately 4,447 MW (69 % of 
the installed capacity). Applying the same ratio only to PV 
facilities connected to LV grids, it follows that the PV facil­
ities connected to LV grids had an aggregated production 
of approximately 3,340 MW.
4.3.3.2.2	
Analysis
This section presents an analysis of the data provided 
by the two inverter manufacturers. The analysis 
focuses on inverter trips from 10:00 until the blackout, 
aiming to assess whether there is a link between these 
disconnections, the transmission grid voltage and 
changes in the TSO–DSO flow. In addition, this section 
includes an estimate of the total disconnected PV produc­
tion resulting from these trips.
4.3.3.2.2.1	 Analysis of disconnections aggregated in 5-minute intervals
As explained in Section 4.3.3.2.1, inverter manufac­
turer M#1 provided their data in 5-minute intervals, 
while inverter manufacturer M#2 provided their data in 
10-second intervals. To compare the two datasets, the 
data received from manufacturer M#2 were therefore 
aggregated into 5-minute periods (by summing the data 
from 30 consecutive 10-second intervals).
Global view
Figures 4-70 and 4-71 show, for each 5-minute period, 
the proportion of inverter trips due to overvoltage, sepa­
rately for the two manufacturers. This proportion is calcu­
lated across all regions, i. e., for Spain as a whole. The 
figures also show the voltage evolution on the 400 kV 
grid (top) and the changes in TSO–DSO flows (bottom).
For both datasets, similar correlations (trends) can be 
observed between the number of overvoltage-related 
trips, grid voltage and changes in TSO–DSO flows. For 
example, it appears that a higher proportion of over­
voltage trips is registered during the 11:05 – 11:10 
period, during which the TSO–DSO flows and the grid 
voltage increased significantly and a first oscillatory 
episode took place around 11:06. A similar trend/corre­
lation is observed during the 11:25 – 11:50 period, as 
well as during and/or after the two major oscillatory 
periods (12:05 – 12:10 and 12:25 – 12:30). 
Hence, it cannot be excluded that a certain share of PV 
inverter overvoltage trips was associated to these three 
oscillation episodes. However, the 5-minute aggre­
gation of overvoltage-related trips is not sufficiently 
detailed to accurately assess the possible link between 
these phenomena.
Furthermore, because the blackout occurred in the 
middle of a 5-minute period (12:30 – 12:35), an analysis 
based on a 5-minute aggregation does not allow for 
deriving any correlations between the PV inverter trips 
and the phenomena that occurred during the incident.

4.3.3.2.2.3	 Estimation of the total amount of disconnected generation (units <1 MW) based on the 
10-second resolution dataset from inverter manufacturer M#2
33	
This simplification assumes that the grid parameters (voltage and frequency measured at inverter terminals) immediately return into the required normal 
operating ranges after a disconnection has happened. Under real conditions, this might often not be the case, which means that the total time between 
disconnection and reconnection of a tripped inverter can last significantly longer.
The purpose of this subsection is to estimate the extent 
to which it is possible to correlate the TSO–DSO flow 
changes with the total amount of disconnected gener­
ation units <1 MW.
The methodology used, described below, is based on 
several assumptions and simplifications in the absence 
of further information. These factors should therefore 
be taken into account when interpreting the results.
The methodology used is based on the following 
assumptions and simplifications:
»	Dataset: To estimate the total amount of disconnected 
generation <1 MW at a given moment, a relatively 
accurate timestamp for each inverter trip is required. 
Therefore, the dataset of manufacturer M#1 cannot be 
used in this context, as a 5-minute temporal resolution 
is insufficient. On the contrary, the 10-second resolution 
available in the dataset from manufacturer M#2 is 
appropriate. Hence, only the dataset from manufacturer 
M#2 can be used to perform this estimation. This does 
not imply that the data from M#2, particularly regarding 
the number of trips, are necessarily more accurate than 
those from M#1. In particular, the Expert Panel does 
not know whether the tripping behaviour of the M#2 
inverter fleet overestimates, underestimates, or is in 
line with the actual total disconnected generation of 
the entire population of PV units <1 MW.
»	Reconnection time of tripped inverters: As described 
in Section 4.3.3.2.1, the minimum time between 
the disconnection after a trip and the automatic 
reconnection of an inverter is equal to approximately 
240 seconds (4 minutes). For the sake of simplicity, in 
the context of this methodology, it is assumed that every 
tripped inverter always33 reconnects after a fixed time 
of 4 minutes. While trip/disconnections of inverters at 
e. g., timestamp 12:00:00 lead to an increase of the total 
amount of disconnected generation (i. e., a decrease 
of production infeed to the DSO grid), automatic 
reconnections of the same inverters at timestamp 
12:04:00 lead to the decrease of this same value (i. e., 
an increase of production infeed to the DSO grid).

»	Reference value regarding actual aggregated 
production from PV facilities <1 MW: Since the 
applied dataset from M#2 solely contains information 
about inverters connected to LV grids, the Expert Panel 
decided – in line with Section 4.3.3.2.1. – to consider 
3,340 MW (69 % of the actual aggregated production 
from PV facilities <1 MW) as the reference value of the 
actual aggregated PV production from 10:00 onwards 
on 28 April. With this approach, it can be ensured that 
the disconnection behaviour of the LV-connected 
inverters in M#2 is linked only to the estimated actual 
generation from PV facilities <1 MW with a connection 
point at the same voltage level. However, this also 
means that the applied methodology can lead to an 
underestimation (by approximately 30 %) of the total 
amount of disconnected generation <1 MW, since the 
potential effect of voltage variations on medium-
voltage (MV) connected inverters is not considered in 
the calculation.
In order to estimate the total amount of disconnected 
generation <1 MW the following calculation steps are 
applied:
»	1.	 Calculate sum of trips (= overvoltage + 
[undervoltage + overfrequency + under­
frequency]34) for each 10-second window.
34	
Even though these trips do not play a significant role, they are included for the sake of completeness.
»	2.	 To take into account the disconnection 
and reconnection behaviour of tripped 
inverters, apply a sliding window with 
a span of 4 minutes (= 24 periods of 10 
seconds) and create the sum of all trips that 
have been calculated in step 1) within this 
sliding window.
»	3.	 Calculate the proportion of disconnected 
inverters from Step 2 relative to the total 
number of inverters in the fleet from M#2/
»	4.	 Extrapolate the percentage value from Step 
3 to the estimated total PV production at the 
low-voltage level (3,340 MW; see Section 
4.3.3.2.1).
The result of this methodology is shown in Figure 4-79 
(bottom graph), which correlates the estimated amount 
of disconnected generation based on the proposed 
methodology with the TSO–DSO flows. It appears that 
the significant changes in the TSO–DSO flows during the 
11:05 – 11:10, 12:05 – 12:10, and 12:25 – 12:30 periods 
occur nearly in parallel with the changes in the esti­
mated disconnected generation.
Since both y-axes in the bottom graph of Figure 4-79 
have the same scale, it is also possible to estimate the 
ratio of disconnected generation compared to the overall 
TSO–DSO flow changes for the relevant time periods:

4.3.3.2.2.4	 Sensitivity of the amount of disconnected generation to the inverters’ reconnection time
As described in Section 4.3.3.2.2.3, a fixed reconnection 
time of 4 minutes has been applied to estimate the total 
amount of disconnected generation <1 MW.
The purpose of this subsection is to estimate the influ­
ence of the reconnection time TReconnect on the estimated 
total amount of disconnected generation <1 MW. For 
this purpose, four different reconnection times were 
selected:
»	10 seconds (equivalent to an immediate recon­
nection since the M#2 dataset has a temporal 
granularity of 10 seconds)
»	1 minute
»	2 minutes
»	3 minutes
»	4 minutes
Figure 4-81 shows the effect of the selected reconnec­
tion time on the total amount of disconnected genera­
tion <1 MW.
A more detailed zoom on the 11:00 – 11:30 timeframe in 
Figure 4-82 reveals that TReconnect significantly influences 
the peak in total disconnected generation for TReconnect 
values between 10 seconds and 2 minutes. When TReconnect 
increases further, the peak continues to increase but at 
a smaller rate of change, while the amount of discon­
nected generation is maintained for a longer time
However, the estimation results with a selected TReconnect 
of just 10 sec (= almost immediate reconnection) and 
1 min clearly indicate that the peak values of discon­
nected generation are significantly lower compared to 
the estimation variants mentioned before. Essentially, 
the same applies to the persistence of the disconnected 
generation.
Taking these findings into account, the fundamental 
question arises as to what extent the choice of TReconnect 
and the design of the automatic reconnection procedure 
of small PV inverters in general may affect the interoper­
ability of the TSO and DSO networks.
It therefore seems appropriate to perform further 
­analysis of the automatic reconnection behaviour of 
small PV inverters (particularly for events with a high rate 
of disconnection events).

4.3.3.3	
Voltage Dependency of Loads
4.3.3.3.1	
Introduction
The voltage dependency of loads is an inherent property 
of electrical power systems. It is rooted in the funda­
mental design of electrical devices and describes how a 
device’s power consumption varies with changes in the 
supply voltage.
In large power systems, the total load is usually a 
time-varying mix of thousands of different electrical 
devices. While some electrical devices always draw the 
same amount of power, others consume more or less 
depending on whether the voltage is higher or lower 
than the nominal voltage.
According to the well-known ZIP model, loads can be 
categorised into the following three categories (Figure 
4-83):
»	Constant impedance (Z):  Current changes 
directly with voltage (e. g., heating, lighting).
»	Constant current (I): Current remains constant, 
so power changes linearly with voltage.
»	Constant power (P): The device draws constant 
power by adjusting current as voltage changes, 
often seen in regulated electronics, which can 
cause instability.
Figure 4-83:  ZIP load types

4.3.4	
Conclusions
The analyses developed in Chapter 4.3 allow drawing the 
following conclusions related to the observed changes in 
TSO–DSO flows on 28 April 2025:
»	Changes in TSO–DSO flows can only slightly be 
linked to aFRR/mFRR activations.
»	Changes in TSO–DSO flows are, to a certain 
extent, linked to overvoltage tripping of gener­
ation units <1 MW connected to low-voltage 
grids:
–	 the proportion of overvoltage trips shows a 
high correlation with the increase in voltage 
on the transmission grid;
–	 the estimated total amount of disconnected 
generation is strongly correlated with the 
changes in TSO–DSO flows;
–	 the total amount of disconnected generation 
is highly dependent on the actual number 
of trips and on the total time between the 
disconnection and the reconnection of the 
disconnected inverters;
–	 the methodology used to estimate the total 
amount of disconnected generation is based 
on several assumptions and simplifications.
These factors should therefore be taken into account 
when interpreting the results.
»	The Expert Panel recommends performing 
further analysis of the voltage-related discon­
nection and automatic reconnection of small 
PV inverters (see Recommendation 11 in 
Chapter 9).
»	Because voltage dependency of loads is an 
inherent property of power systems, it can 
also be linked to a certain extent to the load 
increase at the DSO level (and hence changes 
in TSO–DSO flows):
–	 A correlation is established between a simpli­
fied load model and DSO measurements.
–	 However, detailed models, information on 
load composition, and additional representa­
tive DSO measurements would be needed to 
accurately model the detailed behaviour of 
all TSO/DSO interfacing points (including the 
location and load/generation composition, 
especially the share of PV supply at the LV 
level).
»	Furthermore, based on the calculations 
performed to estimate the total amount of 
disconnected generation, it appears that the 
net load increase of 317 MW observed between 
12:32:00 and 12:32:57 (Event 1 in Table 3-1) 
is partially due to the disconnection of PV units 
connected to the LV grid. However, due to the 
assumptions made and the uncertainties in the 
available data, it is not possible to precisely 
determine what proportion of this net load 
increase can be attributed to LV-connected PV 
units, nor whether estimates for LV-connected 
units can be applied to MV-connected inverters.

Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  297 
4.4	
System Stability and Defence Plans
The purpose of the analyses outlined in this section is 
to elucidate the phenomena that occurred in the final 
stages preceding the blackout of the Iberian Peninsula 
and to present various sensitivity studies concerning the 
principal external variables that may have been pivotal 
to the event, from both frequency and voltage stability 
standpoints.
4.4.1	
Methodological Framework for Analysis
The simulation model was developed starting from the 
latest available state-estimator snapshot prior to the 
blackout event, time-stamped at 12:25. This snapshot 
ensures full alignment with the actual system condi­
tions preceding the incident, in particular with respect 
to system topology, power flows, and voltage profile, 
thereby establishing a robust and realistic initial oper­
ating point for the dynamic simulations.
The static snapshot includes a complete and detailed 
representation of both topology and operating point of 
the Spanish and Portuguese power systems, along with 
the portions of the French and Moroccan grids close to 
the Spanish borders. The remainder of the European 
grid is represented through equivalent generators at the 
model boundaries.
Based on this initial model, several adjustments were 
needed to make it suitable for RMS dynamic simula­
tion purposes. Synchronous generator-based power 
plants were represented in the greatest possible detail, 
including step-up transformers and auxiliary loads, 
ensuring an accurate depiction of their electrical inter­
face with the transmission network. Renewable gener­
ation plants were modelled as individual generators, 
including generator busbars, transformers, auxiliary 
loads, etc. In addition, very small generation units 
connected to medium and low voltage levels of the 
distribution network were estimated and modelled as 
aggregated equivalent generators at the distribution 
level. Throughout this adaptation process, the voltage 
magnitudes, voltage angles, and line power flows of the 
initial snapshot were preserved.
Once the study model was adapted to the level of detail 
required for dynamic studies, comprehensive dynamic 
models were incorporated to reproduce the behaviour 
of all relevant system components. Each generator was 
associated with a specific dynamic model based on 
owner and manufacturer information, technology type, 
and applicable grid code requirements, including the 
controls necessary to provide the prescribed response to 
disturbances, as well as protection models aligned with 
the robustness requirements defined by the regulations.
In addition, dynamic models of load behaviour were 
implemented, along with area-based load-shedding 
protection schemes, where the percentage of discon­
nection was updated based on the most recent esti­
mated real values. Line protection models for loss of 
synchronism at the interconnections with France were 
included, as well as dynamic representations of HVDC 
links, STATCOM devices, and additional system operator 
models developed for reporting and result analysis.
With respect to HVDC representation, an equivalent 
model at the points of connection was modelled, 
providing a consistent and robust reproduction of the 
HVDC’s dynamic behaviour during the event.
Overall, this modelling framework enables reliable RMS 
simulations, ensuring consistency with the validated 
steady-state operating point while accurately capturing 
the dynamic interactions relevant for voltage stability 
assessment.
For the sake of full transparency, it is important to 
mention that the construction of such a detailed repre­
sentative model of the Iberian Peninsula and neigh­
bouring power system required the Expert Panel to 
strictly collaborate with the affected TSOs, particularly 
Red Eléctrica, which were deeply and primarily involved 
in this process. These results could not have been 
achieved without strong and transparent collaboration, 
while simultaneously ensuring the confidentiality of 
third-party information relevant to system security. The 
Expert Panel monitored all developments and guided 
the investigation by defining modelling requirements, 
validating assumptions and intermediate results, and 
ensuring methodological consistency and technical 
rigour throughout the entire analysis process.

===== PAGE 298 =====
298  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
4.4.2	
Frequency Stability
This section outlines the analyses and conclusions on 
frequency stability, based on RMS dynamic simula­
tions conducted using the detailed model described in 
section 4.4.1. 
The simulations allow for the reproduction of frequency 
evolution during the incident and assess the role of 
inertia and the behaviour of the defence plan during 
the event.
4.4.2.1	
Reproduction of the Frequency Trajectory During the Incident
4.4.2.1.1	
Adjustments to the Snapshot
The model described in section 4.4.1.1 was used to analyse the dynamic behaviour of the system in the final phases 
of the event, starting from 12:33:16. To ensure the highest level of accuracy, the steady-state equilibrium point was 
further adjusted to reflect the system conditions at that specific time. These changes were made as a series of modifi­
cations and load flow convergences of the initial snapshot:
»	1.	 The production of generation technology 
was adjusted to match the generation mix 
at 12:33:16.
»	2.	 The international exchanges with France, 
Portugal, and Morocco were adjusted to the 
values provided by PMU measurements for 
12:33:16.
»	3.	 Power plants based on renewable energy 
sources, cogeneration, and waste-to-­
energy were converted to the fixed power 
factor control mode, according to Royal 
Decree 413/2014 (cosδ = 0,985 inductive).
»	4.	 A set of topological changes was modelled 
to reflect the state of the transmission 
network at 12:33:16, including tap changes 
of the Arkale phase-shifting transformer, 
line closures and openings, and reactor 
connections/disconnections carried out by 
the TSO between 12:25:00 and 12:33:16, 
as indicated in the incident chronology 
in Chapter 3.
»	5.	 The disconnection of the transformer in 
the province of Granada that occurred at 
12:32:57 was modelled, as well as the 
loss of the active and reactive generation 
connected to it (Event 3 in Chapter 3).
»	6.	 The active and reactive power injections of 
the generation subject to the requirements 
applicable under P.O. 7.4 (synchronous 
generators of > 30 MW) were modelled 
according to the measurements available 
for each unit as 12:33:16.
»	7.	 Demand by zones was adjusted to reflect 
the power variation in demand trans­
formers between 12:25:00 and 12:33:16.
»	8.	 PMU measurements (63 buses at 400 kV and 
220 kV) were used as a reference to adjust 
the voltage profile for the transmission 
network of the adapted model to better 
represent the situation during the event.

4.4.2.1.2	
Validation of the Model and Simulation Results
To validate the model and build confidence in its ability to 
effectively replicate system behaviour, a simulation was 
run to reproduce the evolution of electrical quantities in 
the moments leading up to the incident. Specifically, a 
dynamic simulation beginning with the disconnection 
of generation at Badajoz (Event 4 in the list presented in 
Chapter 3) was carried out, and the evolution of the main 
system variables was compared with the available PMU 
measurements. 
It is important to note that in the simulation, all genera­
tors disconnected automatically through the triggering 
of their individual protection models. Only the tripping 
of a combined cycle power plant (12:33:20.100), the 
L/Loeches–Arganda 220 kV line (12:33:19.971), and of 
the Spain–Morocco interconnections (Puerto de la Cruz–
Beni Harchane 400 kV at 12:33:20.229 and Puerto de la 
Cruz–Mellousa 400 kV at 12:33:20.473) were time-based 
disconnections due to the lack of proper protection 
models and/or the lack of information about the cause 
of the disconnection.
Figure 4-89 and Figure 4-90 show the frequency and 
voltage at the La Cereal 400 kV substation, located north 
of Madrid near the centre of the Iberian Peninsula, 
compared to the real-world PMU measurement at the 
same location. As shown, the simulation model captures 
the general trend of the frequency, showing an accurate 
match between the simulation and the real-world meas­
urement data.

4.4.2.2	
Role of the Defence Plan Performances
This simulation aims to investigate the impact of a 
“perfect” load-shedding scenario on the incident. In 
this case, “perfect” load shedding refers to the exact 
implementation of shedding percentages at each acti­
vation threshold. To perform this variant, load-shedding 
protection models were modified to include the theo­
retical percentages of demand that had to be discon­
nected at each step (slightly increased). Figure 4-93 
and Figure 4-94 show the Spain–France active power 
exchange and the frequency at the La Cereal 400 kV 
substation for the base case (blue), the case with the 
theoretical load-shedding percentages (green), and the 
PMU measurements (red). 
Initially, both simulations are identical, and the blocking 
of load-shedding protections due to reverse power flow 
does not affect the initial disconnection of generation 
as imports increase and synchronism is lost. However, 
at around t = 5 s (12:33:21.000), the simulations begin 
to diverge, with the simulation using theoretical 
load-shedding percentages exhibiting a slightly slower 
frequency decrease caused by the increased load shed­
ding. However, the loss of synchronism remains mini­
mally affected, and at the end of the simulation, the 
frequency at La Cereal is still decreasing rapidly. Hence, 
even “perfect” load shedding would not have avoided 
the blackout.

4.4.2.3	
Role of Inertia
Role of increasing the total system inertia
This simulation aims to investigate how additional 
system inertia could have affected the transient evolu­
tion during the incident. For this purpose, the dynamic 
models of the conventional generators, turbines, and 
other rotating masses were modified to increase the 
inertia constant. After these modifications, the total 
system inertia increased +20 % compared to the base 
case. Figure 4-95 and Figure 4-96 show the Spain–France 
active power exchange and the frequency at the La Cereal 
400 kV substation for the base case (blue), the case with 
a +20 % increase in total system inertia (green), and the 
PMU measurements (red). The two simulations are very 
similar, and only a slight delay in the loss of synchronism 
can be observed. These results indicate that additional 
system inertia had a minimal impact on the degree of 
system evolution in the final moments of the incident. 
To better understand Figure 4-96, it is worth to note that 
a higher inertia makes the peninsular system inject and 
absorb energy with the rest of Europe in a slower (and 
slightly stronger) way during the loss of synchronism than 
in the base case. This makes the transient unloading of the 
system higher and, therefore, the overvoltage disconnec­
tions happens before than in the base case, making the 
frequency evolve in a steeper way towards blackout.

4.4.2.4	
Role of HVDC Power Reversal Mode
This simulation aims to investigate the impact of the HVDC 
power reversal mode on the Spain–France exchange, the 
loss of synchronism, and the evolution of frequency. This 
functionality allows for rapid inversion of the power flow 
on the HVDC link to counteract the overall system imbal­
ance. To simulate this functionality, it is assumed that after 
the exchange reaches its maximum import capacity from 
France to Spain, the HVDC power reversal mode activates 
and immediately changes from exporting approximately 
1 GW to importing 1 GW. Figure 4-97 and Figure 4-98 
show the Spain–France active power exchange and the 
frequency at the La Cereal 400 kV substation for the base 
case (blue), the case with the HVDC power reversal mode 
(green), and the PMU measurements (red). 
Before the activation of the HVDC power reversal 
mode, both simulations are identical. At t = 3.5 s 
(12:33:19.5000), the power reversal mode is activated 
and the Spain–France active power exchange exhibits 
a sharp step, increasing the import to 4.7 GW. However, 
the simulation results show that the loss of synchronism 
is not affected by the sudden increase in imports, and 
the frequency drops significantly faster due to generator 
disconnections caused by fast transients in the electrical 
quantities. These results indicate the activation of the 
HVDC power reversal mode when the Spain – France 
exchange reaches its maximum in the import from 
France to Spain does not have a positive impact on the 
incident.

The above analyses indicate that, even under the 
assumption of perfect execution of defence plan actions, 
neither these measures nor additional inertia would 
have been sufficient to prevent system collapse. Further­
more, a rapid intervention on the HVDC interconnection 
between France and Spain aimed at restoring the Iberian 
Peninsula’s system balance could have actually wors­
ened system behaviour due to fast transient phenomena.
4.4.3	
Voltage Stability
This section outlines the analyses and conclusions 
regarding the voltage stability perspective. This study 
employed two different models to efficiently assess 
phenomena related to voltage dynamic behaviour 
across different characteristic time scales. In particular, 
the model described in section 4.4.1 was used to 
reproduce the final moments of the incident (section 
4.4.3.2), providing a detailed representation of the 
dynamic behaviour of all components. Conversely, a 
quasi-dynamic model was specifically developed to 
reconstruct the voltage evolution in the minutes leading 
up to the incident, allowing for a better understanding 
of elements that contributed to voltage volatility. 
Additional details about this model are provided in the 
sections below.
4.4.3.1	
Analysis of Voltage Transient Between 12:25:00 and 12:33:16 
The aim of this section is to simulate the entire time window between 12:25:00 and 12:33:16 to gain insight into the 
voltage variations before the high voltage cascade that occurred at 12:33:16.
4.4.3.1.1	
Description of the Model
As previously noted, the simulation of these long-term 
phenomena is based on a quasi-dynamic model of the 
system, built using the open-source tool Dynawo.30 An 
anonymised version of the static snapshot described in 
section 4.4.1 was imported to prevent the disclosure 
of sensitive third-party information while allowing the 
Expert Panel to conduct independent analyses. The simu­
lations were performed using the DynaFlow31 approach 
implemented in Dynawo.
Specifically, the approach used in this study allows for 
long-term time-domain simulations even when detailed 
dynamic models of components (such as generators or 
loads) are not available. It relies on simplified time-­
domain representations, allowing an approximation 
of the system’s dynamic response without requiring 
in-depth knowledge of the internal dynamic behaviour 
of each individual component. This makes the approach 
suitable for analysing the overall system evolution 
over longer time scales; however, it is not intended to 
accurately reproduce the fast dynamics that characterise 
the final seconds of the incident, where more detailed 
models are required to accurately capture system behav­
iour. Therefore, the divergence of this quasi-static model 
by real measurands in the last part of simulated tran­
sients is not considered.
4.4.3.1.2	
Base Case
The snapshot at 12:25:00 is the initial point of the simu­
lation. The main events affecting the voltage have been 
forced into the simulation:
»	Variations in active power loads in Portugal and 
Morocco to match the measured flow exchange with 
Spain.
»	Variations in distribution loads (active and reactive 
power) in Spain to match the measured exchanges 
from TSO to DSO. These simulated variations include 
both load and generation variations at the DSO level.

===== PAGE 305 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  305 
»	Variations of active and reactive power of photovoltaic 
and wind generation under 50 MW connected to the 
transmission system, to match measured active and 
reactive power. Other generation categories connected 
to transmission were not modified, as their variations 
were minimal during this period.
»	12:25:23: Closing of the Guadame–Cabra 400 kV line
»	12:26:01: Closing of the Tordesillas–Galapagar 
400 kV line
»	12:26:54: Closing of the Vitoria shunt reactor

»	12:27:52: Closing of the Guadame 2 shunt reactor
»	12:28:01: Closing of the Morata shunt reactor
»	12:32:57: Event ID 3 400 kV TS1–Granada, 355 MW 
disconnection
»	12:33:16.4: Event ID 4a 400 kV TS1–Badajoz, 582 MW

»	12:33:16.9: Event ID 4b 400 kV TS2–Badajoz, 145 MW 
disconnection
»	12:33:17: Event ID 5a1 400 kV TS1–Segovia, 23 MW 
disconnection

To verify the quality of the simulation, Figure 4-99

The simulation closely matches the measurements,

The main observation is that the exchange with Portugal 
decreases throughout the simulation, with a sharp drop 
of 500 MW between 12:30:48 and 12:31:29, increasing 
the exchange from Spain to France while simultane­
ously reducing voltage. These results provide an initial 
indication of the sensitivity of this exchange to voltage 
volatility in southern Spain, where resources for voltage 
regulation were limited.
4.4.3.1.3	
Parameters Affecting Voltage Variations
Starting from the base case, several simulation variants 
were developed to better understand the influence of 
the different exogenous factors affecting system behav­
iour. In each variant, a single exogenous variation was 
applied individually, while all other conditions remained 
the same as in the base case.
This approach allows the effect of each factor to be 
isolated and its individual contribution to the observed 
voltage evolution to be evaluated. By comparing the 
results of each variant with the base case, the relative 
importance of each exogenous driver in shaping the 
voltage profile during the minutes leading up to the 
incident can be assessed.
Analysis 1: No variation in the exchange between Spain and Morocco
In this analysis, the power exchange between Spain and Morocco was assumed to remain constant at the value 
observed from the snapshot at 12:25. 
Although the variations in power exchange between 
Spain and Morocco are relatively small (around 180 MW, 
see Figure 4-103), they lead to non-negligible voltage 
changes, highlighting a slight sensitivity of the voltage 
to this flow. 
In particular, the power flow on the Spain–Morocco 
border is directly correlated with voltage. Maintaining a 
higher value has little impact on the power flow on the 
opposite Spain-to-France border (as power variations 
there are minimal), but increases local flows, which in 
turn lowers voltages in southern Spain. 
Figure 4-103:  Fixed exchange on the Spain–Morocco border: voltage at the 
400 kV substation in southern Spain.

at the France–Spain border.

the Spain–Portugal border exceed 900 MW over the time

about 500 MW started at 12:30:48. These fluctuations 
cause voltage deviations in southern Spain (specifically, 
an increase in voltage levels), demonstrating the signifi­
cant impact of cross-border flows on voltage in the area.
The simulations results depicted in Figure 4-105 and 
Figure 4-106 allow to conclude that the Spain to Portugal 
power flow was negatively correlated to the voltage 
variation, since keeping a higher power flow on this 
border lowers the power flow on the opposite Spain 
to France border, with the effect of higher voltages in 
southern Spain.

reproduce the exact system trajectory, but rather to high­

The variation in PV generation connected to DSOs consists

The simulation results depicted in Figure 4-109 and

generation, consistent with the behaviour observed for

Analysis 5: Voltage variations without closing 400 kV lines for oscillation damping improvement
In this analysis, a variant of the base case was developed 
in which the closing of 400 kV lines intended to improve 
oscillation damping (10 lines from 12:07 to 12:26) was 
not applied. The switching actions performed during the 
event were therefore removed from the simulation to 
evaluate their influence on voltage behaviour.
As expected, Figure 4-111 shows that the topological 
changes implemented to counteract the oscillations 
have a non-negligible impact on voltage levels in 
southern Spain. The closing of the 400 kV lines reduces 
the network impedance and redistribute the active and 
reactive power flows of lines, which in turn increase the 
voltage profile in the area.
This observation confirms that the corrective actions 
taken by the operators to successfully dampen the oscil­
lations, in accordance with the procedures in place and 
discussed in Section 4.2, had an impact on the voltage 
level in the South of Spain.
Figure 4-111:  No line disconnection to counteract oscillations: voltage at the

Analysis 6: Additional reactive power margins from conventional generation 
The aim of the simulation is to evaluate the voltage tran­
sient assuming additional reactive power margins to 
the generators spinning at 12:32, showing as additional 
reactive power absorption could contribute to stabilise 
the voltage behaviour of the system. 
The simulation results reported in Figure 4-112 are 
obtained with the long term analysis approach that take 
into account in steps by 1 second the dynamic evolution 
of the system. It is important to underline that, although 
the dynamics of the AVR are represented, the model 
does not capture the existing effects of AVR limiters 
but considers the physics of the generators adopting as 
reference capability of the generators a square curve, 
available by the snapshots. These assumptions are not 
limiting the simulation but necessary to give the needed 
general evaluation about system needs. The simulation 
shows how additional margin could improve the reac­
tive power management increasing the total physically 
available reserve.
