4.4.3.2.1	
Role of Voltage Regulation from Additional Synchronous Condensers 
To further explore the concept of reactive power 
margins for voltage regulation, an additional variant 
was developed to investigate the impact of additional 
dynamic voltage support provided by new synchronous 
condensers distributed across the transmission network. 
A total of eight 250 MVA synchronous condensers were 
modelled in the base case, including the step-up trans­
former, according to the Spanish Network planning 
modification (Modificación de aspectos puntuales (MAP) 
2021 – 202632) approved on 14 July 2025. The dynamic 
model of the synchronous condensers and step-up trans­
formers was based on standard models from the library 
with typical parameters for the technology.
After these changes, a dynamic simulation was 
conducted for the same conditions as in the base case 
simulation. Figure 4-114 and Figure 4-115. show the 
Spain–France active power exchange and the frequency 
at the La Cereal 400 kV substation for the base case 
(blue), the case with eight new synchronous condensers 
(green), and the PMU measurements (red).
Similar to the previous analyses, the increased voltage 
control capabilities provided by the synchronous 
condensers create a safer situation to address the 
initial incidents, avoiding cascading generation trips 
and allowing the system to reach a stable operating 
point (as seen in the frequency and the Spain–France 
exchange) compared to the base case simulation and 
PMU measurements.

4.4.3.2.2	
Role of Defence System Effects on Voltage Transient
This simulation aims to investigate the effect of blocking 
underfrequency load-shedding protections when volt­
ages rise above a critical threshold. During the event, 
load-shedding protections were activated to mitigate 
the active power imbalance and slow the frequency drop 
caused by the cascade generation tripping. However, an 
undesired effect was the reduction of litne loading and, 
consequently, the voltage increases at the nearby buses 
as lines became increasingly capacitive. To perform this 
variant, the load-shedding dynamic models were deac­
tivated. Figure 4-116 and Figure 4-117 show the Spain–
France active power exchange and the frequency at the 
La Cereal 400 kV substation for the base case (blue), the 
case with the load-shedding protection blocked (green), 
and the PMU measurements (red). 
Initially, the simulations are identical, and the blocking 
of load-shedding protections does not affect the initial 
disconnection of generation with the import increase 
and the subsequent loss of synchronism. However, 
around t = 5 s (12:33:21.000), the simulations begin 
to diverge. The simulation with load-shedding protec­
tions blocked shows a significantly faster decrease of 
frequency, reaching 47 Hz several seconds earlier than 
observed in the PMU measurements. These results 
indicate that, despite having a potentially negative 
effect on increasing voltage due to the reduction of line 
loading, the activation of load-shedding protections 
has a significantly positive effect on system frequency, 
reducing the active power imbalance and mitigating 
the frequency drop.

4.4.3.4	
Conclusions Regarding Voltage Stability simulations
The voltage stability was investigated with a set of 
simulations aimed at obtaining the system sensitivity to 
different voltage control strategies.
The simulations demonstrated that, at time of the inci­
dent, the voltage of the Spanish power system was sensi­
tive to any variations — whether related to exchanges 
with Portugal, France or Morocco, TSO-to-DSO flows, 
or generation below 50 MW — resulting in significant 
voltage fluctuations.
According to the results, the real capacity of the system 
to manage a certain excess of capacitive reactive power 
is the key point that explains the loss of voltage control.
In detail, the results of simulations can be summarised 
as follows:
»	exchanges between Spain, Marocco and France 
confirm that voltage is strongly sensitive to the 
power flows
»	exchange with DSOs shows a more evident 
sensitivity on voltage than the previous one
»	reclose some transmission lines, which is a 
correct and effective maneuver to reduce oscil­
lations, had the side effect to generate addi­
tional reactive power, worsening the voltage 
profiles
»	automatic connection of shunt reactors 
during the voltage rise would have helped 
maintaining voltage within acceptable limits. 
By limiting the voltage increase, this action 
prevents further disconnections and therefore 
avoids cascading effects that could ultimately 
lead to a blackout.
»	Increase the quantity of reactive power 
absorbed by synchronous machines (enlarging 
capabilities into the simulations to obtain 
a wider support by generators or adding to 
the rotating park synchronous condensers) 
confirms a good control of voltage, avoiding 
the rise out of control. That could be obtained 
adding more synchronous generators or 
in future, more synchronous condensers/­
STATCOMs, enabling voltage regulation by static 
generators
4.4.3.5	
System Defence Performance
This section evaluates the performance of low-frequency demand disconnection (LFDD) in the Iberian Peninsula 
power system during the incident.
4.4.3.5.1	
TSO Level
Red Eléctrica provided the oscillographic records for all 
load-shedding relays installed at transmission network 
substations. 
A detailed analysis of this information enables accurate 
verification of the load shed at transmission positions for 
each step, as well as identification of the exact instant 
of the trip, the amount of load shed, and the frequency 
value at the moment of pickup and tripping of the 
load-shedding relays. 
Likewise, an exhaustive assessment of the behaviour of 
the load-shedding relays was carried out, confirming 
that in all cases, the relays operated correctly according 
to their intended design, in line with the pickup thresh­
olds and time delays established for each step of the 
load-shedding scheme. 
The blocking function in case of reverse active power 
flow was activated as designed in those LFDD relays 
installed on the transmission network that require it. 
Therefore, it can be concluded that the performance of 
the LFDD at transmission level positions was correct and 
in accordance with the design.

===== PAGE 317 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  317 
Figure 4-122:  Example of oscillographic record.
4.4.3.5.2	
DSO Level
The DSOs provided the load-shedding demand data asso­
ciated with each step at each distribution network posi­
tion. Some also provided the instant of disconnection. 
The overall assessment of the LFDD was satisfactory. In 
general, no deviations from the applicable requirements 
were observed in the LFDD operation by DSOs. Never­
theless, an analysis of the information received by DSOs 
revealed certain limitations that may serve as a starting 
point for potential improvements in future evaluations 
of the system defence plan:
»	Oscillograph records from every individual 
load-shedding relay that operated were 
not provided to the Expert Panel, making it 
impossible to thoroughly verify their individual 
performance. 
»	The number of LFDD relays with blocking 
functionality for reverse active power flow 
in the distribution network is very limited, as 
this requirement has only applied since the 
Demand Connection Network Code came into 
force in 2016.
»	Most DSOs reported having very limited means 
to detect the volume of unwanted disconnec­
tion of DER less than 1 MW along with loads, 
due to their volatile influence over time. This is 
especially important for selecting feeders with 
lower DER penetration to avoid disconnecting 
generation.

===== PAGE 318 =====
318  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
4.4.3.6	
Conclusion Regarding LFDD Performance
LFDD is a system protection scheme designed to auto­
matically shed predefined loads when the system 
frequency falls below set thresholds. Its main objective 
is to prevent a widespread system collapse by rapidly 
reducing demand to restore frequency and stop its 
decline. 
In this incident, although the LFDD scheme operated 
according to design, its contribution was not sufficient to 
preserve system stability under the specific conditions of 
this event. The incident was not just caused by a gener­
ation deficit and the resulting frequency drop, but was 
accompanied by a widespread overvoltage scenario, 
both prior to the activation of the LFDD and during the 
load disconnection following the activation of all steps, 
as explained in previous sections. 
During the period in which the underfrequency 
load-shedding steps were activated, it was observed 
that, despite fully shedding the demand associated 
with each step, the system frequency continued to drop, 
because the generators were simultaneously tripping 
due to overvoltage. In addition, the voltages continued 
to rise for two reasons. 
On one hand, the load shedding reduced currents, 
causing voltage drops in line and cable sections, resulting 
in a higher residual voltage and higher reactive power 
generated by the transmission lines. On the other hand, 
the simultaneous disconnection of generators reduced 
active voltage control and reactive power absorption, 
resulting in higher residual voltage.
LFDD was designed and activated to protect the system 
against frequency drops in line with the applicable 
requirements. However, it was not intended to stabilise 
the system under conditions of widespread overvoltage 
across the network. 
Simulations indicate that if the LFDD relays had been 
blocked due to overvoltages – which means no load 
shedding for frequencies below 49.0 Hz – the frequency 
would have collapsed even faster than in reality. The 
actual LFDD scheme – without blocking in case of over­
voltages – did not worsen the outcome. On the contrary, 
it managed to delay the system collapse, which could 
unfortunately not be avoided due to other effects for 
which the LFDD scheme was not designed.

Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  319 
4.5	
Management of alarms related to voltage
The provisions applicable to voltage control and reactive power management under the Commission 
Regulation (EU) 2017/1485 of 2 August 2017 establishing a guideline on electricity transmission system 
operation (SO GL) provide as follows: 
30	
The applicable national regulation in Spain is the PO 1.4, in Portugal is the “Manual de Procedimentos da Gestão Global do Sistema do setor elétrico” (MPGGS) 
and in France is the Code de conduite du réseau de transport C1-1 - French Regulation: Décret No. 2003-588 Article 2 - EU Regulation: No. 2017/1485 Article 27 
and Annex II Table 2.
31	
In accordance with Article 29 (5) of Regulation (EU) 2017/1485.
»	Each TSO is responsible for maintaining voltage 
at transmission system connection points 
within the defined steady-state ranges during 
normal operating conditions, as provided 
in Article 27 Obligations of all TSOs regarding 
voltage limits. 
»	If the voltage at any connection point deviates 
from these ranges, the TSO must implement 
appropriate voltage control and reactive power 
management actions to restore compliance, 
in accordance with Article 29 Obligations of 
all TSOs concerning voltage control and reactive 
power management in system operation.
In real-time operation, alarms are configured to signal 
when operational thresholds for loading or voltage 
are reached, as defined by established procedures and 
practices. When the measured voltage at a substation 
exceeds the specified threshold, an alarm is displayed 
on the dispatcher’s interface and may trigger additional 
alerts in the control room (e. g., audible signals such as 
a bell).
Subsequently, alarm management practices were 
analysed within the control centres of TSOs, DSOs and 
generation facilities. In addition, an analysis was 
conducted of the voltage alarms received from 12:00:00 
to 12:33:17 at the control centres, and the voltage 
manual control actions taken by operators.
4.5.1	
Alarms at the TSO level
This section addresses alarm management within the 
TSO control centres of RTE, REN and Red Eléctrica.
TSO control centres receive real-time alarms in their 
SCADA systems whenever voltage levels at transmis­
sion grid nodes approach or exceed the voltage limits 
defined by the applicable requirements on national30 
and European levels respectively, based on measured 
data collected at intervals ranging from one minute to 
seconds. These thresholds are customised to meet each 
TSO’s voltage control requirements, such as applying 
stricter limits due to contracts with transmission-con­
nected consumers or producers or HV equipment, 
or based on node categorisation for voltage moni­
toring or alignment with the TSO–DSO voltage control 
agreement.31

32	
Pilot nodes for voltage control are nodes distributed throughout the transmission network and represent the voltage proﬁle of each area. Pilot nodes for 
voltage agreement represent the voltage at the connection point between the TSO and the DSO. Border and near interconnections nodes represent the voltage 
close to interconnections.
In general, these voltage alarm thresholds remain 
constant across all system states, both in real-time opera­
tion and in operational planning. However, it is foreseen 
that temporary extended limits may be applied under 
exceptional circumstances, such as during top-down 
restoration strategies for very short periods of time, or, 
in the case of RTE, under N 1 conditions as specified in the 
applicable regulations.
The TSOs have also implemented additional tools for 
voltage control monitoring:
»	RTE provides a voltage heat map that issues 
audible and visual alarms when under- or over­
voltage limits are exceeded, with a geograph­
ical representation.
»	REN uses a dedicated SCADA display showing 
all busbar voltage values in a tabular format. 
When limits are exceeded, the corresponding 
values blink in red.
»	Red Eléctrica operates complementary screens 
that display measurements from generation 
units with dynamic voltage control capability, 
the status of discrete elements, and voltage 
trends at pilot nodes in each zone. Operators 
can also access zonal maps displaying voltage 
values received from each substation. When 
the first level limits are exceeded, the corre­
sponding values turn red.
The TSOs have simulation tools capable of performing 
N and N-1 analyses in real time. RTE and Red Eléctrica 
analyse short-term scenarios to anticipate random reac­
tive power losses caused by any element tripping.
For alarm management, the TSOs primarily rely on 
SCADA data rather than PMU data or other sources. In 
the absence of direct measurements or if necessary for 
specific tools, estimated or calculated data may be used.
Regarding alarm prioritisation, each TSO has imple­
mented its own approach using different classification 
methods, such as alarm levels, colour codes or audible 
or visual alerts, to help operators quickly identify and 
prioritise actions. Alarms function independently of the 
generator type connected to each node and are trig­
gered immediately once the threshold is exceeded. As 
shown in the defined thresholds, the alarm thresholds 
defined by RTE, REN and Red Eléctrica are stricter than 
the limits for remaining connected without damage or 
disconnection – under both steady-state and temporary 
conditions – applicable to generation connected to the 
transmission network, as defined by the applicable 
requirements (Sections 3.2.1.1 and 3.2.1.2). This ensures 
an operational margin in line with the applicable 
requirements. In RTE’s case, the starting time above the 
threshold is displayed.
Operators continuously monitor voltage levels and 
alarms to implement preventive measures before 
threshold limits are reached. If limits are exceeded, 
corrective actions are carried out in accordance with 
the applicable requirements, established based on, 
among others, national (TEN-101 and TEN-102) or 
regional instructions for RTE; operational handbooks and 
training documentation for REN, and national (PO 7.4) 
and European regulations (SO GL) and training docu­
mentation for Red Eléctrica. Voltage control actions are 
executed through SCADA systems, market platforms or by 
phone, depending on the measure to be applied. If any 
action affects the DSO network or a specific generator, 

===== PAGE 321 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  321 
Red Eléctrica informs the affected DSO or Generation 
Control Centre (GCC) in advance. When established by the 
applicable requirements or mutual agreement, certain 
actions, such as load transfers performed by the DSO or 
voltage and reactive power adjustments carried out by 
the GCC, are executed at the TSO’s request.
Each operator acts within its scope of responsibili­
ties: the TSO maintains transmission network voltage 
within the limits defined by the applicable require­
ments, the DSO ensures supply quality in the distribution 
network, and GCCs operate their generators to align 
with the requirements applicable to the voltage control, 
33	
For the purposes of this assessment, a targeted sample of relevant distributors – those connected to transmission network with a large volume of customers 
(> 100.000, in the case of DSOs connected to the Spanish electricity system) – was contacted. It should be noted that the Spanish electricity system comprises 
more than 300 distributors.
following TSO voltage instructions in the case of REN or 
RTE, or as established by the applicable requirements 
(PO 7.4 and RD 423/2014) in the case of Red Eléctrica.
When a TSO, DSO or GCC detects a voltage issue, they 
notify the need to coordinate the necessary actions or 
apply national procedures and agreements (such as TSO–
DSO voltage control agreements) under the TSO’s guid­
ance. Coordination in these cases can be undertaken by 
phone or via tools that link the different control centres.
4.5.2	
Alarms at the DSO level
This section contains the information that relevant 
distributors33 provided regarding the management of 
voltage alarms in their control centres. The DSO control 
centres receive alarms related to voltage levels in their 
respective distribution networks, with varying alarm 
thresholds among distributors.
The reported values and criteria are summarised below, 
whereby one DSO corresponds to the Portuguese elec­
tricity system, while the remaining ones belong to the 
Spanish electricity system:
»	DSO 1: Has two alarm levels, normally set at 
±1.05 p.u. and ±1.07 p.u. with respect to the 
operating voltage, indicating that these ranges 
may vary at certain points in the network.
»	DSO 2: Has three alarm levels for undervoltage 
and overvoltage, defined within the limits 
defined by the applicable requirements and 
adjustable according to the connected load, 
always below ±1.10 p.u. with respect to the 
nominal voltage.
»	DSO 3: Confirms the existence of voltage 
and reactive power alarms without speci­
fying thresholds. It indicates that these vary 
depending on the network area and are 
defined with sufficient tolerance to allow 
the necessary operations to keep voltage 
within the limits defined by the applicable 
requirements.
»	DSO 4: Has one alarm level for overvoltage 
(1.07 p.u. with respect to nominal voltage) 
and two levels for undervoltage (0.93 p.u. 
and 0.60 p.u. with respect to nominal voltage), 
applied uniformly.
»	DSO 5: Sets alarms at 1.04 p.u. from normal 
operating values for each transformer and 
busbar. In some cases, these thresholds are 
readjusted to meet the operational require­
ments of certain facilities.
DSOs do not specify whether these alarms are coor­
dinated with the trip thresholds of the generation 
connected to their network. Some also state that the 
generation connected to their network must align with 
the thresholds defined by the applicable requirements.
If alarm thresholds are exceeded, DSOs indicate that 
the primary solution to resolve voltage deviations is the 
on-load tap changer of their transformers (automatic 
or manual), while they also have capacitor banks. If the 
high-voltage side is significantly deviated, they contact 
the TSO to take appropriate actions or to apply the TSO–
DSO voltage control agreement at the interconnection 
point. In particular, the Portuguese DSO indicates that it 
may take additional actions, such as changing the reac­
tive power control mode or the setpoint of RfG-com­
pliant type B, C and D generators, as well as transferring 
or switching off loads. Additionally, DSO control centres 
have alarms for transformer tap status (extreme tap 
position). In one specific case, supervision has also been 
implemented for changes in short-term international 
exchange programmes between Spain and neigh­
bouring systems, due to their impact on regional voltage.

===== PAGE 322 =====
322  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
In general, DSO control centres have established alarm 
prioritisation based on purpose, generating both visual 
and audible alerts. These alarms are triggered based 
on information received through each control centre’s 
SCADA system.
Regarding the use of other tools, two DSOs describe the 
use of heat maps, real-time evolution graphs of elec­
trical magnitudes or graphical representations of these 
with applied colour codes. Additionally, one DSO reports 
that its control centre performs day-ahead contingency 
analyses.
4.5.3	
Alarms at the GCC level
This section presents the analysis of GCC responses 
regarding voltage control alarm management. The 
Expert Panel requested information from 12 control 
centres, selected as being the most representative, from 
which 10 responses were received: four from centres 
managing generation in Portugal and six in Spain.
Some GCCs have real-time voltage measurements 
through their SCADA systems, obtained from signals 
transmitted by local control units or connection nodes. In 
most cases, GCCs receive voltage alarms for conventional 
generation and hydro, but not for renewables.
Voltage-related alarms in GCCs are primarily triggered by 
the following causes:
»	Activation of protections associated with gener­
ating units (under/overvoltage trips), reported 
in four of the GCCs analysed.
»	In some cases, deviation of the reactive power 
delivery or voltage levels from the limits 
defined by the applicable requirements, as 
observed in five of the GCCs analysed.
»	Exceeding alert thresholds defined according 
to the protection settings of generating units, 
reported in one of the GCCs analysed.
In most control centres, the type of generation unit 
determines the criteria for voltage alarms and actions by 
control centre operators. For example, in conventional 
units, voltage is typically managed on site rather than 
via generator control centres. In the case of hydro plants, 
voltages are managed in the control centres. Renewable 
generation does not have voltage violations but rather 
alarms are raised in the case of over/under voltage trips.
Some control centres report no alarms for certain gener­
ators, as voltage control in these cases is performed 
locally. However, other GCCs implement multiple types of 
alarms. Typically, these criteria are applied consistently 
across all plants within the same technology.
Based on the type of alarm received, certain GCCs have 
indicated that operators may implement one of the 
following actions:
»	Restore the lost generator.
»	Request information or instructions from the 
relevant system operator.
»	Request information from the generator.
Each GCC has established its own alarm prioritisation 
based on mechanisms such as audible alarms, colour 
codes and flashing indicators, depending on criticality. 
In general, alarms are received through each control 
centre’s SCADA system.
Additionally, some GCCs indicate that if the operator 
identifies anomalous voltage values or any disturbance, 
they contact the TSO’s control centre to report the situ­
ation and, if necessary, adapt operations in accordance 
with the TSO’s instructions.

»	The number of voltage alarms was approx­

»	The deactivation of alarms is finalised only 
when the voltage leaves the ±2,5 kV deadband. 
This means that voltages dropped below the 
high-voltage alarm threshold or exceeded the

durations extracted from the alarm log.
»	Two of the analysed time intervals showed a 
significant number of alarm events triggered 
below the low-voltage alarm thresholds, with

which have no generation units connected.
–	 It should be noted that voltage alarm thresh­

levels approach the limits defined by the 
applicable requirements in Spain.
»	In the last two periods analyzed, the trans­

one alarm event represented approximately 
30 % and 35 % of the total nodes, respectively,

setting HVDC voltage setpoints) were effective 
in bringing voltage back within the alarming 
threshold within minutes in most cases (typi­
cally less than 5 minutes).
»	The manual corrective actions were carried 
out within humanly realistic time frames. The 
measured response times between the first 
recorded alarm exceeding the high-voltage 
alarm threshold and the execution of the first 
voltage control remedial action 1 min 33 s in the 
northern zone and 2 min 11 s in the southern 
zone take into account the time required for 
the operator to detect the alarm, analyse the 
issue, assess the most appropriate action while 
taking its impact into account, and implement 
it. In the final analysed period, Red Eléctrica’s 
dispatchers were unable to implement manual 
voltage control actions due to the very short 
duration of the event (38 seconds). In such 
timeframes, only dynamic voltage control – 
i. e., generator voltage regulation together 
with STATCOM and HVDC voltage control – can 
effectively mitigate voltage deviations.

»	Alarm log distribution exhibited clear zonal 
clustering: the southern and eastern zones 
repeatedly stood out for low-voltage alarm 
events, while the interior, southern and 
northern zones showed the greatest concen­
tration of high-voltage alarm episodes.
»	A non-trivial portion of alarms were triggered 
outside the transmission network, for which 
the TSO is not responsible for voltage control 
management. They were mainly registered 
in the south. Furthermore, it should be noted 
that not all non-transmission network nodes 
generate voltage alarms at Red Eléctrica’s 
control centres, so the actual number of alarm 
activations in the non-transmission network 
may have been higher than Red Eléctrica could 
observe.
4.5.10	 Conclusions from alarms recorded in REN’s control centre and their 
operational handling
»	The number of 400 kV voltage alarms exceeded 
the number of affected nodes because alarms 
are triggered per busbar and at two identical 
thresholds, leading to multiple alarms often 
referring to the same issue. No alarms at 220 kV 
were triggered during this period.
»	Within this interval, two consecutive periods 
were identified in which 10 and 14 under­
voltage alarms were recorded, reaching a 
minimum voltage value of 377.9 kV. This was 
followed by a third period with 56 overvoltage 
alarms, all above 420 kV and affecting a larger 
number of nodes compared with the previous 
undervoltage periods. Throughout the entire 
interval between 12:00 and 12:33:17, no 
voltage control actions were carried out by the 
control centre, as the alarms cleared within a 
few seconds and dispatchers are not expected 
to perform manual actions in such a short 
timeframe.
4.5.11	 Conclusions from alarms recorded in RTE’s control centre and their 
operational handling
Before 12:33:17, the voltage levels at the 225 and 400 kV 
RTE south-west substations were within normal limits, 
and no specific action was taken.
As a result of the tripping, the voltage values exceeding 
the thresholds were processed and recorded as expected 
in the tools (voltage heat map and SCADA).
4.5.12.	 Conclusions from alarms recorded in the analysed distribution 
control centre
»	During this period, a total of 4,150 alarms were 
recorded due to voltage levels exceeding the 
distributor’s voltage threshold, affecting 308 
nodes. The maximum recorded voltage was 
1.10 p.u. in the distribution network and 
1.11 p.u. at the 220 kV level, for which the DSO 
is not responsible for voltage control.
»	In the first interval, most alarms occurred at 
45 kV and 15 kV. In the second interval, while 
45 kV and 15 kV remained the most affected 
levels, there was a significant increase in alarms 
at 220 kV. In the third interval, the majority of 
alarms were concentrated at 220 kV and 45 kV.
»	Although these intervals coincide with periods 
during which voltage alarms exceeding high-
voltage thresholds were recorded in the trans­
mission network, in the first interval, both the 
duration and the number of affected nodes 
were considerably higher than those recorded 
in the transmission network.
»	No analysis has been conducted regarding the 
voltage control actions applied by the distrib­
utor during any of the three intervals.

4.5.13	 Conclusions from alarms recorded in the analysed generation 
control centre
»	The generation control centre recorded a total 
of 165 alarms related to voltage deviations 
from the nominal value, including 102 above 
nominal and 63 below nominal. These alarms 
were triggered in a small but recurring group 
of nodes, mainly in the southern and north­

»		The voltages below nominal occurred across 
two intervals, affecting the same six nodes, 
with minimum voltage values of 0.88 p.u. at 
the 11 kV level and 0.93 p.u. at the 132 kV level.
»	Voltages above the nominal value were 
recorded across three periods, affecting four 
to five nodes per interval, with maximum 
voltage values of 1.10 p.u. at the 45 kV level 
and 1.09 p.u. at the 220 kV level. Several of 
these nodes appeared repeatedly across 
different periods, indicating a notable level of 
recurrence.
»	These intervals correspond to the time frames 
in which voltage alarms were triggered in the 
transmission network.
4.5.14	 Summary from recorded voltage alarms and their 
operational handling
The high number of alarm logs recorded in Red ­Eléctrica’s 
control centres is explained by the alarm system’s config­
uration: multiple alarms were triggered at the same 
node, and several were recorded at nodes outside the 
transmission network, beyond the TSO’s voltage control 
responsibility.
Most voltage alarm events were triggered at values 
within the voltage limits defined by the applicable 
requirements, and most low-voltage alarms occurred 
during the oscillatory period. Before 12:33:17, only 
sporadic activations occurred at voltages above 435 kV 
(1.1 % of the total events above high voltage alarm 
thresholds) or below 375 kV (0.6 % all lowvoltage alarm 
threshold events) but cleared in a few seconds.
In the last two periods analyzed, about 30 % and 35 % of 
the transmission network nodes triggered at least one 
alarm event, whereas in the prior periods the propor­
tion was substantially lower, around 10 %. During the 
same time interval on the previous Monday, the share of 
transmission network nodes that activated at least one 
voltage alarm was only 2.5 %.
The dispatcher’s corrective actions restored voltage 
within thresholds within a few minutes. During the 
assessed period, between 12:25 and 12:28, the response 
times between the first alarm event above the high 
voltage threshold and the execution of the first reme­
dial voltage control action are considered operation­
ally reasonable, as they include the time needed for 
the operator to detect the alarm, analyse the issue and 
determine and implement the most appropriate action.
In the final analysed period, after 12:32, Red Eléctrica’s 
dispatchers were unable to implement manual voltage 
control actions due to the very short duration of the event 
(38 seconds). In such time frames, only dynamic voltage 
control can effectively mitigate voltage deviations.
With respect to the alarm events recorded in REN’s 
control centre, the number of 400 kV voltage alarms 
exceeded the number of affected nodes because alarms 
are triggered per busbar and at two identical thresholds. 
Throughout the entire timeframe, no manual voltage 
control actions were taken by the dispatchers, as the 
undervoltage alarms cleared within seconds and the 
short duration of the overvoltage final event prevented 
dispatchers from performing control actions.
The distribution control centre received only alarms 
associated with voltage levels exceeding the distribu­
tor’s established limits, coinciding with the time inter­
vals in which high voltage alarm threshold events were 
recorded in the transmission network. The duration of 
the events in the distribution network was longer than 
that observed in the transmission network.
The GCCs also recorded alarm events related to under- 
and over-nominal voltage values at a recurring group of 
nodes, corresponding to the same time periods during 
which voltage alarms were triggered in the transmission 
network.
Area of attention/improvement:The Expert Panel 
suggests that all TSOs undertake any developments 
that they deem necessary in the design of their alarm 
system and associated operators’ responses to further 
enhance their ability to detect and address any relevant 
phenomena.

4.6	
Root Cause Tree
The description of the events that occurred and led to the 
blackout on 28 April 2025, as detailed in chapters 2 and 
3 of this report, combined with the technical analyses 
described in the sub-chapters 4.1 to 4.5, allow the Expert 
Panel to identify the main elements that caused the inci­
dent and the relationships between them. The result is 
the Root Cause Tree that is presented in Figure 4-124. 
The methodology applied to find the proper relation 
between the elements of the incident is the so-called 
Root Cause Analysis (RCA), which is a method of prob­
lem-solving used for identifying the root causes of faults 
or problems. This methodology systematically asks the 
question “why?” an event happened until all causes are 
identified, starting in the present case from the question 
“Why was there a system blackout on 28 April 2025?”
The methodology followed here is loosely based on the 
Five Whys exercise which is a questioning technique for 
going beyond symptoms of problems to identify the 
underlying or root causes of a problem. It follows several 
logical steps: 
»	State the problem as accurately and briefly as 
possible; 
»	List the possible causes of the problem by 
asking the question “Why?” or “Why did that 
happen?”; 
»	For each of the causes, again ask the question 
“Why?”, and list answers again; 
»	Continue this process at least 5 times or until 
having reached the source of the problem, the 
lowest level; 
»	This level is where something can be done 
about avoiding the event in the future. 
The identified causes can then be analysed further 
to see whether this is only a circumstance which 
­eventually contributed to the chain of events or if the 
concerned cause shall be subject to improvement 
and ­recommendations. It must be stressed that not all 
causes will identify an issue; some causes might be 
­unavoidable, like for instance the fact that load varies 
with voltage, they will not be catalogued as a cause 
requiring further improvements. 
In Figure 4-124, the blue boxes refer to the causes for 
which the panel considers it useful to make one or more 
recommendations aimed at improving the resilience 
of the European electricity system. These recommen­
dations are explained in Chapter 9 of this report. The 
number of the recommendation related to a specific 
cause is mentioned next to the box describing the cause. 
The structure of the tree is divided into two parts and 
the chain of the events can be explained accordingly. 
The bottom part of the tree shows the identified issues 
(several of these are structural, some of them coinci­
dental or event-driven) which contributed to the fast 
voltage increase that occurred from around 12:32:00 
onwards. From these identified elements the tree high­
lights with blue colour those ones which can be influ­
enced by proper measures and subject to recommen­
dations. The upper part of the tree represents the last 
sequence of the event which relates to system defence 
and final steps before the blackout. Some of these 
elements are also subject of recommendations which 
are also highlighted with blue colour.

Although the role of the different elements of the tree is explained as part of a detailed technical analysis in the chapters 4.1 – 4.5, some further explanation on 
what is the relation of those elements to each other and how they contributed to the blackout is necessary due to the complexity of the incident. The order of 
the list below as well as the arrangement of the boxes and branches in the root cause tree do not reflect the importance of these key factors.
1.	The reactive power output of 
several conventional generators 
reached Q-reference in less than 
75 % of the samples (hourly).
The Operational Procedure 7.4 (2000) 
applicable in Spain on the day of the 
incident determined the minimum reac­
tive power contribution (absorbing or 
injecting depending on the voltage) by 
large conventional generators when the 
voltage is outside of a margin around the 
voltage reference set by the TSO. Based 
on the result of performed evaluations 
of SCADA-data of RE several conven­
tional units provided less reactive power 
support than the calculated values based 
on the procedure without prejudice to 
any potential derogations. More reactive 
power absorption would have led to a 
decrease in voltage. 
This factor contributed to a non-effective 
voltage control by conventional genera­
tors, especially in some regions. 
2.	The reactive power framework 
for conventional generators did 
not provide for explicit criteria 
concerning dynamic behaviour 
and there were no economic 
consequence if the requirements 
regarding voltage control were 
not met.
The framework in place the day of 
the incident did not include explicit 
­specifications for the dynamic voltage 
control. Moreover, the Procedure 
prescribed penalties in the event that 
generators would not comply with 
the procedure; however, the penalties 
were not applicable in practice, since 
the economic scheme required by the 
Operating Procedure had not been 
developed by the designated entity. 
The existence of a financial scheme 
could have incentivised the generators 
to implement improvements in voltage 
control performance.
This factor contributed to a non-effective 
voltage control by conventional genera­
tors, especially in some regions. 
3.	RES power plants follow fixed 
power factor. 
A fixed power factor control mode means 
that the reactive power contribution is 
inherently proportional to active power 
injection. RES plants in Spain followed 
this mode. 
First, this meant that for every active 
power change (e. g. schedule change) 
the generators injected into the system a 
proportional reactive power change (and 
hence a voltage change);
Secondly, fixed-power-factor-mode 
resources provided no reactive power 
support that would compensate voltage 
fluctuations, since their reactive power 
output did not respond to conditions in 
the grid. 
4.	Design of voltage control of local 
generation networks (behind 
connection point) not aligned 
with system needs.
The design of some non-regulated 
local generation networks in Spain 
(incl. voltage control/disconnection 
settings) was not aligned with system 
needs, meaning, among others, a more 
challenging voltage control and higher 
risk of disconnection. Voltage control in 
such networks was insufficient in some 
cases, due to a combination of fixed 
power factor control mode of generators, 
fast generation ramps, physically slower 
changes of tap-changing transformers.
5.	No limitation on ramping for 
generators with fixed power factor. 
Fast decrease of active power infeed of 
generators with fixed power factor lead 
naturally to a reduction of reactive power 
absorption. Thus, fast ramping down 
of such units resulted in fast increase of 
voltage as well.
6.	Shunt reactors are operated manu­
ally – requiring decision-making 
and processing time.
Shunt reactors in Spain were operated 
manually. The time needed to manu­
ally connect shunt reactors is longer 
than what is needed when voltage 
changes very fast. Due to the speed 
at which voltage rose after 12:32:00, 
disconnected shunt reactors could not 
be connected in time due to the needed 
processing time for manual switching.

===== PAGE 334 =====
334  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
7.	Many overvoltage disconnection protection 
settings diverged from applicable requirements 
or were not aligned with system needs.
Some generation units (or connecting transformers 
or lines) disconnected at their voltage level before 
the voltage disconnection conditions at the transmis­
sion connection point and time delay conditions were 
met. This led to a loss of absorption of reactive power, 
resulting in a steep increase in voltage. 
8. Converter-driven instability and interaction with 
other generators in the same area
A converter-driven instability combined with interaction 
with other generators in the same area led to forced 
oscillations which endangered the system as frequency 
and voltage can severely fluctuate then within seconds. 
9.	Absence of PSS on some large units and 
­insufficient actions by existing ones.
Power System Stabilisers (PSS) installed on generators 
side are able to damp oscillations. The more PSS installed 
the better oscillations can be mitigated. Not all large 
generation units were equipped with PSSs and the 
action of the existing PSSs was insufficient to damp the 
oscillations.
10.  First (forced) Oscillation of 0.63 Hz and second 
(inter-area) Oscillation of 0.2 Hz
Oscillations are a major threat to system security. 
Thus, initiating mitigation measures in order to damp 
­oscillations has highest priority from operational 
perspective. On the day of the incident, the dispatchers 
implemented mitigation measures during both 
­oscillatory episodes, which successfully damped the 
oscillations but contributed to increase the voltage.
11.  Voltage-related disconnections of small 
embedded generators < 1 MW
Based on data of two inverter companies, and subject to 
the assumptions and simplifications explained in chapter 
4.3, it can be considered that there was a significant 
number of overvoltage trips of small PV units connected 
to the low-voltage DSO grids. These units tripped during 
periods of high voltage ramps in the transmission 
network but also during and around periods of high 
voltages and voltage fluctuations (slow/fast changes, 
oscillations).
This led to changes in load flow pattern of the transmis­
sion grid resulting in voltage changes. 
12.  Spanish 400 kV grid operated at a wider 
voltage range than in other EU countries, 
enabled by the specific provisions applicable 
to Spain.
Operating the system with a voltage range 380 – 435 kV, 
while generators were to remain connected up to 435 kV 
or 440 kV (depending on commissioning date) meant 
that the voltage margin was low or non-existent. 
13.  Activation of system defence plan in 
ES/PT – pump shedding/load shedding.
Load and pump shedding as part of the system defence 
plan aim to reduce the consumption of active power 
in order to stop and restore frequency drops. When 
­disconnecting grid users, that absorb reactive power 
at the same time, it naturally increases the voltage. 
Thus, the activated load shedding helped the system 
to ­stabilise frequency, but on the other hand some 
­automatic disconnections, e. g. pump power plants 
absorbing reactive power at time of disconnection, have 
intensified the overvoltage problem. 
14.  Despite load shedding, frequency decreases 
in ES/PT due to cascade of overvoltage and 
underfrequency disconnections of generators 
in ES/PT.
As the effect of further loss of generators due to over­
voltage was higher than loss of load due to activated 
load shedding, frequency continued to decrease until 
system totally collapsed and blackout occurred.

5	
RESTORATION PROCESS 
The objective of this chapter is to explain the restoration process in the systems 
affected by the incident, namely the Portuguese and Spanish systems. In the case 
of the French system, the incident only impacted a local area, as described in 
Section 5.4. 
This chapter is divided into ten sections:
5.1	 Preconditions and strategies for the restoration 
process
5.2	 The restoration sequences in the Spanish system
5.3	 The restoration sequences in the Portuguese system
5.4	 French local area restoration by RTE
5.5	 Generation and load recovery
5.6	 Steps after system restoration
5.7	 Market restoration
5.8	 Behaviour of distributed energy resources and load 
during restoration
5.9	 Voice communication and remote control problems 
during restoration
5.10	Conclusion 
5.1	
Preconditions and strategies for the restoration process 
Restoring electrical grids in continental Europe after the 
occurrence of a significant disruption is a complex and 
coordinated process. TSOs work collaboratively in accord­
ance with Regulation (EU) 2017/2196, which sets out the 
Network Code on Electricity Emergency and Restoration 
(hereinafter NC ER), to re-establish electricity supplies 
through a mixture of “top-down” and “bottom-up” 
approaches. The top-down approach utilises voltage 
from neighbouring, healthy parts of the network, while 
the bottom-up approach relies on the black-start capa­
bility of power plants. Black-start capability enables 
certain power plants to start up independently without 
any external power supply, which is vital for gradual 
restoration when no external voltage is available.
5.1.1	
Red Eléctrica preconditions and strategies for the restoration process
The restoration process in Spain used a combination of 
top-down and bottom-up restoration strategies. For the 
top-down strategy, support was activated through the 
neighbouring countries, creating three zones with stable 
frequency and voltage that gradually increased and 
subsequently synchronised with the remaining areas. 
Specifically, the following supports were activated: 
»	Support from France via the interconnections 
through the País Vasco
»	Support from France via one of the 
­interconnections through Cataluña
»	Support from Morocco via one of the 
­interconnections through Andalucía
In the bottom-up strategy, implemented in parallel, 
re-energisation was initiated using hydropower plants 
(HPP) with black-start capability. 
The restoration plan for the Spanish peninsular (i. e. 
mainland) electrical system divides the network into 
seven specific areas, as shown in Figure 5-1. Each area 
contains at least two HPPs with black-start capability, 
with one serving as backup to the other, in line with the 
applicable requirements.

5.1.2	
REN: preconditions and strategies for the restoration process 
In Portugal, the “Plano Nacional de Reposição de 
Serviço” (“National Service Restoration Plan”) was acti­
vated. This procedure sets out the restoration strategies 
to be adopted following a generalised blackout of the 
Portuguese system. The strategies used differ depending 
on whether the generalised shutdown is national 
(top-down restoration, with support from the Spanish 
system) or Iberian (bottom-up restoration, without 
support from the Spanish system). 
In line with the applicable requirements, the Portuguese 
system has two power plants with black-start capa­
bility, one serving as backup to the other. The National 
Service Restoration Plan provides for the restoration of 
the Portuguese system from one of these power plants, 
or from the start-up of both, depending on operational 
conditions.
The restoration was started by the two power plants with 
black-start system capability in Portugal (the bottom-up 
strategy): the Combined Cycle Gas Turbine Powerplant 
(CCGT) 1-Norte, located near the Oporto area, and HPP 
1-Centro, near Lisbon. 
To restore the system as quickly as possible, the dispatch 
centre operators (located in Sacavém) and the network 
operation centre operators (located in Vermoim) were 
divided into two teams: the first team was in charge of 
establishing an electrical island with HPP 1-Centro, and 
the second team was in charge of establishing an elec­
trical island with CCGT 1-Norte.
In a phone call at 12:34, it was verified with Red Eléc­
trica that the blackout had affected the entire Iberian 
Peninsula.
At 12:38, the Portuguese system state was changed from 
normal to blackout in the EAS. At 17:04, it was changed to 
the restoration state.
Figure 5-1: Specific restoration plans for the Spanish system – Red Eléctrica

5.1.3	
RTE: preconditions and strategies for the restoration process 
There was only one 63 kV substation (SS) without voltage 
on the RTE grid (Arriosse), as shown in Figure 5-2. This 
had a limited impact on customers, as by 12:49 they 
were already being supplied via the DSO network. 
Consequently, the restoration plan was not activated, 
and this SS was re-energised at 13:57.
The nuclear power plant that tripped also had a limited 
impact. The restoration plan was therefore not activated, 
and the plant was re-energised on the next day, 29 April, 
at 16:15.

Red Eléctrica control centres. Additionally, some of these 
distribution companies experienced issues in receiving 
telemetry and remote-control signals at their facilities.

and HPPs were progressively connected to the system.

Bottom-up restoration of the Extremadura 1 island in Spain
»	At 12:55 on 28/4/2025, HPP Extremadura 1 was started 
up using its black-start capability, to supply auxiliary 
services to a nuclear power plant and stabilise the load

power higher than the load in the island at the moment 
of synchronisation. The DSO in this area was not able to 
increase the load in time (probably due to autonomous 
reconnection of a small RCW < 1 MW).

5.2.4	
Top-down restoration of the Southern zone in Spain 
»	At 13:04 on 28/4/2025, voltage was received from 
Morocco, initiating the restoration of the Southern zone. 
»	At 14:27, the load in the Southern zone supplied from 
Morocco had reached approximately 55 MW when an 
underfrequency relay tripped the cable at 49.50 Hz, as 
shown in Figure 5-15.
»	The under-frequency situation at 14:27 was due to an 
imbalance in the power system of Morocco, since there 
was no additional load increase in the Spanish system 
at that moment.
»	At 14:34, the network energisation from the 400 kV 
Tarifa SS was restarted to enable voltage supply to the 
thermal groups in the Southern area of Spain.
»	The frequency in the Moroccan system, including the 
Southern island of Spain, was very volatile, because 
the link between Morocco and the large continental 
European system was not available at that time.
»	At 19:32, the L-400 kV Almaraz–C. Rodrigo was switched 
on, synchronising the Southern zone with the Northern 
zone.
»	The Expert Panel recommends to the TSOs of Spain 
and Morocco that they investigate the possibilities for 
temporarily changing the under-frequency threshold 
on the interconnector during the initial steps of the 
top-down restoration scenario to a less conservative 
value, equal to (or a few millihertz above) the first 
load-shedding frequency threshold in the Moroccan 
system. It also recommends that they provide for the 
possibility of switching back to the original frequency 
threshold when the Spanish system is reconnected to 
the Continental European system.

5.2.5	
Bottom-up restoration of the East Asturias island in Spain 
»	At 13:06 on 28/4/2025, unit 2 of HPP East Asturias was 
started up using its black-start capability, to energise 
a 132 kV distribution system in the East Asturias area. 
Figure 5-16 shows the active and reactive power 
exchange between unit 2 and the island grid.
»	At 13:23, unit 2 of HPP East Asturias was tripped by an 
under-frequency protection at 49.50 Hz, causing the 
collapse of the East Asturias electrical island.
»	This frequency drop corresponded to an increase in 
active power production by unit 2 of HPP East Asturias, 
most probably due to a load increase at that moment in 
the distribution system. The exact size of the load step 
could not be identified from the recordings.
»	The setting of the under-frequency protection to 
disconnect the production unit at a threshold of 49.50 Hz 
deviate from the applicable requirements under the 
Spanish operational procedure, which prescribes that 
the underfrequency protection of generation facilities 
must be coordinated with the frequency-based load-
shedding system. This means that production facilities 
may only disconnect from the grid if the frequency falls 
below 48 Hz, with a minimum delay of 3 seconds. 
»	The Expert Panel regrets that neither the operator of 
the production unit nor the DSO that was in charge 
of operating the distribution system in East Asturias 
were able to provide recorded measurements of the 
frequency in the island during the restoration period. 
The Expert Panel therefore recommends improving 
observability for TSOs and DSOs of any production 
and storage facilities involved in scenarios for the 
bottom-up restoration of distribution systems.

5.2.6	
Bottom-up restoration of the Galicia island in Spain 
»	At 13:26 on 28/4/2025, unit 1 of HPP Galicia 1 was 
started up using its black-start capability, initiating the 
Galicia electrical island, which was designed to supply 
load in Galicia and critical loads, and to energise the 
auxiliary services of several thermal power plants 
(TPPs).
»	With the progressive creation of the black-start island 
and the connection of multiple loads, unit 3 of another 
hydropower plant, HPP Galicia 2, was synchronised at 
approximately 16:02; this unit was also intended to 
absorb reactive power.
»	Due to insufficient frequency control by unit 1 of 
HPP Galicia 1 (see Figure 5-17), which could not be 
resolved upon request by the TSO, frequency control 
was switched to unit 3 of HPP Galicia 2 at 16:11. Unit 1 
of HPP Galicia 1 was assigned a fixed active power 
setpoint.
»	At 16:18, unit 3 of HPP Galicia 2 was tripped by the 
overexcitation protection (ANSI 24), also known as 
“Volt-over-Hertz (V/Hz)” protection. Prior to this, a 
brief increase in grid voltage was recorded, indicating 
a deficiency in voltage regulation, possibly caused by 
the activation of the under-excitation limiter on unit 3 
of HPP Galicia 2, or by a manual voltage regulation 
malfunction. After the trip, the plant operator of HPP 
Galicia 2 informed the TSO that a single unit at the plant 
could not control voltage and frequency at the same 
time. Unit 1 of HPP Galicia 1 took over additional active 
power injection, thereby initially stabilising the island.
»	At 16:27, unit 2 of HPP Galicia 2 was synchronised first, 
with the aim that it would take over frequency control 
from unit 1 of HPP Galicia 1. 
»	At 17:46, unit 3 of HPP Galicia 2 was synchronised, with 
a defined active power setpoint and voltage regulation.

»	At 18:11, unit 1 of HPP Galicia 1 was tripped due to 
power reversal protection. According to Figure 5-17, 
the synchronisation of unit 3 of HPP Galicia 2 led to a 
reduction in the active power output of unit 1 of HPP 
Galicia 1. This indicates issues with the active power-
frequency control in unit 1 of HPP Galicia 1, as the 
assigned fixed active power setpoint could not be 
maintained.
»	At around 18:17, the DSO informed the TSO that, due 
to a remote-control problem, no further loads could 
be connected in the Galicia island. The only remaining 
option for expanding the grid island, in the absence 
of any additional loads, was synchronisation with 
a neighbouring part of the system that was already 
energised.
»	Prior to the synchronisation attempt, around 18:40, 
several transmission lines were disconnected to reduce 
the reactive power absorption of the HPPs. After the 
disconnection, voltage variations appeared, probably 
due to an unstable behaviour in the AVR of the HPPs. 
During the oscillation, at around 19:15, a transmission 
line was connected, and units 2 and 3 of HPP Galicia 2 
tripped due to an overvoltage event.
»	With this, the Galicia electrical island had completely 
collapsed. Due to the proximity of voltage from the 
Northern zone, it was decided not to restart the island.
5.2.7	
Bottom-up restoration of the Levante island in Spain 
»	The restoration plans (PRS-0-003 “Restoration of 
Levante Zone” and PRS-0-010 “Supply of nuclear power 
plants auxiliary services”) provide for the creation of 
two separate islands:
–	 Island 1: use unit 1 of HPP Levante 1 with black-start 
capability to energise one busbar (“busbar 1”) in the 
nearby 400 kV substation and further energise the rest 
of the Levante zone. Additionally, this group would be 
used to supply the auxiliary services of power plant 
HPP Levante 2 in order to connect more groups to this 
Levante island.
–	 Island 2: use unit 2 of HPP Levante 1 with black-start 
capability to energise another busbar (“busbar 2”) in 
the same nearby 400 kV substation, to energise the 
auxiliary services of the NPP in the northern Levante 
area. 
»	At 13:06 on 28/4/2025, unit 1 of HPP Levante 1 was 
started up using its black-start capability. According to 
the producer, this group supplied the auxiliary services 
of the nearby HPP Levante 2, through a 20 kV link. This 
went on until 29 April, with no trips or incidents.
»	At 13:52, unit 2 of HPP Levante 1 was started up using 
its black-start capability, initiating the Levante electrical 
island, which was designed to energise the auxiliary 
services of the NPP in the northern Levante area. 
»	At 14:02, the 400 kV/66 kV transformer at the nuclear 
power plant was energised at nominal voltage. Unit 2 
of HPP Levante 1 was able to withstand the transformer 
inrush current. However, although a soft start 
re-energisation procedure was foreseen, the operators 
of the TSO and the producer finally agreed with the 
nuclear power plant to energise the transformer at 
nominal value.
»	At 14:08, the producer was requested by the TSO 
to connect unit 1 of HPP Levante 1 to “busbar 1” of 
the nearby 400 kV substation to create island 1. For 
unknown reasons, the high voltage breaker of this 
group could not be closed, meaning that “busbar 1” 
remained without voltage.
»	At 14:36 and 14:50, the producer tried to energise 
“busbar 1” by closing the high voltage breaker of unit 2 
of the nearby HPP Levante 2, which was started using 
auxiliary power from unit 1 of HPP Levante 1. Both 
attempts were unsuccessful, leaving “busbar 1” at zero 
voltage.
»	At 14:54, the producer tried unsuccessfully to energise 
“busbar 1” by closing the high voltage breaker of unit 1 
of HPP Levante 2, leaving “busbar 1” still at zero voltage.
»	At 15:19, due to the unsuccessful attempts to energise 
“busbar 1” from the 3 above-mentioned units, the 
TSO decided to close the busbar coupler between 
“busbar 1” and “busbar 2”, with the aim of continuing 
the restoration process to the rest of the Levante zone. 
Busbar 2 was already energised from unit 2 of HPP 
Levante 1. From this point onwards, the TSO progressed 
the restoration with one island instead of two separate 
islands.

»	At 15:29, the TSO energised a 40 km 400 kV overhead 
line, causing unit 2 of HPP Levante 1 to increase reactive 
power absorption from 11 Mvar to 45 Mvar, as shown 
in Figure 5-18. The black-start unit initially remained 
stable after this line connection. 
»	The energisation of the 400 kV line at 15:29 caused the 
voltage at the nearby 400 kV substation to increase to 
452 kV, as shown in Figure 5-19.
»	At 16:00, another network component in the 
distribution grid was connected, leading to a further 
increase of reactive power absorption by unit 2 of HPP 
Levante 1 (from 45 to 50 Mvar) and a further voltage 
increase (up to 455 kV).

»	At 16:03, unit 2 of HPP Levante 1 tripped, due to the 
action of the “Volt-over-Hertz” (V/Hz) protection set 
at 1.1 p.u., losing the Levante electrical island. The 
generator was no longer able to absorb more reactive 
power and the UEL (Under Excitation Limit) was 
activated. The reactive power absorption limitation 
raised the voltage level and the generator tripped on 
the V/Hz function.
»	At 16:30 and at 16:43, two new attempts were made to 
create the Levante electrical island from HPP Levante 1 
unit 2, but the unit tripped each time due to Volt-over-
Hertz protection.
»	At 17:23, the nearby 400 kV substation was energised 
from the Eastern zone, and at 17:59, HPP Levante 1 
unit 2 was connected to it. After synchronisation, 
damped voltage oscillations were observed at the 
nearby 400 kV substation.
»	The TSO and the producer are currently reviewing the 
restoration plan for the Levante area and clarifying the 
technical possibilities of power plants with black-start 
capability.
»	In general, the Expert Panel recommends that HPPs 
are started at voltages under the nominal value, as 
stated in the restoration plans, to allow the operation 
of the 400 kV lines at reduced voltage. This would limit 
reactive power production by the grid elements, and 
avoid activation of the V/Hz machine protection during 
the first restoration steps.
5.2.8	
Bottom-up restoration of the Duero 2 island in Spain 
»	At 14:11 on 28/4/2025, unit 1 of HPP Duero 2 was 
started up using its black-start capability, initiating 
the Duero 2 electrical island, which was designed to 
supply critical loads, other HPPs, and synchronise with 
the other islands. 
»	At 17:49, the Duero 2 island synchronised with the 
Northern zone via the 220 kV line Tordesillas-Arroyadas.
»	At 18:46, the Duero 2 island was decoupled from 
the Northern zone due to the tripping of the 220 kV 
Arroyadas–Renedo line (see Figure 5-20), which was 
caused by stability issues arising from the very long 
220 kV corridor and high power flow between the 
Northern zone and the Duero 2 island. The Duero 2 
electrical island did not collapse, but several 220 kV 
lines and generating units within the Duero 1 island 
were disconnected. 
»	At 18:54, synchronisation was quickly restored through 
the 220 kV Arroyadas–Renedo line. Subsequently, 
reinforcement of the interconnection between the 
zones was carried out via the 400 kV network.

5.2.9	
Bottom-up restoration of the Cantabria island in Spain 
»	At 14:05 on 28/4/2025, unit 2 of HPP Cantabria was 
started up using its black-start capability, initiating 
the Cantabria electrical island, which was designed 
to supply load in the Cantabria area, supply auxiliary 
services for several TPPs, and synchronise with the 
islands created in the Asturias area. It is established in 
the Restoration Plan to start this island with the largest 
possible number of groups operating in parallel.
»	At 15:23, HPP Cantabria unit 1 was connected to 
stabilise the island, as shown in Figure 5-21. 
»	At 15:53 and 15:57, respectively, the step-up 
transformers of units 3 and 4 of HPP Cantabria were 
magnetised from the 220 kV side, causing an inrush 
current, which was supplied from units 1 and 2. Units 3 
and 4 were not synchronised to the island formed by 
units 1 and 2.
»	As from 15:53, the active power of unit 1 started to 
increase, reaching 20 MW at 16:02, while at the same 
time the active power of unit 2 was pushed back to 
zero, and even to negative values. 
»	Figure 5-22 shows that the frequency remained close 
to 51 Hz during this period. This behaviour suggests 
that an additional load of approximately 10 MW was 
connected to the island and that there was a problem 
with the load sharing between units 1 and 2. 
»	At 16:02, an unknown event triggered a frequency 
decrease leading to slow oscillations of increasing 
amplitude in the active power between units 1 and 2. 
This led, at 16:06, to the disconnection of unit 2 due to 
reverse power flow and of unit 1 due to over frequency, 
with the loss of the entire Cantabria electrical island. 
»	Considering the proximity and progress of the Northern 
zone, the re-energisation of the Cantabria area from the 
zones with stable voltage and frequency was prioritised 
in order to speed up the restoration of this zone.

5.2.11	 Bottom-up restoration of the West Asturias island in Spain

–	 At 15:29: unit 1 of HPP West Asturias II 
–	 At 15:48: unit 2 of HPP West Asturias II

be reviewed.

5.2.14	 Bottom-up restoration of the Toledo island in Spain 
»	At 15:16 on 28/4/2025, HPP Madrid was started in 
132 kV distribution network, using its black-start 
capability. The objective was to supply the auxiliary 
services of a TPP and some stabilisation loads in the 
Toledo area.
»	At 15:19, a technical problem during the switching on 
of the auxiliary services led to the tripping of the unit.
»	At 15:36, after the restart of the black-start unit, an 
initial connection of loads – approximately 30 % of the 
machine’s nominal power – caused the unit’s speed to 
drop and subsequently led to the unit being tripped by 
the turbine controller.
»	Further attempts to create a stable black-start island 
were unsuccessful for various reasons:
–	 16:01 – Trip due to overvoltage, accompanied by 
variations in the grid voltage
–	 16:22 – Trip due to speed drop, coinciding with load 
connection
–	 17:57 – Trip by the protection system due to an 
external cause
»	Despite several attempts, it was not possible to create 
the island. Due to the advanced stage of grid restoration 
in the other zones, priorities were reassessed.
5.3	
The restoration sequences in the Portuguese system
This section describes the restoration sequences in Portugal in detail, from the initial actions through to the total 
restoration of the Portuguese system.
Due to confidentiality constraints, the names of the generation units are anonymised for external publication.

Restoration process timeline
»	At 12:35(CEST) on 28/4/2025, REN requested the black-

»	At 12:43, REN requested the black-start mode start-up 
of CCGT 1-Norte. Following the restoration plan, the 
black-start operation mode was carried out using 
one generation unit in each of these power plants to 
establish electrical islands.
»	At 12:45, HPP 1-Centro was operating in black-start

Centro island are described in detail in section 5.3.3.
»	At 12:49, HPP 1-Centro tripped, after which the producer

small hydro units.

to Canelas and Recarei SSs and progressively increased 
load supply until 17:26, when the unit tripped (see 
section 5.3.2.)

second restoration area.

5.3.2	
Bottom-up restoration of the Norte island in Portugal 
»	At 12:43 (CEST) on 28/4/2025, REN requested the black-
start mode start-up of CCGT 1-Norte. 
»	In the first few hours, CCGT 1-Norte was unsuccessful 
in closing the generator circuit breaker to energise 
the unit transformer, due to unexpected problems in 
the control and command systems in the power plant 
substation. According to the producer, an interlock 
between excitation and the generator circuit breaker 
prevented the energisation of the generator step-up 
transformer. This interlock was identified and modified 
during this period.
»	At 16:38, CCGT 1-Norte started, and voltage was 
propagated to the 220 kV busbar of the power plant SS. 
»	At 16:54, voltage was propagated to the Canelas and 
Recarei SSs, and there was a progressive load supply. 
»	At 17:23, a synchronous compensator was started 
using Unit 2 of HPP 1-Norte to support voltage control 
in the island, as provided for in the National Service 
Restoration Plan. For the reasons explained below, this 
caused the unwanted tripping of CCGT 1-Norte. 
»	During the start-up process of unit 2 of HPP 1-Norte 
as a synchronous condenser, its auxiliaries consumed 
approximately 17 MW in forcing the remaining water 
out of the hydro turbine and bringing the machine to 
synchronous speed. This additional load to the Norte 
island slowed down the CCGT 1-Norte generator and 
reduced the island frequency from 50 Hz to 49.7 Hz. 
»	The operator in charge at CCGT 1-Norte changed to load 
control in an attempt to increase the load set point and 
stop the speed drop. When changing to load control, 
the unit adopts the actual load as the load set-point.
»	After 25 seconds, the auxiliary compensator’s 
consumption dropped back to 0 MW. The sudden load 
drop after the manual change to load control was not 
anticipated by the operator. CCGT 1-Norte accelerated 
and was disconnected from the grid by its overspeed 
protection, as shown in Figure 5-35. CCGT 1-Norte 
did not trip, and continued on house load operation. 
Upon the opening of the HV circuit breaker, CCGT 
1-Norte switched automatically from load control to 
speed control. A few minutes later, the switchyard was 
re-energised.

5.3.3	
Bottom-up restoration of the Centro island in Portugal 
»	At 12:35 (CEST) on 28/4/2025, REN requested the black-
start mode start-up of HPP 1-Centro using unit 3. 
»	At 12:45, HPP 1-Centro was operating in black-start 
mode and propagating voltage to the 220 kV busbar 
of Zêzere SS. 
»	At 12:49, when connecting the 220/60 kV Transformer 
4 of Zêzere SS with a rated power of 170 MVA, unit 3 of 
HPP 1-Centro tripped. This was due to the activation of 
the maximum voltage protection relay of the 400 V AC 
busbar (auxiliary system). 
Figure 5-38: Active power, reactive power and voltage in the Centro island between 12:45 and 12:49
»	HHP-Centro is composed of 3 main HPP generators and 
two small HPP generators that serve to energise the 
auxiliaries of the large HPPs. Following the activation 
of the maximum voltage protection relay of the 400 V 
auxiliary system, the small HPP generators could not 
stop in an appropriate way. 
»	The producer initiated several unsuccessful attempts 
to start the auxiliary services of HPP 1-Centro. The 
automation control function that triggered the urgent 
stop event in both the small HPP generators could not 
be reset until a diesel unit was connected to the low 
voltage busbar. 
»	After this, the low voltage busbar of the power plant 
was energised and the black start procedure of the 
main units was started.

»	REN confirmed that the restoration procedure has been 
updated following the incident to stipulate that the 
lowest possible voltage setpoint should be applied on 
the main black-start source before the transformers are 
energised, so as to minimise inrush currents by keeping 
the operating point of the transformer within the linear 
part of the (current – magnetic flux) characteristic curve 
and avoiding the saturation zone.
»	Alternatively, where technically possible, progressive 
voltage restoration (also known as “soft-start”) 
is recommended to reduce transformer inrush 
phenomena. REN explained to the Expert Panel that 
it has increased the number of black-start facilities 
from two to four in Portugal. The two additional black-
start facilities are hydropower plants with soft-start 
possibilities.
»	The Expert Panel recommends that production and 
storage facilities involved in bottom-up restoration 
scenarios improve the accuracy of the measurements 
for key parameters, such as active power, reactive 
power, voltage and speed/frequency, to facilitate 
ex-post analysis.

5.5	
Generation and load recovery
The restoration of electrical grids after a total blackout 
is a complex and demanding coordinated process. 
TSOs worked collaboratively to re-establish electricity 
supply through a mixture of top-down and bottom-up 
approaches. Generation and load recovery occurred 
simultaneously, as the grid was being restored. This 
sub-chapter describes the generation and load recovery 
once system balance had been achieved.
5.5.1	
Spain
The restoration of the Spanish transmission system from the Red Eléctrica side was concluded at 04:00 on 29 April. 
The restoration continued at the distribution system level, concluding at 07:00 on 29 April.
Evolution of generation and load during and after restoration
The restoration of the interrupted power supply began at 
12:43 on 28 April with the support received through the 
Spain — France interconnection. Additionally, as noted in 
the previous sections, in the minutes following the inci­
dent, islands were created from hydroelectric plants with 
autonomous start-up across different electrical zones.
At 13:04, support was established through the Spain — 
Morocco interconnection. Subsequently, starting at 
15:14, combined-cycle plants were progressively 
connected to contribute to the restoration of the power 
supply.

Figure 5-45: Evolution of the generation and load in the Spanish system through to the end of 29 April – Red Eléctrica
Evolution of renewable generation during restoration
Supervision and control of RCW in the Spanish electrical 
system is carried out by CECRE, which was commissioned 
in June 2006.
Under the Spanish regulation established in Royal 
Decree 413/2014, all single RCW facilities, or clusters 
sharing the same connection point with a total installed 
power greater than 1 MW, are required to send real-time 
telemetry of the active power they produce to CECRE. 
Additionally, all single RCW facilities, or clusters with a 
total installed capacity greater than 5 MW, receive active 
power setpoints from CECRE, with which they must 
comply.
CECRE, therefore, receives real-time telemetry from RCW 
facilities, and can issue real-time limits for maximum 
production in the RCW facilities connected to both the 
transmission and distribution network. 
This real-time information is collected from the plants 
by the Renewable Energy Control Centres (RESCCs) and 
channelled to CECRE via the ICCP links connecting these 
control centres. 
To minimise the number of points of contact with CECRE, 
the RESCCs serve as the sole real-time interface with the 
Spanish TSO. In other words, RESCCs act as intermediaries 
between CECRE and the RCW facilities. Each RCW facility 
is free to choose its preferred RESCC, regardless of the 
technology it uses or its connection point to the network. 
Generation control is managed by CECRE, which sets indi­
vidual limits for each facility through its corresponding 
RESCC. 
Therefore, on the one hand, RESCCs collect real-time 
information from RCW facilities and send this to CECRE 
(supervision), while on the other hand, they collect the 
setpoints established by CECRE and send these to the 
facilities (control).
After the incident, at 13:38, CECRE sent a setpoint of 0 MW 
to all RCW facilities.

Portugal 
Evolution of generation and load during and after restoration
