Evolution of renewable generation (wind and solar) during restoration
According to the established Portuguese regulations, all 
single renewable power plants, or sets of power plants 
sharing the same connection point with a total installed 
power greater than 1 MW, should be observable and 
controllable (via setpoints) from REN’s National Control 
Centre. However, no setpoint was sent to limit renew­
able production during the restoration phase.
According to the National Service Restoration Plan, the 
connection points of the renewable power plants (solar 
and wind generation) connected to the transmission 
system were not energised during the restoration of the 
transmission system. After the restoration, they were 
energised by REN throughout the day on 29 April, and 
instructions for production permissions were provided 
by phone. 
For the wind generation connected to the transmission 
system (2,774 MW of installed capacity), production 
permissions were given from 16:00, while solar genera­
tion (1,767 MW of installed capacity) received permission 
from 21:00 on 29 April. 
The renewable power plants connected to the distri­
bution system began to be energised shortly before 
the end of the transmission system restoration, in coor­
dination between REN and E-REDES. For the wind and 
solar generation connected to the distribution system 
(2,634 MW and 2,620 MW of installed capacity, respec­
tively), production permissions were given from 23:00 
on 28 April. 
5.5.3	
France 
The D-1 commercial nomination on the Spain — France 
border for business day 28 August was scheduled from 
France to Spain (up to 1,688 MW) between 13:00 and 
15:00, and then from Spain to France between 16:00 and 
21:00 (1,800 MW from 16:00 to 18:00, then 3,000 MW).
As RTE supplied Red Eléctrica in the afternoon and 
evening of 28 April and in the morning of 29 April, RTE 
activated bids on the French balancing mechanism (up 
to 4,500 MW; total activated energy for 28 and 29 April: 
51.9 GWh) and sought support from other TSOs (up to 
500 MW, including 3,000 MWh from Swissgrid on 28 April 
and 8,850 MWh from Amprion on 28 and 29 April).

===== PAGE 388 =====
388  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
5.6	
Steps after system restoration
This section describes the steps taken to ensure system balance after the network restoration.
5.6.1	
Spain
The day-ahead market session for 29 April was 
conducted, but its results were not incorporated into 
system operations. The remaining electric market activ­
ities for 29 April in the Spanish system were suspended. 
They were re-established for 30 April. As the system 
restoration progressed, orders were given to synchro­
nise all available hydraulic and thermal generators in 
the system. As they were synchronised, instructions were 
given to each of these generators by phone to adjust 
their generation to demand.
The master aFRR controller was connected at 00:06 on 
29 April. The synchronised hydraulic and thermal gener­
ators with secondary regulation capacity were included 
in this system, thereby providing a significant volume of 
secondary regulation to manage variations in demand 
and generation.
From 01:38 to 07:00, the limitations on RCW generation 
were progressively removed to allow their inclusion in 
the system, as described in section 4.3.
Throughout 29 April, the synchronised hydraulic and 
thermal generators were instructed by phone to adjust 
their generation to demand and maintain adequate 
levels of secondary reserve. 
From 00:00 to 24:00 on 29 April, export capacities with 
France, Portugal, and Morocco were reduced to 0 MW to 
enable all system demand to be supplied with the avail­
able generation.
From 06:30 to 11:00, due to the insufficient availability 
of synchronised generation to supply the demand, a 
support import programme was requested from France 
(800 MW from 06:30 to 08:00 and from 10:00 to 10:30, 
1,500 MW from 08:00 to 10:00, and 400 MW from 10:30 
to 11:00).
In the last hours of 29 April, hydraulic and thermal gener­
ators were instructed to adjust their generation to their 
market programmes, starting from 00:00 on 30 April.
5.6.2	
Portugal
The day-ahead market session for 29 April was 
conducted, but the results were not incorporated into 
system operations. The remaining electric market 
activities for 29 April in the Portuguese system were 
suspended. They were re-established for 30 April.
As the system restoration progressed, HPPs and TPPs 
were given instructions by phone (non-market-based 
central dispatch). As they were synchronised, each of 
these generators received instructions by phone to adjust 
its generation to demand.
During the afternoon of 29 April, the production limi­
tations on renewable generation (wind and solar) 
connected to the transmission grid were progressively 
removed to allow their inclusion in the system, as 
described in section 4.3.
Throughout 29 April, instructions were issued by phone 
to the synchronised hydro and thermal generators 
to adjust their generation to demand and maintain 
adequate secondary reserves. The AGC was put into 
service at 20:25 on 28 April, following an interconnec­
tion schedule programme at 0 MW, as agreed with Red 
Eléctrica.

5.7	
Market restoration
This section describes the restoration of market activities in Spain and Portugal after the restoration and stabilisation 
of the systems.
5.7.1	
Spain
On the morning of 29 April, the Iberian NEMO was 
informed by phone of the forecast for the completion 
of the system restoration and the resumption of market 
activities, starting with the clearing of the daily market 
for energy delivery on April 30.
At 11:39 on 29 April, in coordination with the Iberian 
NEMO, the Spanish TSO published a statement in the 
System Operator Information System (ESIOS) to all actors 
indicating that the restoration state would last until 
23:59 that same day:
Following the incident in the peninsular electricity 
system that occurred at 12:33 p.m. yesterday, April 28, 
and until 11:59 p.m. today, April 29, market activities 
are suspended in accordance with Operating Procedure 
P.O.3.9. Therefore, no energy or capacity schedules or 
allocations made through market mechanisms for the 
periods within this time frame will be considered valid.
The energy settlement will be carried out in accordance 
with sections 5 and 6 of the aforementioned procedure.
The System Operator has already informed the NEMO that 
market activities will resume starting with the day-ahead 
market for energy delivery April 30.
This information was also published on the privileged 
information platform of the System Operator.
Due to the incident in the Spanish Peninsular electrical 
system at 12:33 PM on April 28th, market activities 
for delivery April 29th are suspended, following both 
Article 35 of Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/2196 and 
Spanish Operational Procedure 3.9. Market activities for 
delivery April 30th have been restored. 
The following milestones in particular are highlighted:
»	Participation in the single day-ahead coupling 
took place on 29 April at 12:00 for energy 
delivery on 30 April. For 30 April, the intercon­
nection capacity between Spain and France, 
as well as between Spain and Portugal, was 
limited. 
»	The intraday market for 30 April was enabled 
at 23:00 on 29 April.
»	Connection to the European platform for mFRR 
(MARI) at 00:15 on 30 April.
»	Connection to the European platform for RR 
(TERRE) at 00:26 on 30 April.
»	Connection to the imbalance netting platform 
(IGCC) at 11:55 on 30 April.

5.7.2	
Portugal
On 29 April at 14:43 (CEST), REN validated the results of 
the daily market for 30 April.
On 29 April at 16:23, REN published a statement and 
an urgent market message indicating that the resto­
ration and stabilisation of the system would last until 
23:59 that same day: 
Following the blackout situation that occurred on 28 April 
2025, in the Portuguese electrical system and the subse­
quent, ongoing process of restoration and stabilisation 
that is taking place on 29 April, it is reported that: 
»	The interconnection capacity between Portugal 
and Spain will be set on 30 April (CEST – Central 
European Summer Time), at 0 MW in the import 
and export direction. 
»	Transactions will resume in the day-ahead 
market, intraday market sessions, and the contin­
uous intraday market for the delivery periods 
relating to 30 April (CEST) 
»	Contracts will resume, inclusive from 30 April 
(CEST), in the various markets and processes 
managed by REN – Rede Eléctrica Nacional, S.A., 
namely the processes for resolving technical 
restrictions, the replacement reserve (RR) market, 
the frequency restoration reserve market with 
manual activation (mFRR) and the secondary 
regulation band market 
Additionally, on 29 April at 18:26, a notification was sent 
to all market players indicating that the restoration state 
would last until 23:59 that same day. 
REN reconnected to the balancing platforms as follows: 
»	IGCC: The reconnection occurred on 30 April at 
19:08. 
»	TERRE: REN began submitting its requirements 
for RR for the delivery periods between 03:00 
and 04:00 on 30 April. 
»	MARI: The reconnection occurred on 30 April for 
the quarter-hour from 19:30 to 19:45.
5.8	
Behaviour of distributed energy resources and load 
during restoration
The Expert Panel asked the DSOs if they had observed 
any disturbing behaviour in DERs or any unexpected 
load behaviour (EVs, BESS, heat pumps, etc.) after 
re-energisation.
The DSOs replied that generation units < 1 MW connected 
to the DSO network currently have no obligation to 
provide real-time information to the DSO. DSOs do not, 
therefore, have visibility over DERs, their status, or their 
electrical parameters, meaning that it would have been 
difficult to detect any unwanted effects if they did occur. 
One DSO explained that its choice of preferring urban 
areas at the start of the restoration was because this 
allowed the energised network to maintain a stable load 
with minimum impact from DERs.
Another DSO explained that the MV feeders that were 
switched on were selected before the blackout for 
having few DERs, ensuring a more stable load.
Prior to the initiation of the restoration process, all MV 
feeder switches were opened by the DSOs to ensure the 
complete disconnection of all loads and generators. 
Subsequently, a controlled reconnection sequence of 
loads and generation was carried out in coordination 
with the Spanish TSO.

===== PAGE 391 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  391 
5.9	
Voice communication and remote-control problems 
during restoration
The Expert Panel asked the DSOs if they had experienced 
any issues with voice communication systems during the 
first 24 hours after the blackout.
A first contact between Red Eléctrica and one particular 
DSO control centre in Spain could not be established until 
17:48, when it was made through the control centre of 
another DSO. Until that moment, there was no informa­
tion about the condition of that particular DSO network 
following the incident.
Around 16:00, the South Control Centre of a DSO in 
Portugal experienced a failure in its primary communi­
cation system with the TSO Control System. As a contin­
gency, satellite phones were used. By 18:00, the DSO had 
successfully implemented VOIP over the internal commu­
nications network, resolving the need for satellite phone 
use at the South Control Centre. The public earth-based 
and cell telecommunication networks failed. The DSO 
in Portugal resorted to private internal communication 
systems and satellite phones. The North Control Centre of 
that DSO can act as back-up for the South Control Centre 
to receive and execute instructions from the TSO.
A DSO in Galicia reported a clear degradation of its voice 
communication service during the first six hours after the 
start of the blackout, culminating in a complete service 
drop at 18:25. This was due to problems at the public 
telecom operator complicating the usual call routes. The 
DSO used redundant point-to-point lines and alternative 
communication centres to maintain communication with 
the TSO. The public operator’s service was fully restored 
at around 01:15 on 29 April. Coordination and opera­
tional continuity were maintained throughout, with 
critical service continuity being prioritised.
The TSO confirmed major difficulties in contacting this 
DSO due to this drop in the voice communication system, 
with a significant impact on the restoration processes 
in Galicia. From 17:17 to 20:45, the TSO was not able to 
contact this DSO through the usual call routes, except on 
one occasion at 18:17.
The TSO explained that from 21:10 to 22:04 and from 
22:27 to 00:02 the following day, it was unable to 
contact the DSO control centre in Sevilla due to commu­
nication issues at this DSO, although the TSO had no 
problems communicating by phone with other parties at 
that time. Several attempts were made to reach different 
phone numbers at their control centre, but none of these 
were successful. During these two periods, the restora­
tion process for the demand in Andalucia was paused. 
At 00:02 on 29 April, communication was finally estab­
lished using cloud-based communication software.
From 18:30 until 04:00 on 29 April, the TSO and a DSO 
control centre in Barcelona were only able to establish 
telephone communications occasionally due to commu­
nication issues at the DSO, although the TSO was able to 
communicate by phone with other parties without any 
problems at that time. This slowed down the restoration 
process in Cataluña, Galicia and León.
Another Spanish DSO reported that in all its DSO control 
centres, a priority phone line was available for commu­
nications with the TSO control centre, as requested in the 
applicable regulations. Nevertheless, between 18:00 
and 19:00, voice communication issues were recorded 
with the TSO control centre, and linked to the latter’s 
communication system. The TSO, however, rejects this 
hypothesis, as it was able to communicate by phone 
with other parties without any problems at that time, It 
reported that telephone calls made between the TSO and 
this DSO went through an automatic warning message 
that significantly delayed communications, since the call 
did not reach the DSO operator until the message had 
finished. In some cases, there were delays of more than 
2 minutes before the load restoration instructions could 
be transmitted.
The TSO reported that at 18:17, a DSO informed them 
that some time earlier, they had lost remote control of 
their facilities in the Galicia and Madrid zone. This caused 
a significant, hours-long delay in the restoration of the 
Galicia and Madrid zone.

===== PAGE 392 =====
392  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
The TSO reported that one DSO informed them that from 
the start of the restoration process, they had neither 
remote control nor visualisation of many of their substa­
tions in the Andalucia distribution network. To supply 
demand from those substations as they received voltage 
from the transmission network, they had needed to 
dispatch personnel to the affected substations to recover 
remote control and telemetry signals. This situation 
delayed the restoration process. The DSO explained 
that some of these communication outages arose due 
to dependencies on the public telecommunications 
operators. Consequently, operational resources were 
deployed to the facilities in anticipation of a potential 
local intervention, and mobile power generators were 
placed on some communication repeaters. The public 
telecommunications operator’s network lost coverage 
due to the failure of the autonomous power supply 
systems at its communication repeaters and switching 
centres. This loss of coverage varied depending on the 
location of the communication infrastructure and the 
timing of re-energisation.
Multiple DSOs explained that in areas where communi­
cation via public operators was lost, satellite terminals 
were used, for example, to enable communication 
between control centres and field personnel. The 
Spanish TSO reported that some generation companies 
had reported problems in communicating with their 
combined cycle power plants. This caused delays in 
the process of energising the auxiliary services of those 
plants, and consequently in their synchronisation.
5.10	 Conclusion
The Expert Panel would like to recognise the dedication, 
commitment and good cooperation of the operators and 
employees of TSOs, DSOs, producers, renewable energy 
control centres, and other stakeholders. Their expertise 
and experience were instrumental in the successful 
restoration of the Spanish and Portuguese power 
systems following a blackout of unprecedented scope 
and magnitude.
The information gathered in the aftermath of the resto­
ration has enabled the Expert Panel to identify key 
challenges and develop recommendations for further 
improving future restoration processes in the event of 
any similar incidents.
Restoration efforts proceeded most smoothly in areas 
that could be re-energised “top-down” from stable 
neighbouring transmission systems, which provided 
essential voltage support and system stability. 
Regions farther away from healthy systems required 
parallel energisation from dedicated power plants – 
primarily hydropower facilities, but including one 
gas-fired plant serving Northern Portugal – equipped 
with black-start capabilities and following the estab­
lished restoration procedures. 
In Spain, renewable energy, cogen and waste facilities 
or clusters with an installed capacity greater than 5 MW 
were instructed to produce zero output during the first 
twelve hours of system restoration, to prevent uncon­
trolled energy injection. Once the system had stabilised, 
these production restrictions were gradually lifted, 
allowing these resources to be reintegrated. 
The investigation found that some local restoration 
scenarios encountered challenges that led to delays in 
load recovery. These issues highlight the complexity of 
rebuilding an “islanded” section of the grid from a single 
source without broader system support. Nevertheless, 
certain areas energised through local black-start sources 
were able to successfully synchronise with the larger 
system.

===== PAGE 393 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  393 
Technical difficulties identified include issues with: 
»	power and frequency control of multiple power plants 
in the same island, as encountered in Extremadura 1 
(section 5.2.2), Galicia (5.2.6), Cantabria (5.2.9), 
Extremadura 2 (5.2.10), and Norte island Portugal 
(5.3.2)
»	synchronisation of the islands, as happened between 
Duero 1 and Duero 2 (section 5.2.3)
»	machine protection settings, as encountered in the 
Centro island in Portugal (section 5.3.2) and the East 
Asturias island in Spain (5.2.5)
»	inappropriate voltage control in certain generators 
leading to limits in their reactive absorption capability, 
as encountered in Galicia (section 5.2.6) and Levante 
(5.2.7)
»	start-up and HV breaker closing with black-start plants, 
as encountered in Levante (section 5.2.7), Andalucía 
(5.2.13), Toledo (5.2.14) and both Portuguese black-
start islands (5.3.2 and 5.3.3)
»	impact from distributed energy resources, as encoun­
tered in Extremadura 1 (section 5.2.2)
The incident underscored the critical need for reliable 
and redundant (voice) communication among key 
restoration actors, especially when public telecommu­
nications are unavailable. In regions lacking such backup 
communication (Galicia, Sevilla, Barcelona and Madrid), 
load recovery was significantly delayed, as explained in 
section 5.9.
The Spanish system was fully restored within 16 hours, 
while the Portuguese system was back online within 
12 hours after the blackout. Looking at restoration expe­
riences following historic blackouts of similar magni­
tudes in other developed power systems, the restoration 
times in Spain and Portugal are within comparable limits, 
allowing for the specific complexities of grid restoration, 
and the limited interconnection of the Iberian Peninsula 
with Continental Europe, which reduced the possibilities 
for a top‑down restoration strategy. 
The restoration procedures and fallback strategies, 
combined with the full commitment of well-trained 
operators, enabled a rapid and effective restoration. 
Nevertheless, this experience highlights the ongoing 
importance of regular black start testing and joint oper­
ator training, frameworks for managing distributed 
energy resources during restoration, robust independent 
voice communication and remote control systems for 
DSOs and SGUs, and the value of high-resolution real-
time measurements across both the transmission and 
distribution networks for the effective analysis of any 
future incidents.
Key recommendations to further improve future restora­
tion processes in the event of similar incidents include:
»	Regular live black start testing involving all relevant 
parties.
»	Regular joint training sessions on restoration scenarios 
for all key stakeholders (TSOs, DSOs, producers).
»	Ensuring that renewable energy sources in the 
distribution grids do not disturb the delicate restoration 
process.
»	Ensuring that blackout-proof voice communication 
between key actors and critical remote control functions 
is available when public telecommunication networks 
are down.
»	Making available high-resolution measurement data 
from SGUs in the transmission and distribution grids, to 
allow better after-incident analysis.

6	
OPERATIONAL PLANNING
6.1	
Introduction
This chapter addresses operational planning activities 
relevant to the incident under analysis, covering both 
regional-level processes performed by the Regional 
Coordination Centres (RCCs) and national operational 
planning procedures implemented by Red Eléctrica de 
España (RE) in its role as the Spanish transmission system 
operator (TSO). The chapter provides a comprehensive 
overview of the operational planning activities coordi­
nated at the regional level and national levels.
With regard to regional coordination, the chapter 
presents the investigation and analysis performed by 
the RCCs in accordance with their responsibilities for 
Regional Incident Analysis and Reporting (RIAR). RIAR is a 
legally mandated task pursuant to Article 37 (i) of Regu­
lation (EU) 2019/943, requiring RCCs to carry out post-op­
eration and post-disturbance analysis and reporting 
activities. The RCC Post-Operation and Post-Disturbances 
Analysis and Reporting Methodology was approved by 
ACER through decision No. 04/2022 and entered into 
force on 1 April 2022. 
The RIAR task interfaces with the incident investiga­
tion process conducted by the ICS Expert Panel. In line 
with the applicable methodology, an RCC Investigation 
Subgroup is established within the ICS Expert Panel when 
the RCC investigation threshold is met. As confirmed in 
Chapter 8 of the Factual Report, this threshold has been 
met for the incident under consideration. Consequently, 
an RCC Investigation Subgroup was established and 
conducted a detailed investigation in accordance with 
Article 37 and Annex I of Regulation (EU) 2019/943. The 
conclusions of the RCC investigation are incorporated 
into this chapter of the ICS Final Report. This chapter 
also describes the national operational planning regu­
lation in force in Spain on 28 April 2025, applied by RE 
and Spanish electricity undertakings. The explanations 
of the underlying procedures were provided by RE and 
are included to allow for the assessment of the implica­
tions of the RE operational planning environment on the 
incident. Accordingly, the following sections detail the 
RCC investigation, as well as the relevant operational 
planning procedures implemented by RE.

6.1.2	
Regional Coordination SWE
The SWE System Operation Region (SOR), established 
under Regulation (EU) 2019/943, comprises Portugal, 
Spain, and France. The RCC appointed for the region is 
Coreso.
The Portuguese and Spanish power systems are char­
acterised by a high penetration of renewable energy 
sources (RES), particularly wind and solar generation. 
As a result, regional power flows are highly dependent 
on wind and solar generation patterns and forecasts. 
Owing to the variability of these sources, intraday (ID) 
system conditions may differ from those anticipated in 
the day-ahead (D-1) market time frame, notably during 
periods of high wind and/or solar output combined 
with low demand, when renewable reduction through 
market mechanisms may be required.
Under such conditions, the Portuguese TSO (REN) may 
identify tight downward regulation margins. This infor­
mation is provided to the RCC for situational aware­
ness. The situation is not a comparable limitation in 
the Spanish system, where a large share of renewable 
generation participates in balancing services. Relevant 
forecasts and system conditions are communicated 
to the RCC within the SWE day-ahead security analysis 
(SA DA) process and during regular coordination calls 
between TSOs.

===== PAGE 397 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  397 
In Spain, additional operational constraints arise from 
the geographical separation between major generation 
areas and load centres. During low-load conditions, 
long 400 kV transmission lines may exhibit capacitive 
behaviour, leading to high voltage levels. To manage 
these conditions, TSOs identify and implement additional 
operational measures (topological remedial actions 
(RAs)), such as the temporary disconnection of transmis­
sion lines. Consequently, D-1 grid models often include 
a higher number of lines out of service compared to the 
models stemming from the week-ahead (W-1) outage 
planning coordination (OPC) process. This difference is 
consistent with the respective objectives of the plan­
ning processes: W-1 coordination focuses on identifying 
potential incompatibilities among long-term planned 
outages, whereas D-1 and ID security analyses assess 
system security under expected operational conditions 
and determine the need for additional operational 
measures.
From an interconnection capacity calculation perspec­
tive, Coreso assesses the Portugal–Spain and Spain–
France borders independently, as interactions between 
them remain limited due to the Spanish transmission 
network located between the two borders. Accordingly, 
capacity calculation in the SWE region is based on the net 
transfer capacity (NTC) methodology rather than a flow-
based approach.
6.1.3	
Geographical Scope of RCC SA in SWE
In line with the System Operation Guidelines (SO GL), 
RCC activities dealing with a representation of the grid 
focus on a defined subset of assets of the three TSOs’ 
grids, defined on the basis of their cross-border impact, 
pursuant to the relevant regional methodologies. These 
processes, together with their applicable methodolo­
gies, are:
»	Coordinated capacity calculation (CCC), in 
line with regional methodology pursuant to 
Article 21 of Capacity Allocation and Congestion 
Management (CACM), for the critical network 
elements (CNEs) and contingencies determined 
by applying the regional methodology and in 
line with Article 22 of CACM
»	Coordinated security analysis (CSA), described 
in Articles 75 and 76 of the System Opera­
tion Guideline (SO GL) and its corresponding 
pan-European (PE) methodology for coordi­
nating operational SA (CSAm) and regional 
methodology for regional operational secu­
rity coordination (ROSC), which applies to the 
assets determined pursuant to Article 14 of 
CSAm
»	OPC, described in Article 80 of the SO GL, which 
applies to the assets pursuant to the method­
ology for assessing the relevance of assets for 
outage coordination (RAOCm), implementing 
Article 84 of the SO GL
The RCC security assessment and coordination process 
applies to only a subset of elements of the national TSO 
network, assessed as cross-border relevant in line with 
the methodologies, and does not cover the entire control 
areas of the TSOs. In line with the SO GL, the network 
elements relevant for CSA and OPC tasks are defined as 
follows:
»	Relevant for the CSA, cross-border relevant 
network elements (XNEs), defined as those 
above the influence threshold determined in 
the SWE region in line with the ranges specified 
in Annex I of CSAm
»	For outage coordination, the relevant assets are 
defined as those above the influence threshold 
determined in the SWE region pursuant to 
RAOCm
The ROSC process that implements SWE regional 
mandated methodology pursuant to Article 26 of the 
SO GL is still under implementation (expected in Q3 
2027). Currently, an interim regional security assess­
ment is performed by Coreso as a coordinated approach 
agreed with REN, RE, and RTE. However, the current 
security assessment and outage coordination processes 
are supported by a legacy, non-automated optimisation 
tool that selects RAs in case a constraint or an outage 
incompatibility is detected. Coreso and the TSOs (RE, REN, 
and RTE) have agreed to limit the coordinated selection 
of RAs in the current SA and in OPC processes to cases 
where the simulated contingencies violate the limits 
of a subset of elements of cross-border relevance. This 
subset is referred to as the “Main area”, reflecting the 
need for close coordination between the affected TSOs as 
per their agreement. Constraints related to less relevant 
XNEs are addressed by the concerned TSOs at the national 
level, with the potential to initiate bilateral coordination 
where and when necessary.

agreed by the involved TSO(s) and ensures coordination 
between all involved parties.

Figure 6-1: Relevant RCC tasks and their time horizons.
As shown above, RCCs perform two key PE tasks on a 
weekly basis following a rotational principle: OPC and 
short-term adequacy (STA). Coreso additionally performs 
the regional OPC service, which incorporates an SA, 
ensuring grid security through load-flow computations 
and SA.
6.2.1	
OPC
The OPC process is designed to support the planning of 
grid element outages while ensuring the operational 
security of the interconnected European power system. 
This is achieved through procedures carried out at both 
the PE and regional levels.
Building on the PE OPC process, RCCs also conduct 
regional OPC processes, commonly referred to as regional 
OPI assessments. These aim to evaluate whether the 
outage plans of European TSOs are feasible from a grid 
security perspective. If potential congestions are iden­
tified, the process involves proposing RAs, verifying the 
feasibility of the coordinated unavailability plan (UAP) 
with respect to security limits, and issuing recommenda­
tions to address any detected incompatibilities in outage 
planning.
6.2.1.1	
PE OPC Process
The PE OPC tool supports the coordination of outages 
by enabling the exchange of UAPs and maintaining a 
database of relevant assets. Relevant assets are grid 
elements that TSOs deem critical for regional coordina­
tion. A standardised procedure ensures data quality and 
consistency through the validation of planned statuses 
for cross-border lines managed by TSOs. All RCCs carry out 
the PE OPC process on a rotational basis. During the week 
of this incident, the RCC acting as the merge operator was 
SEleNe CC.
The W-1 OPC cycle covers Saturday to Friday, with TSOs 
required to submit preliminary disconnection plans by 
Wednesday at 12:00. After a series of validations and 
merges (first at 12:00, second at 16:00), RCCs perform 
security assessments. TSOs can adjust plans and request 
further analysis until Thursday at 16:00 (third merge). 
Final plans are reviewed in the weekly operational 
teleconference (WOPT) on Fridays at 10:25, for the CORE, 
Italy North (IN), and SWE regions, moderated by TSCNET. 
Final changes must be submitted by Friday at 13:00 
(fourth merge), which defines the official plan. Outages 
submitted after that are deemed unplanned. RCCs use 
CGMs to evaluate outage impacts and propose RAs or 
cancellations if operational security limits are at risk.

6.2.1.2	
Regional OPI Assessment for SWE
As explained in 6.2.1.1, the PE OPC process merges individual UAPs four times. Once the second merge UAP is available, 
the regional OPI assessment starts at Coreso for all relevant regions. 
The main steps performed by the OPC operator at Coreso include:
»	Building the single OPC scenario to be analysed 
in detail for all regions. This is based on two 
main factors: the level of exchanges from 
reference cases provided by TSCNET and the 
volume of simultaneous relevant planned 
outages from TSOs. The operator selects one 
time stamp (TS) that reflects the most critical 
scenario – typically with the highest exchanges 
and most outages.
»	Identifying any outage planning security 
constraints (OPSC) or OPIs at the regional 
level by running an SA using a contingency list 
supplied by TSOs (the same list used in the SA DA 
SWE). It should be noted that the SA considers 
static limits of power flows and voltages, rather 
than dynamic (transient) stability security 
limits. This approach is appropriate in the SWE 
case because:
–	 Steady-state limits are reached before 
dynamic security limits in a statistically over­
whelming majority of dispatching situations.
–	 The subsequent SA process performed by 
TSOs, using an up-to-date scenario, captures 
potential dynamic stability risk in the tran­
sient regime associated with contingencies.
»	Proposing solutions to TSOs when constraints 
are found, prioritising non-costly RAs (e. g. 
PST tap changes or outage rescheduling). 
Costly measures like generation redispatch or 
commercial exchange adjustments are consid­
ered only when necessary. The key distinction 
is that OPIs may involve costly measures and 
could even result in the cancellation of planned 
outages by the respective TSO.
»	Sharing results during the WOPT and coordi­
nating with other RCCs/TSOs when issues affect 
multiple regions, ensuring transparency and 
third-party awareness. 
»	Publishing Regional OPSC/OPI reports for each 
region. These reports summarise the analysed 
outages, cross-border physical flows, contin­
gency outcomes, and proposed solutions. They 
are also shared internally to support upcoming 
capacity calculation and SA processes, 
­especially for tracking postponed outages or 
agreed RAs.
The W-1 process is repeated weekly and remains flexible 
to accommodate last-minute changes, including urgent 
outage notifications requiring ad hoc analysis.
Focus on BD 28/04 TS 12:30
The W-1 Regional OPI assessment for Week 18 was 
carried out on Thursday and Friday, 24 – 25 April 2025. 
Results were distributed to all participating TSOs imme­
diately after completion.

===== PAGE 402 =====
402  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report

point in the list above) scenario for the CORE, IN, and

(considering those of BD 21/04, TS 18:30) and the

6.2.1.3	
Conclusion
The PE and regional OPC processes for Week 18 were 
executed in accordance with the defined procedures 
and timelines. All required W-1 merges were completed, 
relevant UAPs were exchanged, and the PE and regional 
security assessments were carried out as prescribed. 
The identification of BD 28/04 at TS 12:30 as the single 
scenario for detailed regional OPI assessment was based 
on the level of exchanges and the concentration of 
relevant planned outages across the CORE, IN, and SWE 
regions.
The regional OPI assessment for the SWE region did not 
identify any OPI requiring costly RAs or outage cancella­
tions. One OPSC was detected and addressed through a 
non-costly RA (PST tap change), reducing the overload 
to within acceptable limits. Consequently, based on 
the planned transmission asset unavailabilities and the 
commercial exchanges used in the OPC grid model, the 
system was assessed as secure for the analysed scenario. 
Nevertheless, the underlying SAs assess power flows 
under steady-state conditions and do not cover dynamic 
or voltage-related operational security limits.
As the OPC was performed the week before, some struc­
tural limitations must be noted, such as the differences 
between the commercial exchanges considered and 
the actual real-time cross-border flows. In addition, the 
scope of the OPC process does not include generation or 
demand asset unavailabilities.
Accordingly, the OPC process, as designed and applied, 
was not intended to identify or prevent events arising 
from real-time operational conditions outside the scope 
of planned transmission outages. Within its defined 
remit, the OPC task was performed correctly and in line 
with existing procedures.
6.2.2	
Short-Term Adequacy
The purpose of the STA service is to investigate whether 
the reliable available expected production capacity can 
meet the expected consumption using both upward and 
downward regulation at the regional level, pursuant to 
Article 81 of the SO GL. The calculation takes place daily, 
and the time horizon of the process is D-7 to D-1. The 
STA process is complementary to the adequacy analysis 
locally performed by TSOs pursuant to Article 104-107 of 
the SO GL. Although this incident was not related to any 
adequacy issues, a summary of the STA data and results 
is available in the following sections. 
All SWE TSOs (RTE, RE, and REN) and RCCs participate in the 
PE (also known as cross-regional) STA process. 
For the daily process, all TSOs are required to submit input 
data for the calculations. The process is then executed 
automatically and monitored by the main or backup RCC. 
The regional STA process can also be triggered if the 
results of the deterministic calculation indicate inade­
quacy for a time horizon of D-3 or shorter. This situation 
rarely occurs. The Nordic RCC was the main adequacy 
assessment agent (AAA) for the PE process in the week 
when the incident occurred. No regional process was 
triggered on the days preceding the incident, and the 
focus of the analysis will be the process of the previous 
day. The process did not detect any adequacy issues for 
the day of the incident.
6.2.2.1	
Input Data
All required input data (NTC files, W-1 generation, and 
W-1 load files) relevant for all affected and neigh­
bouring TSOs were received before the STA calculations 
were performed on 27 April 2025 (the day before the 
incident). These files successfully passed validation and 
were used in the calculation. 
The first file uploaded by RE for the W-1 generation was 
rejected, as it lacked information on installed generation 
for biomass, oil, pumped storage, water reservoir, other 
renewables, and waste. RE automatically sends two sets 
of input files for demand and generation forecasts. 
The files are sent at 3 am and 8 am to cover the possibility 
of failure of the first set of files. During the day on 27 
April, the second set of generation input files was auto­
matically correctly uploaded. 
To assess the accuracy of some of the input data provided 
by the affected TSOs, a comparison was made between 
the STA input data (forecast values) and the realised 
values (obtained from the ENTSO-E Transparency Plat­
form (TP)) for solar and wind generation.

6.2.2.2	
Calculation Results
STA calculation was completed within the standard 
time frame typical for the daily STA process. The auto­
matic deterministic and probabilistic calculations 
were triggered at 09:00, finishing at 09:05 and 09:20, 
respectively. 
The entire STA process was completed successfully, with 
no system failures or issues reported through the STA 
tool’s ticketing system. The deterministic results for the 
period did not reveal any adequacy issues in affected 
and/or neighbouring TSOs after the STA calculation. Final 
exchanges between the affected TSOs and the remaining 
capacities (RCs) after the calculation are presented in 
Figure 6-4. As part of the daily procedures, the Nordic RCC 
operator on duty reviewed the deterministic results and 
emailed the rest of the RCCs along with the TSOs facing 
adequacy issues. RE, REN, and RTE were not among the 
countries identified with adequacy concerns.
Regarding the probabilistic calculations from the PE tool, 
no inadequacy was identified in the SWE region during 
the relevant time frame. 
Furthermore, the results for all the SWE TSOs showed 
considerably high RCs, as shown in Figure 6-4. RC repre­
sents each TSO’s ability to meet its load using available 
generation. These results indicate no adequacy issues 
and no reliance on imports from neighbouring areas. 
Figure 6-4: RC statistic – final state per BDZ in SWE for the period 28/04/25 to 03/05/25.
A recently developed feature in the STA process allows 
the assessment of potential curtailment at the bidding 
zone level. This assessment is optional for TSOs, and only 
some currently use it. This analysis depends on input data 
classified as inflexible generation – generation that must 
run. The calculations then evaluate whether curtailment 
may be necessary and identify any surplus inflexible 
generation that cannot be consumed, while also consid­
ering the capacity to export this excess.
The must-run calculation results from RTE indicated no 
need for curtailment, as inflexible generation remained 
below the expected load. In the case of REN, the tool 
encountered a calculation error, so no meaningful results 
were available. For RE, no relevant data were provided 
for this feature; therefore, no calculation results are 
available. RE has already planned for the IT development 
to implement this capability in the STA process, with 
delivery planned in 2026.

6.2.2.3	
Analysis
The outcomes of the STA calculation are dependent on 
the quality of the input data received from the TSOs. This 
data is crucial for defining the deterministic scenarios 
with the expected cross-border flows and serves as the 
basis for the probabilistic scenarios. Unrealistic input 
data could result in incorrect adequacy predictions or 
failure to identify inadequacies.
To determine whether the difference in forecast accuracy 
was an isolated event occurring only before the incident 
or a more systematic discrepancy, the scope of the anal­
ysis was extended to the entire month of April 2025. 
Several metrics were then used to evaluate the forecast 
quality, including accuracy and coverage of probable 
events.
The accuracy was evaluated by the difference between 
the realised values (from TP) and the forecasted input 
data (from TSOs) for all MTUs. The results, displayed in 
Table 6-5, show that there is no significant difference 
between the incident day and the observed values 
throughout the month. The difference is even smaller on 
the incident day, except for the wind forecast in Portugal. 
It can also be observed that the magnitude of the differ­
ence values is significantly reduced compared with the 
installed capacity of the generation, shown in Table 6-6.

The most frequently observed values fall outside the 
90 % probability range, indicating a significant deviation 
from the forecast. This is evident for the solar forecast, as 
the timing of the forecast prevents the inclusion of RES 
limitations. The wind forecast shows accurate alignment. 
There is also a high frequency of wind forecasts in the 
upper range for Portugal, showing that actual values 
often exceed predictions, while the opposite trend is 
observed for France.
The analysis of input data quality reveals significant 
discrepancies between the forecasted values provided 
by the TSOs and the actual observations, particularly for 
solar forecasts. Nevertheless, the results of the process 
would remain unchanged, without any adequacy issues.
It is worth mentioning that, given the timing for the fore­
cast, limitations that affect RES (primarily solar in Spain) 
cannot be considered for the inputs to STA.
The second part of the analysis assesses the impact of 
those differences and forecast uncertainty on STA results, 
specifically whether the output would change if the 
input data were more accurate. A study was performed 
to assess the impact of input data on the results, where 
the forecast input data from the TSOs was replaced with 
the observed values for the day of the incident. The 
results indicate that cross-border flows are distinct, but 
the overall output of the STA process remains unchanged, 
with no issues in terms of adequacy and minimal impact 
on available capacity to meet demand.
6.2.2.4	
Conclusion
The STA process for the period preceding the incident 
was performed in accordance with its defined method­
ology, scope, and timelines as set out in Article 81 of the 
SO GL. All required input data were received prior to the 
execution of the D-1 calculations, successfully passed 
validation checks, and were used in the STA assess­
ment. The deterministic and probabilistic calculations 
were completed within the standard operational time 
frame, and no technical issues were reported during the 
process. The results were reviewed by the designated 
RCC operator, and no adequacy concerns were identified 
for the SWE region or the affected TSOs.
The STA results indicated sufficient RC for all relevant 
bidding zones, with no reliance on imports, and no 
identified risk to adequacy for the day of the incident. 
No regional STA process was triggered, and the outcome 
of the assessment was consistent with the absence of 
adequacy issues in real-time operation. Accordingly, the 
STA task was performed correctly and delivered results in 
line with its intended objective of assessing the balance 
between expected load and available generation 
capacity.
Regarding the incident under investigation, the STA 
process was not designed to identify or prevent events 
arising from operational security phenomena unrelated 
to adequacy. The STA process, within its defined scope, 
would not have been expected to identify or avert the 
incident. 
Nevertheless, the investigation identified limitations 
related to the quality and representativeness of input 
data, particularly for solar generation forecasts. Differ­
ences between forecasted and realised values were 
observed, and the coverage of probabilistic forecast 
ranges was found to be limited. These limitations did 
not affect the final conclusions for the incident day; even 
when the STA input data was retrospectively replaced 
with realised generation values, the overall outcome of 
the adequacy assessment remained unchanged, with 
no inadequacy detected. Nevertheless, they highlight 
areas where the robustness of the STA process could be 
enhanced, particularly in data quality monitoring. The 
monitoring of STA process performance is a continuous 
activity, undertaken jointly by RCCs and TSOs in dedicated 
ENTSO-E Task Teams. Work is ongoing to improve data 
quality monitoring, forecast accuracy, and methodolog­
ical alignment, in line with Articles 42 and 43 of the ACER 
decision on the amendment of the CSAm (13 May 2024).
Overall, the STA process fulfilled its intended function and 
was executed correctly. The results were reviewed, and 
no adequacy concerns were identified for the SWE region 
or the affected TSOs. While improvements in input data 
quality and forecast representativeness could further 
strengthen the accuracy of the assessment, they would 
not have altered the outcome of the STA assessment, nor 
enabled the identification or prevention of the incident 
under investigation.

6.2.3	
Common Grid Model
37	
UCTE DEF: Union for the Co-ordination of Transmission of Electricity Data Exchange Format.
38	
CGMES: Common Grid Model Exchange Specification.
As outlined in Table 6-3, the creation of common grid 
models (CGMs) is a responsibility assigned to RCCs under 
EU Regulation 2019/943, Article 37 (c). This task must 
be carried out in accordance with the methodologies 
and procedures established under the SO GL, developed 
pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 714/2009, as well as 
CACM and forward capacity allocation (FCA). CGMs serve 
as the foundation for regional and PE processes such as 
CSA, OPC, and CCC, and are produced by merging the indi­
vidual grid models (IGMs) provided by TSOs.
An IGM is a detailed model of a TSO’s control area, 
containing information on network topology, load, 
generation, and relevant operational data. Each TSO is 
responsible for creating and maintaining its own IGM 
using a standardised format to ensure compatibility with 
other TSOs’ models. Currently used standards include the 
Union for the Co-ordination of Transmission of Electricity 
Data Exchange Format (UCTE DEF)37 and Common Grid 
Model Exchange Specification (CGMES).38 UCTE DEF is 
a legacy standard created by the UCTE, which was the 
predecessor organisation to ENTSO-E. CGMES is an IEC 
(International Electrotechnical Commission) technical 
specification based on the IEC CIM (Common Information 
Model) family of standards.
In sum, a CGM is a consolidated network model produced 
by merging multiple IGMs from different TSOs. This 
provides a representation of a larger, interconnected 
portion of the power system, which is then utilised for 
system-wide processes. The CGM merging processes for 
different time horizons and regions are described in the 
following subsections.
6.2.3.1	
PE CGM in CGMES
The PE CGM is created by merging the IGMs of European 
TSOs while considering reference data programmes (PEVF 
or CGMA files) and boundary sets (BDSs). It is created for 
four different time horizons: ID, D-1, Two-Day-Ahead 
(D-2), and Year-Ahead (YA).
In accordance with SOC Decision Number 11 dated 
4 December 2019, the CGM is developed based on a 
rotational principle. Under this approach, CGM creation 
responsibilities are divided into groups based on time 
frames: Group 1 handles the D-1 and D-2 time frames, 
Group 2 is responsible for the ID time frame, and Group 
3 manages the YA time frame. Each group operates with 
two roles: main and backup.
At any given time, one RCC assumes one role within a 
specific group and carries out the CGM creation accord­
ingly. The rotation among RCCs occurs every four weeks – 
except for the YA time frame, which rotates annually – 
following a predefined schedule. The use of both main 
and backup roles ensures redundancy, as two RCCs work 
in parallel on the same time frame, ensuring that at least 
one CGM will always be available, even if the main RCC 
encounters technical or operational issues. 
The merging process using the CGMES format during 
the period when the disturbance occurred was facing 
challenges. Convergence issues are often encountered, 
and certain CGMs are not published. During the devel­
opment phase, one tactic used to identify problematic 
input files was to exclude them. This allowed the quality 
of the process to be assessed using the remaining files. To 
comply with the CGM methodology, RCCs jointly decided 
to discontinue this practice in the production environ­
ments as of Q3 2024. The end of this pre-emptive exclu­
sion practice led to lower publication rates for CGMES 
CGMs. However, the published CGMs fully considered all 
available input data and were in line with the European 
Merging Function (EMF) requirements.
According to the CGMM and following the adopted 
timings in the CGM building process (implemented on 21 
April 2025), the D-1 CGMES process begins at 18:00 – by 
which time all IGMs should be submitted – and concludes 
by 18:30, when validated CGMs for the relevant scenario 
become available via OPDE. Similarly, the D2CF CGMES 
process starts at 19:50 and ends at 20:00, with vali­
dated CGMs also made available through OPDE. For both 
processes, according to the rotation calendar, Coreso 
acted as the main RCC responsible for the merging, while 
SCC served as the backup RCC.

===== PAGE 409 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  409 
The intraday congestion forecast (IDCF) process operates 
on an hourly basis, with validated CGMs released every 
hour via OPDE. TSCNET served as the main RCC for the IDCF 
CGMES process, and Baltic RCC acted as the backup. 
For BD 28/04/25, all three SWE TSOs submitted valid 
D-2 and D-1 IGMs on time. However,11 TSOs from other 
regions did not provide D-2 IGMs, and five TSOs did not 
provide D-1 IGMs. Coreso’s D-1 merge was successful for 
eight out of 24 TSs, while the remaining 16 – including 
the 12:30 TS – were non-convergent. The backup D-1 
model from SCC for 12:30 was also non-convergent. 
For the D-2 process, neither Coreso’s nor SCC’s models 
converged for any TS.
For the ID merge, RTE delivered three batches (on 27 April 
2025 at 20:41 UTC and 28 April 2025 at 04:40 and 12:40 
UTC), REN delivered once, with 24 IGMs (on 27 April 2025 
at 21:27 UTC), and RE delivered four batches (27 April 
2025 at 20:47 and 23:08 UTC, and 28 April 2025 at 04:52 
and 12:51 UTC). The transition to more frequent ID IGMS 
of these TSOs is pending. Seven other TSOs did not deliver 
any valid ID IGMs for this business day. TSCNET, as the 
main merge operator, performed hourly merges for the 
business day, which were all non-convergent. The latest 
merge before the incident took place at 11:12. For this 
latest merge, the IGMs from all but two TSOs were more 
than one hour old. As the backup merge operator, Baltic 
RCC was able to create a convergent model at 07:51 by 
substituting models based on additional validation rules 
not yet harmonised at the European level. This was the 
latest convergent PE CGM in CGMES before the incident.
Overall, the merging process in the CGMES format is still 
undergoing improvements, and the resulting models 
were of only limited use. Since all regional and cross-re­
gional assessments are still based either on the legacy 
UCTE DEF merge or a regional CGMES merge, this had no 
impact on the incident under investigation. All security 
assessments regionally coordinated by Coreso, such as 
contingency assessments carried out within the capacity 
calculation process or the D-1 security assessment 
(legacy process), are performed using other models. The 
missing input data from other regions had no relevant 
impact on SWE.
In conclusion, while there were no available PE D-1 and 
D-2 CGMs in CGMES format at the time of the incident – 
only regional models for SWE, as explained below – this 
would not have made a difference.
6.2.3.2	
Regional CGMES CGM
In addition to the PE CGMs, Coreso carries out a regional 
merge of the D-2 and D-1 CGMES IGMs from REN, RE, and 
RTE on a daily basis, producing CGMs that are manda­
tory inputs for the D-1 and ID capacity calculations, 
respectively. 
For capacity calculation, the TSOs in SWE deliver: 
»	In D-2 (approximately 15:15 UCT), 24 models 
representing each hour of the day “D”, used for 
capacity calculation in D-2
»	In D-1 (approximately 15:30 UCT), 24 models 
representing each hour of the day “D”, used for 
capacity calculation in the first IDCC.
For both capacity calculation processes, CGMs are 
produced each evening for six TSs (02:30, 05:30, 09:30, 
12:30, 15:30, and 19:30) and shared with the TSOs as 
part of the process outputs. 
The latest regional SWE CGMES merge was completed 
before 19:30 on Sunday. All required input data was 
valid and delivered on time. The merge and load flow 
simulations were successfully executed for both time 
horizons.
6.2.3.3	
Continental Europe CGM in UCTE DEF
UCTE DEF is currently used for data exchange in various 
operational processes, including SA for SWE and other 
regions, and CCC in other regions. UCTE DEF is currently 
being replaced by CGMES. One major difference between 
UCTE DEF and the CGMES-based PE CGM implementation 
lies in the modelling approach: in UCTE DEF, models 
are built for all of Continental Europe, and each RCC 
additionally generates CGMs specifically for their own 
region. For example, for the day-ahead congestion 
forecast (DACF), Coreso produces a D-1 CGM for the SWE 
region (including applied model improvements), while 
SEleNe CC creates CGMs for southeast Europe. In this way, 
each RCC is responsible for developing CGMs tailored to 
its specific region.

===== PAGE 410 =====
410  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
The process of submitting and merging these individual 
models includes data validation. Detected issues are 
categorised by severity, which impacts the data’s suita­
bility for analysis:
»	Informational: Indicates minor data conditions 
or deviations that do not prevent the use of the 
model.
»	Warning: Signifies data inconsistencies or 
potential inaccuracies. Models with warnings 
may be used, but the associated data should 
be treated with caution.
»	Fatal Error: Denotes a data issue that makes 
the model unusable for its intended purpose. 
Processing is typically halted until the error is 
rectified.
Currently, UCTE DEF-based IGMs are merged per synchro­
nous area; in other words, the UCTE DEF CGM containing 
Spain, Portugal, and France will not include the Nordics.39 
In this subsection, the availability and validation of the 
affected TSO IGMs and the merge for the Continental 
Europe CGM in UCTE DEF are presented.
Since the IGMs are the starting point, the delivery of IGMs 
for the different time horizons is shown in Table 9. Each 
process has a different expected frequency of IGM crea­
tion. For D-1 and real-time snapshots (RTSN), one IGM 
per TS is expected, whereas for ID, it can go up to hourly 
delivery of IGMs before real time, e. g. after 12:30, new ID 
IGMs for 12:30 are not expected. 
As shown in Table 6-7, most of the IGMs were valid, 
meaning they contained no fatal errors. The missing 
values are due to REN not providing ID or RTSN IGMs, and 
RE not providing RTSN IGMs. The provision of RTSN files in 
UCTE DEF is not mandatory, and both REN and RE already 
provide ID IGMs in CGMES format – one batch for REN and 
four for RE – for the timings referenced in 6.2.3.1. The 
valid UCTE DEF IGMs include informational and warning 
messages. The only invalid IGM is for the ID time horizon 
and was submitted by RE one hour before real time. The 
model for TS 12:30 was generated at 11:16, which was 
the last ID IGM submitted for TS 12:30, since RE does not 
provide IGM every hour. Concerning RTSN, REN and RE 
provided RTSN models generated on demand for the 
incident investigation.

The RE ID IGM created at 11:16 for the 12:30 TS did not 
fulfil the quality check rules. RE ID IGM did not achieve 
convergence in RE’s legacy power system analysis tool, 
and consequently also in the UCTE DEF IGM model, due 
to a malfunction in RE’s tool responsible for modelling 
the status of reactors. High voltage shifts were provided, 
such as a 400 kV busbar operating at 280 kV. A substitution 
mechanism was applied to build up the corresponding 
ID UCTE CGM. Similar problems were observed on three 
separate days within the month: 4 April (one ID IGM), 
14 April (two ID IGMs), and 28 April (five ID IGMs). On 28 
April, out of the five affected models, four corresponded 
to the 10:30 TS and one to the 12:30 TS. The non-conver­
gence of the ES IGM in RE’s legacy power system analysis 
tool was not caused by grid conditions at that time, but 
rather by a bug in RE’s reactor management script.
Concerning CGMs, the DA IGMs are utilised for the DACF 
process. Coreso is the RCC performing the SA for the SWE 
region, which is further described in 6.2.5. During the 
DACF process, four CGM versions were created: at 18:00, 
18:27, 19:57, and 20:10. 
Based on all the provided ID IGMs, CGMs were created. All 
CGMs created that day for the TS 12:30 were convergent. 
It should be noted that invalid IGMs were not included; 
instead, the latest provided IGM was used. For example, 
for the last ID CGM40 created at 12:15, the ES IGM gener­
ated at 10:16 was utilised.

The substitution mechanism applied to the non-con­
verged IGM model delivered at 11:16 enabled the neces­
sary load flow and ID security assessment processes for 
the regions and TSOs using UCTE CGM. In any case, the 
non-convergence of the UCTE IGM RE model delivered at 
11:16 had no impact on the incident. 
6.2.3.4	
Conclusion
The CGM-related tasks relevant to the SWE region were 
performed in accordance with the applicable method­
ologies and operational practices, and any limitations 
observed in the PE CGMES processes did not affect system 
security or contribute to the incident under investigation.
Although convergent PE CGMES CGMs were not avail­
able for the D-1, D-2, and ID time horizons, this situa­
tion resulted from known and documented challenges 
in data completeness and model convergence at the 
European level. In line with the CGM methodology, the 
discontinuation of pre-emptive IGM exclusion ensured 
methodological compliance, even at the cost of lower 
publication rates. These constraints were external to the 
SWE region and did not compromise regional opera­
tional processes.
For SWE, all CGM inputs required for operational 
decision-making were available and fit for purpose. 
Regional grid models in CGMES format for D-1 and D-2 
were successfully created by Coreso using complete and 
timely IGMs from REN, RE, and RTE, and were effectively 
used in the capacity calculation processes. In addition, 
D-1 security assessments relied on legacy UCTE DEF CGMs, 
which were fully convergent and produced in accordance 
with established procedures. Isolated issues affecting 
individual ID IGMs, notably the non-convergent RE 
model at 11:16, were appropriately managed through 
substitution mechanisms and did not affect the validity 
of the resulting CGMs used by other regions, other than 
SWE, for the ID operational security assessment. It seems 
of interest to clarify that the resulting CGM mentioned 
previously, where a substitution strategy was applied 
for the non-converging RE IGM, is not used as input for 
security assessment in SWE. 
Consequently, the CGM creation tasks applicable to SWE 
were executed as intended, and the unavailability or 
limited usability of PE CGMES CGMs had no operational 
impact on SWE security assessments and no causal or 
contributory role in the incident.
6.2.4	
Coordinated Capacity Calculation
The capacity calculation process described in this section 
refers to the regulated task that follows the CACM Guide­
line EU 1222/2015. As explained in 6.1.2, the SWE region 
has some specificities that define how cross-border 
capacities are calculated. Coreso performs the NTC-based 
capacity calculation using a coordinated methodology 
developed by SWE TSOs (REN, RE, and RTE) and approved 
by ACER and the NRAs. This task is currently performed for 
the following time frames:
»	CCC Long-Term (LT) SWE: Currently performed 
on the TSO side. Under development at Coreso.
»	CCC DA SWE: Performed two days ahead and 
calculates total transfer capacities (TTC) for six 
TSs for the DA market.
»	CCC ID SWE: Two different runs apply:
–	 1st run: Performed one day ahead and calcu­
lates TTC for six TSs for the ID market.
–	 2nd run: Performed on the same day and 
calculates TTC for three TSs in the afternoon 
for the remaining ID market gates. This task 
is live as of 22 October 2025. 
Based on a set of inputs from SWE TSOs (namely IGMs, 
GSKs, and CRACs, all in CGMES format), Coreso calculates 
TTC for a limited number of TSs (02:30, 05:30, 09:30, 
12:30, 15:30, and 19:30) and for each border and direc­
tion independently. The calculated TTCs are sent as a 
proposal to the TSOs, who validate the proposal and allo­
cate capacities for the 24-hour period by extrapolation. 
As part of the CCC DA SWE process, Coreso shall ensure 
that the proposed NTC fulfils the minimum capacity 
requirements according to Article 16 (8) of the Electricity 
Regulation.
To achieve this, a threshold is defined over the maximum 
rating of the most limiting CNEC. Using calculated PTDFs 
and NTCs, the margin available for cross-zonal trade on 
the most limiting CNEC is assessed. If this margin is lower 
than 70 % of the rating, an additional NTC (ANTC) is added 
to the calculated NTC to obtain the proposed NTC. This 
virtual capacity is considered non-secure capacity and 
may be limited by a maximum available countertrading 
stated by TSOs within operational and security limits. 
Coreso then processes the TSOs’ feedback to determine 
the final TTC for each border and direction. 

===== PAGE 412 =====
412  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
To calculate the final output sent to markets, NTC, the 
following formula and parameters are applied:
»	NTC = TTC – transmission reliability margin (TRM)
»	TRM is 7.5 % of TTC for the Spain–France border, 
with a minimum of 200 MW.
»	TRM is 1 0 % of TTC for the Portugal–Spain 
border, with a minimum of 100 MW.
Fallback values may be applied either if the TTC cannot be 
calculated or if the calculated TTC values are lower than 
the TRM values listed above. In such cases, the following 
fallback values are applied per process: 
»	For the CCC DA SWE process, the fallback values 
applied are TTC from the CCC LT SWE process. 
»	For CCC ID SWE processes, the fallback values 
applied are the available TTC from previous 
time frames. In the case of BD 28/04/2025, the 
fallback for CCC ID SWE (first run) is to use the TTC 
values from the CCC DA SWE process.
Although the task is well-established in the SWE region, a 
significant milestone was reached in February 2025 with 
the introduction of a new tool for the CCC D-1 process, 
replacing the previous technology. 
In contrast, for the CCC ID process, the new tool was 
launched in March 2025.

6.2.4.5	
 Conclusion 
The CCC task for the SWE region was performed in accord­
ance with the approved methodologies and within the 
defined operational timelines for the relevant long-term, 
D-1, and ID time frames. All required inputs from the SWE 
TSOs were received, validated, and processed, and the 
CCC D-1 and ID calculations for BD 28/04 were completed 
successfully. Where TTC values could not be computed or 
fell below the applicable TRM, the predefined fallback 
procedures were correctly applied, and long-term or D-1 
TTC values were used in line with the approved meth­
odology. The proposed capacities were validated by the 
TSOs and confirmed as final values without adjustment.
For the directions relevant to the real-time exchanges 
observed at BD 28/04, TS 12:30, the TTC and resulting 
NTC values provided to the market were within the range 
of values observed historically in 2025. The application 
of fallback values, including for the ES → FR direction in 
both the D-1 and ID processes, followed the established 
rules and did not result in atypical capacity levels when 
compared to the distribution of past outcomes. No proce­
dural deviations, calculation failures, or validation issues 
were identified in the execution of the CCC task.
With respect to the incident under investigation, the CCC 
process is designed to determine cross-border market 
capacities in compliance with operational security 
constraints, rather than to anticipate or prevent real-time 
system events. The capacities provided to the market 
were based on the contingency analyses and network 
conditions considered within the CCC framework and 
were confirmed by the TSOs during the validation phases. 
Accordingly, the CCC task, as designed and applied, would 
not have been expected to identify or avert the incident.
The investigation did not identify deficiencies in the 
execution of the CCC process. 
Overall, the CCC task was executed correctly and in line 
with the approved methodology. Within its defined 
scope and objectives, it fulfilled its intended function and 
did not contribute to, nor was it capable of preventing, 
the incident under investigation.
The underlying SAs performed by Coreso assess the limits 
associated with power flows and voltage (permanent 
limits and voltage phase angle) related to operational 
security limits.

6.2.5	
Coordinated Security Analysis
The implementation of the CSA methodology via the 
ROSC process, which will eventually replace the current 
SA service, is still under development, with an expected 
go-live of Q1 2027 for the SWE region. SA for the SWE 
region is conducted by Coreso daily using the DACF grid 
models in the D-1 time frame. This analysis is based on 
coordinated procedures and relies on the Continental 
Europe CGM in UCTE-DEF, as described in 6.2.3. Since 
the SA is performed on steady-state grid models, it only 
considers power flows and not dynamic security limits, 
while voltage limits are not assessed regularly due 
to data format and modelling limitations. Regarding 
its scope, SAs are run for the whole day, while RAs are 
proposed by Coreso operators for the worst TS for each 
constraint, in close coordination with the SWE TSOs. 
Currently, SAs in the ID time frame are not operational 
for the SWE region. 
The SA DA process for the CORE, IN, and SWE regions 
unfolds in a tightly coordinated sequence beginning the 
day before16:00 and concluding by midnight. 
It starts with the delivery of IGMs from the TSOs and 
the availability of market results, which serve as the 
foundational inputs for the process. By 18:00, the first 
version of the CGM (CGM V1) is generated. This version 
is then refined through several targeted improvements 
per region. For the SWE region, for example, Coreso 
adapts the tap position of the PSTs on the FR–ES border 
based on N-state loading and TSO operational guide­
lines to ensure the base case reflects a realistic scenario. 
At 18:15, a second, enhanced version of the CGM (CGM 
V2) is produced, incorporating these improvements. 
The process continues at around 18:30 – 18:45 with 
the launch of the SA for all regions and 24 TS, where 
the system’s robustness is assessed against potential 
contingencies. Once the SA results are available, the 
operator interprets them and identifies the most rele­
vant constraints within the Main and Extended area for 
the SWE region, as detailed in 6.1.2. Once selected, the 
worst-case TS for each constraint is analysed, addressing 
N-1 violations through the implementation of RAs. The 
applicability of these proposed actions is then verified 
through direct communication with the relevant TSOs. If 
confirmed, the actions are documented in the report; if 
not, the Coreso operator seeks and proposes alternative 
solutions.
By 21:00, Coreso, in collaboration with the TSOs, evalu­
ates and coordinates RAs to address any identified issues. 
At 21:00, the Daily Operational Planning Teleconference 
(DOPT) is used to exchange and consolidate relevant 
cross-border data. The process then moves into the 
impact and deviation assessment phase at 22:00, which 
includes a specific study for the Central Eastern Europe 
(CEE) region. 
A combined DACF CGM is built with the CGMs of Coreso 
and TSCNET, including all agreed preventive RAs from the 
study. At 22:30, the proposed RAs are confirmed with the 
TSOs, ensuring alignment and readiness. Finally, before 
midnight, the comprehensive D-1 Report (summarising 
the entire SA, including all assessments and confirmed 
actions) is published, marking the conclusion of the SA 
DA process.
As mentioned earlier, for the SWE region, no SA ID 
process is operational on the RCC side: instead, it is 
performed solely on the TSO side. This process is used 
to reassess the security situation with updated inputs, 
enabling more accurate results and solutions. Coreso 
provides SA ID services for the CORE and IN regions and 
supports TSOs from these regions during the close-to-
real-time time frame as part of continuous monitoring 
and when requested. However, these services, which 
are voluntarily contracted by TSOs in other regions, are 
not provided for the SWE region, as the respective TSOs 
have not identified them as necessary or beneficial for 
this region. 
For the 12:30 TS on 28 April 2025, the DA CGM used was 
the last one created around 18:00 on the previous day, 
following the standard procedure for SA DA activities. 
The study reveals that TS 12:30 was a non-stressed TS, 
meaning that no need for coordination of RA was fore­
casted in the D-1 time frame. 

===== PAGE 416 =====
416  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
6.2.5.1	
Overview of the Study for BD 28/04
The study concluded that critical constraints were 
detected on the France–Spain (FR–ES) border, requiring 
countertrading of up to 300 MW at 05:30, along with 
extreme curative tap positions in the Arkale PST to resolve 
the issue. Additional constraints were identified on the 
Spain–Portugal (ES–PT) border and within the internal 
Spanish grid. These were manageable through the usual 
topological RAs and internal redispatch.
Additional relevant information used during the SA DA 
SWE included the planned outage of interconnection 
tie-lines and the tight downwards generation margin 
announced by REN. There was no specific request to 
study N-2 contingencies, as the weather forecast was 
favourable.
