N-state Physical Flows
As explained earlier, the SWE region consists of two 
borders with a lower degree of interaction than in other 
regions, such as CORE. The main consequence is that, in 
general, the difference between commercial and phys­
ical flows is smaller. Consistent with the previous section, 
the highest N-state flows observed on the main corridors 
of the Spain–France border are all in the Spain-to-France 
direction, either in the early morning or evening. Since 
the capacity calculation process accounted for planned 
outages, the reported capacities did not require signifi­
cant tap adaptation to manage flows.
The Spain–Portugal border has a high level of transfer 
capacity due to the nine tie-lines in operation. However, 
their distribution along the border is not balanced, with 
greater meshing in the north than in the south. 
The lower meshing in the south part of the border means 
that the planned outages in the south impact both the 
N-state and N-1 loadings of tie-lines nearby. Addition­
ally, it is worth mentioning the apparent loop in phys­
ical flows in the northern portion of the Spain–Portugal 
border in the morning, where some tie-lines export 
while others import. This behaviour is quite common in 
this part of the border due to the high level of meshing. 
Since none of the high-loading values occurred near 
12:30, the main conclusion is that this period was indeed 
less constrained in the D-1 time frame.
SA DA Study Results
Constraints were detected either in the morning or 
evening hours, mainly on the FR-ES border (Argia–
Hernani, Arkale–Hernani, Hernani–Itxaso) and ES–PT 
border (Falagueira–Cedillo, Aldeadavila–Lagoaca). 
They were resolved using 300 MW countertrading (FR↑, 
ES↓), PST tap changes at Arkale (from 17 to 1 in steps), 
transformer disconnections at Argia, and internal redis­
patch by RE (400 MW) and REN (800 MW). 
Coreso proposed RAs to bring all N-1 loadings below the 
100 % threshold for each of the detected contingency 
constraints for BD 28/04.
6.2.5.2	
Further Analysis
The CSA process relies on input data provided by TSOs. 
The list of contingencies specifies the cases to be simu­
lated, while the list of monitored elements defines the 
elements to be monitored during the process. If a certain 
contingency is not simulated, the state of the grid under 
that scenario is not assessed. Similarly, if a monitored 
element is not included in the list, potential violations 
may go undetected.
Articles 76 and 77 of the SO Regulation constitute the 
legal basis for the regional proposal of CSA (ROSC meth­
odology) and define several specific requirements that 
the methodology proposal should consider. SWE TSOs 
made a proposal in 2019 with an explanatory note.
On 3 December 2020, the SWE NRAs issued a decision, in 
which they agreed on 10 July 2020 to request amend­
ments to the proposed methodology regarding:
»	The definition of the relevant XNE
»	The coordination between TSOs and the RCC to 
select a new set of RAs when a recommended 
RA is no longer needed
»	The “on-request coordinated operational 
security assessment” process and updates to 
the TSOs’ IGMs
»	The implementation timeline
For the contingency scenarios:
According to Article 13 of the SWE ROSC methodology, 
which implements Article 76 of the SO Regulation and 
was approved by SWE NRAs in December 2020, SWE TSOs 
are required to send their contingency list, including 
both ordinary and exceptional contingencies, with each 
clearly classified.

===== PAGE 418 =====
418  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
Even under the same article and in accordance with 
the SO Regulation, contingencies that do not comply 
with the not comply with the N-1 criterion may be 
excluded, provided that such exclusions are properly 
communicated.
Limitations of the current SA DA SWE process:
The current SA DA process in the SWE region is imple­
mented in line with the processes agreed between TSOs 
and Coreso. The geographical scope of the SA DA SWE is 
defined by network elements identified as cross-border 
relevant under the regional methodologies, ensuring a 
focused and proportionate assessment at the regional 
level. Internal network elements outside this scope are 
addressed through national processes.
The SA DA process is currently performed in the D-1 
time frame and does not include an IDCF reassessment 
following ID market trading, such as changes in dispatch 
or voltage management actions. The assessment relies 
on predefined contingency lists and a defined set of 
assessed elements. For cross-border critical outages, 
one target scenario is assessed, and RAs are evaluated 
through established coordination procedures. 
The current SA process performed by RCC is expected 
to evolve with the implementation of ROSC. ROSC will 
extend the temporal scope of CSAs to the ID time frame 
and support more frequent reassessments reflecting 
updated system conditions. It will also enable a broader 
and more systematic coverage of network elements for 
which RAs would be proposed, enhanced contingency 
assessment capabilities, and improved coordination of 
RAs, including voltage-related aspects, thereby strength­
ening the overall robustness and consistency of regional 
SA. The transition from UCTE DEF to CGMES will also enable 
appropriate consideration of voltage limits.
6.2.5.3	
Conclusion
The UCTE DEF-based CSA in the D-1 time frame, currently 
implemented in the SWE region through the SA DA 
process, was performed in accordance with the agreed 
and coordinated operational procedures, not yet in 
line with the applicable regional methodology (ROSC 
methodology pursuant to Article 76 of SO GL). The SA 
DA process for BD 28/04 was executed using the latest 
available CGM generated on the previous day, following 
the standard timeline and incorporating validated TSOs’ 
inputs, market results, planned outages, and declared 
generation margins. SAs were conducted for the full day, 
relevant contingencies were assessed, and preventive 
and curative RAs were proposed and coordinated with 
the concerned TSOs through established processes.
For BD 28/04 at TS 12:30, the SA DA identified this TS as 
non-stressed, with no forecasted need for coordinated 
RAs. Constraints detected in the SA DA process were 
limited to morning and evening periods and were 
addressed through countertrading, PST tap changes, 
transformer switching, and internal redispatch. None of 
the identified constraints or RAs was associated with the 
midday period corresponding to the incident. The CSA 
process, as currently implemented in the SWE region, is 
limited to the D-1 time frame and relies on predefined 
contingency lists, monitored elements, and the available 
information at that stage. 
ID CSA is not operational at the RCC level for the SWE 
region and remains the responsibility of TSOs at the 
national level. The CSA framework is not designed to 
capture real-time operational dynamics or unforesee­
able, rapidly evolving conditions occurring after the D-1 
assessment. Accordingly, the CSA process, as designed 
and applied, would not have been expected to identify 
or prevent the incident under investigation. The SWE 
network is characterised by limited cross-border power 
flow interdependencies, enabling TSOs to adequately 
assess their networks, from a contingency assessment 
point of view, within their observability areas based on 
schedule information and to bilaterally coordinate any 
necessary RAs. Consequently, the added value of closer 
regional coordination performed by an RCC is more 
limited in the SWE region compared to other regions 
with higher structural interdependencies.
The UCTE DEF-based CSA performed by the RCC did not 
foresee the voltage collapse because it is not designed 
to, as elaborated in the previous section.

6.2.6	
Other RCC Tasks
6.2.6.1	
Emergency and Restoration Plans Consistency Check (NC ER)
In accordance with Article 6 of the NC ER, TSOs shall review 
their defence and restoration plans at least every five 
years, with a subsequent consistency assessment. RCCs 
are responsible for evaluating the coherence of specific 
measures, including inter-TSO assistance, frequency 
management, active power support, and top-down 
re-energisation. Following this consultation, the relevant 
RCC will prepare a technical report assessing the consist­
ency of the measures implemented by the TSOs.
This task was last performed and completed in 2024, 
the second time since it was established. Coreso eval­
uated the defence and restoration plans for the SWE 
region and verified the existence of the necessary 
agreements outlining the procedures to be applied 
during emergency, blackout, or restoration states by 
RE, REN, and RTE. TSOs provided Coreso with references 
to the most recent versions of these documents, and 
no inconsistencies were identified between RTE and 
RE, or between RE and REN.
6.2.6.2	
Regional Incident Analysis and Reporting
RIAR is the RCC task based on the requirement outlined 
in Article 37 (1) (i) of EU Regulation 2019/943 and ACER 
decision 04/2022. In this task, all RCCs jointly investigate 
the role of RCC tasks connected with incidents above a 
specific threshold. Since the establishment of the RCCs in 
2022, the only incident before April 2025 that was above 
the threshold was the Scale 3 incident (blackout) in 
South-East Europe (SEE) on 21 June 2024. The system split 
on 24 July 2021 occurred before RCCs were established.
The investigation into the SEE blackout was completed 
on 25 February 2025 with the publication of the final 
report. With this report, the RCCs issued two recommen­
dations for all ENTSO-E TSOs connected to the RCC tasks: 
one aiming at a more frequent update of the ID IGMs, 
the other addressing the voltage accuracy of the grid 
models. Both recommendations are also applicable to 
SWE, but are expected only in mid-2026. As of 28 April 
2025, they were still pending, in line with the recom­
mended timeline. 
The TSOs included an additional recommendation 
concerning RCC tasks, aimed at resolving the tie-line 
rating inconsistencies in the SEE area. Generally, such 
inconsistencies are not limited to SEE but are also 
present in SWE. However, the recommendation only 
addressed the affected TSOs and did not include other 
TSOs. In contrast to the system split on 4 November 
2006 in Germany, the tie-line rating inconsistencies did 
not contribute to the incident in SEE. Since RCCs gener­
ally consider the lower limits in regional processes, 
the impact of such inconsistencies is limited to local 
processes and not considered critical for RCC processes.
In addition to the mandatory RCC task of RIAR, Coreso 
provides a voluntary service to its shareholders: a “post-
event analysis” service, which offers a basic investigation 
of incidents below the threshold. This may also involve 
the use of post-operational data, such as RTSN. 
6.2.6.3	
Crisis Scenarios 
RCCs play a defined role in ENTSO-E’s process of identi­
fying regional crisis scenarios. This role is described in 
the risk preparedness regulation and further elabo­
rated in the methodology for identifying regional elec­
tricity crisis scenarios, which was amended by ENTSO-E 
and RCCs in 2023 and submitted to ACER. The amended 
methodology, which addresses the role of RCCs at the 
different stages of the process for updating the regional 
crisis scenarios, was approved by ACER on 8 March 2024. ​
The methodology describes four stages of updating the 
regional electricity crisis scenarios: ​
»	Establishing a list of regional electricity crisis 
scenario candidates, starting with the previous 
list and providing updates
»	Compiling a list of regional electricity crisis 
scenarios for evaluation
»	Evaluation and ranking of electricity crisis 
scenarios
»	Reporting on the most relevant regional elec­
tricity crisis scenarios

===== PAGE 420 =====
420  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
In all stages, the RCCs are supporting ENTSO-E, and TSOs 
are consulted or informed. ENTSO-E has the final respon­
sibility for the report and the different process steps. 
This process delivers the most severe regional electrical 
crisis scenarios every fourth year. The TSOs are required 
to evaluate the inclusion of the regional electrical crisis 
scenarios in their risk preparedness plans.​
In 2024, the regional electrical crisis scenarios were 
updated. This process resulted in the analysis of 23 
scenarios, which can have different root causes, such 
as natural events (e. g. weather, earthquakes), anthro­
pogenic causes (e. g. physical attacks), or other factors. 
So far, the investigation has identified no correlation 
between the incidents listed in the regional electricity 
crisis scenarios and the incident under investigation.
6.2.7	
Outcome of the RCC Investigation
The RCC investigation reviewed the coordinated tasks 
applicable to the SWE region in relation to the event of 
BD 28/04. The review considered the objectives, scope, 
and execution of each task, considering the conditions 
observed before the incident.
Across all assessed tasks, the investigation found that the 
coordinated processes were carried out in line with the 
applicable methodologies, timelines, and roles defined 
at the regional level. The analyses performed did not 
identify abnormal conditions or elevated risks for the 
time frame corresponding to the event, and the outputs 
of the different tasks were mutually consistent within 
their respective horizons and assumptions. These anal­
yses primarily focus on steady-state power flows and 
do not assess dynamic or voltage-related operational 
security limits.
The review also highlights that each coordinated task 
addresses specific aspects of system planning and oper­
ation, using forecasted inputs, predefined contingency 
sets, and fixed assessment horizons. As such, the RCC 
tasks provide a structured and forward-looking view 
of system conditions, but they are not designed to fully 
represent real-time operational dynamics or to antici­
pate rare, multifactorial events evolving over short time 
horizons.
In the context of the SWE region, the limited level of 
interdependence in terms of flows between borders 
means that many operational situations can be effec­
tively managed at the national level, with regional 
coordination providing additional support where cross-
border impacts are expected. This characteristic influ­
ences both the scope of RCC tasks and the extent to which 
regional coordination contributes to the management of 
events such as the one observed on BD 28/04.
During the incident under investigation, discussions 
highlighted several areas where the effectiveness 
and robustness of coordinated tasks could be further 
strengthened over time. These include improvements 
in data quality and forecast representativeness, closer 
continuity between planning and operational assess­
ments, improvements in the modelling in the CGM used 
in CSA to assess voltage limits, and the extension of CSA 
into the ID time frame through the forthcoming imple­
mentation of ROSC. These developments are already 
underway within the existing regulatory framework and 
reflect the ongoing evolution of regional coordination.
Overall, the investigation concludes that the RCC tasks 
provided an appropriate assessment of system condi­
tions within their defined scope, considering current 
modelling and process limitations. While the event of 
BD 28/04 unfolded outside the temporal and analytical 
reach of the coordinated tasks in place at the time, the 
findings of this investigation are in line with ongoing 
improvements in regional coordination and operational 
security arrangements.

6.3.4	
Technical Constraints Process
49	
It was modified in October 2025.
50	
The Spanish technical constraints market is a local market that provides solutions for technical constraints in the distribution network when it involves the 
redispatch of generation units above 1 MW. 
The technical constraints process of the Spanish power 
system is described in P.O.3.2. The one in force on 
28 April49 is described here. 
In line with P.O. 3.2, a technical constraint is defined as 
“any circumstance or incident in the electrical system 
that, because of its impact on the electricity supply secu­
rity, quality and reliability in line with the applicable 
P.O.s, require, pursuant to the SO technical assessment, 
the modification of the energy programs. In particular, 
Technical Constraints can be identified because of:
a) Non-compliance of the security conditions in steady-
state or after contingency, as defined in the P.O. that 
establish the criteria for the operation and security of 
the power system.
b) Insufficient secondary and/or tertiary reserve.
c) Insufficient reserve capacity to ensure generation-­
demand adequacy.
d) Insufficient reserve capacity to control voltages in the 
transmission network.
e) Insufficient reserve capacity for system restoration.”
The constraints solution process is applied to:
»	The constraints in the transmission grid, which 
are assessed with respect to the requirements 
of Article 34 of the SO GL, and
»	The constraints in the distribution grid,50 
communicated to RE by the distribution SOs. 
As a result, RAs are ordered as needed, considering the 
activation time required.
6.3.5	
Voltage Consideration Within the Technical Constraints Process 
(P.O. 7.4) 
TSO operational security assessments monitor, for each 
element, overloads, short-circuit currents, angular differ­
ences, and voltage values, both in the base case and 
under contingency conditions. 
Load flow calculations are performed as part of the 
operational planning processes described in Title 6.3.4, 
on D-1, ID, and continuously (at least every 10 minutes). 
These calculations verify that the thermal and voltage 
limits specified in P.O. 1.4 are respected for contingencies 
listed in Article 4.3.2 of P.O. 1.1, in line with Article 33 of 
the SO GL.
In accordance with Article 29 (3) of the SO GL, to manage 
voltage variations inherent to the network evolution and 
dispatch conditions, measures are implemented already 
in the base case pursuant to P.O. 3.2 and P.O. 7.4, in force 
on 28 April 2025, requiring the dispatch of conventional 
generation units capable of providing real-time voltage 
control. 
Resources to ensure voltage control are described in 
section 4.1.

6.3.6	
Criteria, Tools, and Data in the SAs Within the Technical 
Constraint Process 
The volume of dispatched units is established by consid­
ering the programmed operational scenarios, which 
are characterised by network status parameters at both 
the global and zonal levels and informed by historical 
cases with similar network conditions and schedules. 
Consequently, units with real-time voltage control capa­
bility that are deemed necessary are programmed for 
scenarios typically characterised by:
»	A low number of scheduled conventional 
power units in one or more regions (based on 
market schedules) and
»	Low transmission network load (based on 
international schedules and renewable gener­
ation forecasts).
Additionally, assessments are regularly performed in the 
control room to check limits in contingency cases. When 
simulated contingencies show a case with voltages out 
of range, an evaluation is conducted and RAs are sched­
uled, including: 
»	Modification of line status (open/close)
»	Shunt reactors switching/disconnection
»	Dispatch of additional conventional power 
units to maintain voltage or to ensure it 
remains within acceptable limits in the event 
of contingencies
The input data and tools used to perform the security 
assessments in operational planning and real time, as 
referred to in the previous paragraph, are: 
»	Forecast cases (PSS/E format) built every hour 
at hh:15 using the GENES tool, covering each 
of the remaining hours of the current day and 
the 24 hours of the following day, with the 
following information:
–	 International schedules (e.SIOS)
–	 Production and storage unit schedules (avail­
able on the e.SIOS platform), including to 
disaggregation of programming units into 
physical units
–	 Grid and production unit unavailabilities 
(DESC and e.SIOS databases) 
–	 TSO forecasts for demand, solar, and wind 
generation (Delfos forecast modules)
»	Real-time (state estimation) cases built at 
least every 10 minutes. Data for the analysis 
are retrieved from SCADA, and load flow calcu­
lations are performed by the state estimator. 
Load flow values and contingency assessment 
results are available in the PCs of control room 
operators responsible for network assessment 
(transmission network operators and network 
operators in regional desks) in the different 
electrical regions. The information is presented:
–	 In predesigned charts and screens tailored 
for each electrical region of the Spanish 
transmission network, allowing continuous 
monitoring of actual and historical voltage 
values at pilot nodes. Additional graphs and 
tables enable tracking of trends and other 
relevant variables.
–	 In tables showing constrained element 
(thermal limits, voltage magnitudes, voltage 
phase angles, and short-circuit currents). 
–	 Real time/state estimation cases manually 
adjusted by the operator, for situations 
deemed necessary when electrical parame­
ters indicate a potential risk of limit violation. 
In such cases, the operator can trigger an ad 
hoc manual contingency assessment. 
Forecast scenarios (GENES) are used for the technical 
constraints process, which runs on D-1 and after the 
first ID auction. They are also used by operators when 
significant changes – like major outages, unavailabilities 
of generation units, or deviations from programming 
units – are communicated by market participants. 
It is current practice for operators to continuously monitor 
the system and trigger specific assessments based on 
their network experience and judgement. This involves 
adjusting real-time cases from the state estimator with 
the forecast information when operators detect poten­
tially risky trends in their regular monitoring of regional 
screens and graphs.
It is important to clarify that the simulations based on 
forecast scenarios, as well as the close-to-real-time 
security assessment performed by the TSO, must comply 
with regulations, consider contingencies in the contin­
gency list, and account for voltage control capabilities 
in line with legally established requirements. Assess­
ments are therefore performed using models and data 
delivered by system users for offline studies and SCADA 
representation.

6.3.7	
Overview of the Security Assessment and Actions for BD 28/04
On 28 April 2025, none of security assessments 
performed by the SO detected the risk of the cascading 
overvoltage that occurred after 12:30. 
The power system parameters were very different at 
12:30 from those assessed in previous operational plan­
ning time frames. Nevertheless, the contingency assess­
ment for the scenario around 12:30, based on structural 
data in line with operational procedures used by the TSO 
, indicated fulfilment of N-1 static security criteria. The 
cascading problem , as described in chapters 3 and 4 was 
unforeseeable by the applied security analysis.Below is 
an explanation of the most relevant decision timings and 
assessments, as well as the conditions considered on BD 
28/04. They can be summarised as follows:
»	At around 14:45 on 27 April 2025, D-1 technical 
restrictions were applied, with dispatching 
orders accounting for differences of approxi­
mately 2 GW in cross-border flows, as well as 
the typical uncertainty and variability of fore­
casts made many hours before real time.
»	At around 22:30 on 27 April 2025, after the 
unavailability of Thermal Unit 4 was declared, 
IDAs 1 and 2 and the continuous market 
showed smaller variations in cross-border 
flows, while still representing 1.6 GW and 
assessing the night period as the most sensible 
from a voltage control perspective.
»	At 9:00 on 28 April 2025, during the decision 
on whether to extend the limitation of Thermal 
Unit 5, a clear and increasing Spanish export 
tendency was observed, along with higher 
certainty in renewables programmes.
»	At 10:17 on 28 April 2025, after a sustained 
tendency towards import reduction, the ID 
market schedules indicated a net exporting 
situation across all periods, with a downward 
trend in gradients. 
»	Schedules following IDA  3 confirm the 
exporting programmes.
A) Day-Ahead Studies: 27 April between 13:30 and 14:45
With regard to units providing voltage support in real 
time, in line with P.O. 7.4 in force, a total of 10 thermal 
units were initially scheduled as a result of the D-1 
market and technical restrictions. These units were 
assessed as sufficient to provide the necessary voltage 
support. 
In particular, in the South zone, one nuclear power plant 
had been scheduled in the market, and two additional 
thermal units were redispatched by the TSO,to support 
voltage variations associated with variability in internal 
and external schedules. 
Those two units were selected in accordance with the 
technical and economic requirements and criteria set out 
in P.O. 3.2, as explained in 6.3.1.
It is relevant to detail the forecasted conditions at the 
time the needs were assessed during the D-1 technical 
restriction process, as well as their evolution in later ID 
assessments. 
On 27 April during the D-1 technical restrictions process, 
the following conditions were observed:
»	Strong gradients of photovoltaic production 
from 8:00 to 9:00 and 19:00 to 21:00.
»	Changes in cross-border programmes: Spain 
exports most hours but imports from Portugal 
at night and from France from 13:00 to 16:00, 
resulting in gradient changes between 2:00 
and 3:00 am and variability from 6:00 am until 
nearly the end of the day. 
»	Market prices (OMIE) – source of uncertainty in 
the production variation in Spain – decreasing 
from around 30 €/MWh to very low values 
(around 0 €/MWh) at 9:00 am, and then 
increasing from very low values at 20:00.

6.3.8	
Dynamic Stability Assessments
This section describes how Article 38 of the SO Regulation is currently implemented in Spain. 
6.3.8.1	
Offline Dynamic Stability Studies
Prospectively, as part of the analysis conducted to assess 
network development needs and the connection of 
new assets to the transmission network, offline dynamic 
stability studies are performed to assess the acceptability 
of dynamic conditions, in particular the maximum access 
capacity for generation per node and the fault clearing 
times These off-line dynamic stability assessments do 
consider transient thermal limits, voltage amplitude, 
rotor angle stability as well as frequency stability. In 
particular off-line dynamic voltage stability is assessed, 
under the perimeter of expected operational scenarios, 
to recommend a number of must-run of synchronous 
generation units, to assess the interest of dynamic 
voltage control network equipment capabilities, or to 
test the technical requirements to certain system users. 
Also, dynamic stability assessments are yearly conducted 
by Red Eléctrica to set the maximum value of the gener­
ation capacity that can be activated by the control room 
operator via the Active Power Reduction System (SRAP). 
Specific projects require ad hoc dynamic studies in close 
coordination with other TSOs, such as the new HVDC 
interconnection with France (Biscay Gulf) or the DSA 
performed in coordination with the neighbouring TSO 
(RTE) to assess the security of future higher cross-border 
exchange scenarios (8 GW). 
Additionally, at the synchronous area level, dynamic 
frequency stability assessments are regularly performed 
using jointly developed dynamic grid models. These 
assessments are coordinated, including, for example, 
discussions on the adjustment of power system stabi­
lisers (PSS) to mitigate inter-area oscillations. 
6.3.8.2	
DSA in Operation 
The DSA tool available in the control centre performs 
stability assessments close to real time every 15 minutes. 
It simulates the dynamics for approximately 20 s, with a 
minimum calculation step of 1 ms, for 35 critical contin­
gencies. Dynamic stability is evaluated with respect 
to frequency, voltage amplitude, phase angles, and 
thermal limits. Results are presented in the form of a 
semaphore indicating the main expected trends and risk 
probabilities. 
The tool is undergoing improvements, with several 
parameters being refined to improve result accuracy. 
On the day of the incident, the tool outputs were not 
integrated with the operative process/alarming system. 
Ex-post verificationretrieval of the DSA tool results 
show that the tool did not indicate any stability risks for 
timestamps 11:50 and 12:25 (just before and after the 
oscillations).

===== PAGE 431 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  431 
6.4	
Perspectives in forecasting oscillatory phenomena
52	
The importance for the TSOs to act quick and avoid the high risk associated to oscillations is also explained and stated in several reports: 
	
–	Spanish oscillation 2016 https://eepublicdownloads.entsoe.eu/clean-documents/SOC%20documents/Regional_Groups_Continental_Europe/2017/
CE_inter-area_oscillations_Dec_1st_2016_PUBLIC_V7.pdf, 
	
–	Italian oscillation 2017 https://www.entsoe.eu/Documents/SOC%20documents/Regional_Groups_Continental_Europe/OSCILLATION_REPORT_SPD.pdf
The prediction of inter-area or forced oscillations in an 
electric power system is a challenging topic still under 
discussion in the technical literature and in the world of 
operation and planning.
The approach to the problem must inevitably consider 
uncertainty factors. First and foremost, the dynamic 
network models needed to correctly represent oscil­
latory phenomena. The process of building detailed 
supranational dynamic models for planning purposes 
is still ongoing and needs to be further improved and 
accelerated, as also suggested in the recommendations 
section of the report.
In addition to a thorough understanding of mathemat­
ical modeling, validation and measurement tools such as 
WAMS and on-site recordings and tests at the generators 
are required.
Having achieved correct system modeling, it is possible 
to evaluate the preventive measures: Power System 
Stabilisers, STATCOMs, Synchronous Condensers, critical 
grid configurations (i. e. lines opening for maintenance, 
generators displacements, …), advanced system stabili­
zation techniques (i. e. Wide Area Control Systems).
The planning and projecting stage can also define correc­
tive interventions, such as Special Protection Schemes, 
advanced on line voltage control systems or Defence 
Plans improvements.
The availability of a correct modelling of the system 
jointly with a comparison with historical series of online 
monitoring of the system (i. e. WAMS) can help to deduce 
correlations between the triggering of oscillatory 
phenomena and particular grid topoligies or scenarios.
Some international research projects provide method­
ologies to forecast in advance with statistical approach 
the arising of an oscillation, but the level of uncertainty 
in the models (further complicated by the variability 
of renewables sources) illustrated thus far makes this 
stream still immature for systematic use, and real-time 
monitoring of the phenomena is more convenient in the 
immediate future.
Forecasting becomes even more challenging if, instead 
of predicting characteristic grid oscillations (e. g., inter-
area), one wishes to predict phenomena related to 
interactions between inverters or between inverters and 
conventional generators. The degree of non-linearity 
and stochastic sequence of events that drive the gener­
ators to amplify an oscillation is really difficult to be 
intercepted in advance. In other words, the operational 
experience shows that in several situations theoretically 
prone to trigger oscillations, the phenomenon does not 
appear and, in some other cases, apparently stable, the 
oscillations arise.
That said, currently real-time modeling and monitoring 
remain the most effective tools available for stud­
ying and defining oscillations control strategies. The 
predictive approach, taking into account the limitations 
described and the efforts required to improve the tools, 
could be a valuable support for operations in the future.
It is important to explain that solving oscillations, more­
over those of high amplitude, is an urgent priority 52 
because of the high risk they entail for the power system. 
The rapidity of the actions is key. Actions shall be taken, 
of course, paying attention to the actual parameters of 
the system. The control room operators’ sensitivity of 
the possible kV variations associated to the topological 
action is key (e. g. the operator is aware of the voltage 
levels in real time and of the few kV that the voltage 
would raise when closing a certain line). Additionally, 
operators have information on certain assets whose 
manoeuvre shall be prevented/limited.

7	
COMMUNICATION OF 
­SYNCHRONOUS AREA MONITORS 
AND BETWEEN TS0s
This chapter outlines the key communications between synchronous area monitors 
(SAMs) and the affected Transmission System Operators (TSOs) during the incident, 
highlighting the exchanges that supported situational awareness and operational 
coordination. In addition to these interactions, it also includes messages exchanged 
via the ENTSO-E Awareness System (EAS) platform, as well as email correspondence 
between SAMs and the TSOs related to this event. 
To maintain conciseness, the focus is on communications between TSOs; however, 
communications with significant grid users were also reviewed and considered 
during the analysis, despite not being detailed in this section.
7.1	
Communication between TSOs
Within the Continental Europe Synchronous Area, control 
actions and reserves are organised in a hierarchical 
structure with scheduling areas, monitoring areas, 
load-frequency control (LFC) areas, LFC blocks, and the 
synchronous area with two coordination centres. The 
coordination centres facilitate communication and 
cooperation among TSOs, helping solve inter-TSO issues, 
and coordinate responses to potential disruptions or 
changes in power demand and generation. The coordi­
nation centres’ role is carried out simultaneously by the 
TSOs Swissgrid and Amprion, with each responsible for 
a specific geographic portion of the synchronous area, 
ensuring that each TSO communicates with only one 
coordination centre. The TSOs affected by the incident on 
28 April 2025 are all serviced by Swissgrid.
In the Continental Europe Synchronous Area, coordi­
nation centres also fulfil SAM obligations according to 
Article 133 of the System Operation Guidelines (SO GL). In 
this role, they monitor the synchronous area’s frequency 
and other parameters and initiate international coordi­
nation, if needed. The SAM role is performed by Swissgrid 
in even-numbered months and by Amprion in odd-num­
bered months; therefore, Swissgrid was the active SAM 
during the event.
In the following, calls shown in blue are those with the 
SAMs designated for the Continental Europe Synchro­
nous Area, namely Swissgrid or Amprion.

CLASSIFICATION OF THE INCIDENT 
BASED ON THE ICS METHODOLOGY
The ICS methodology was originally developed in accordance with Regulation (EC) 
No 714/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 July 2009, as 
repealed the by Regulation (EU) 2019/943 of the European Parliament and of the 
Council of 5 June 2019 on the internal market for electricity (recast), and updated to 
fulfil the objectives and the security indicator requirements laid out in Article 15 of 
Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/1485 of 2 August 2017 establishing a guideline 
on electricity transmission system operation (SOGL). The definitions and concepts in 
this methodology are in line with Articles 15 and 18 of the SOGL and further extended 
to describe the real-time situation of the TSO’s system.

Figure 8-1: Incident classification scale
Figure 8-1 shows the criteria from the methodology and 
the corresponding scale, ordered by descending priority. 
An incident can comprise multiple events and meet 
various criteria. In this case, the highest criterion decides 
the scale of the incidents. In the case of a scale 2 or 3 
event, an investigation is conducted by an Expert Panel. 
While only the highest priority criterion is relevant for 
deciding the scale, the other criteria are also assessed. 

===== PAGE 448 =====
448  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
8.1	
Scale of the Incident
The highest-violated ICS criterion during this incident was a scale 3 blackout (OB3). This criterion is met if there is a 
loss of more than 50 % of demand or a total absence of voltage for at least three minutes, assessed based on the TSO’s 
control area. The lost load on 28 April 2025 was as follows:
»	25,638 MW for Spain (100 % of the demand in 
the Spanish Peninsula before the incident)
»	5,900 MW for Portugal (100 % of the demand in 
mainland Portugal before the incident)
»	7 MW for France (0.01 % of the demand before 
the incident).
Spain and Portugal also suffered a total absence of 
voltage. Therefore, both the loss of load and voltage 
criteria for OB3 were met. 
For France, the lost load was below 100 MW and there­
fore no L criterion was met. France’s highest criterion 
violation was an OV1 due to high voltage during the 
incident.
8.2	
RCC Investigation Threshold
The RCC post-operation and post-disturbances analysis and reporting (RIAR) methodology has been developed to 
define the respective RCC task in accordance with Article 37 (1)(i) of the Regulation (EU) 2019/943 of the European 
Parliament and of the Council of 5 June 2019 on the internal market for electricity. This methodology foresees an RCC 
investigation in addition to the work of the Expert Panel if both of the following criteria are met:
a.	 a TSO has moved from a normal or alert system state 
to an emergency system state as a result of actions 
taken by another TSO being in emergency, blackout, 
or restoration system state, and 
b.	 the incident has been confirmed as at least a scale 2 
incident as defined by the ICS methodology.
Post-analysis confirmed that Spain and Portugal were 
in a blackout and restoration state during the incident, 
meaning that the incident met the RCC investigation 
threshold to initiate the investigation. The conclusions 
of the RCC investigation are added as a dedicated chapter 
in the final report.
8.3	
Scale of all Violations Linked to the Incident
The OB3 was the most severe criterion violated during 
the incident in Spain and Portugal. Several other criteria 
were violated before the blackout occurred, which are 
presented in Table 8-1 and summarised below. When an 
incident meets several criteria, it is classified according 
to the criterion with the highest priority. Additionally, all 
sub-criteria information (i. e., ICS violations or events) 
is also collected. Figure 8-2 presents a timeline view of 
the ICS criteria violated during the incident. It should be 
noted that the violations of the criteria regarding loss of 
generation facilities (G) and loss of load (L) have been 
separated into smaller violations to better visualise the 
sequence of events and correlate the impact of these 
violations with the measured frequency and voltage 
during the incident. The following paragraphs consol­
idate the violations according to the ICS methodology 
and therefore do not fully align with the detailed time­
line presented in Figure 8-2.
In Spain, there was a loss of generation facilities (G0) at 
12:32, followed by a transformer trip at 12:32:57, which 
is classified as a scale 0 loss of network element (T0) 
violation, and a further 355 MW of generation tripped. 
Approximately 20 seconds later, at 12:33:16, there were 
successive trips of power generation facilities. These 
generation trips are classified as one G2 incident as they 
occurred within fifteen minutes and were greater than 
3,000 MW. Further T incidents occurred with the loss of tie 
lines and transmission lines in Spain. The trip of the HVDC 
interconnector was classified as a T2 ICS violation due 
to the impact on a neighbouring TSO with OV (voltage) 
violations in France. The disconnections of all tie lines 
between France and Spain split the Iberian Peninsula 
from CE (involving more than one TSO with a load larger 
than 5 % of the total load of the synchronous area before 
the separation, thus violating the RS2 criterion). The loss 
of load (L2) criteria was met after the generation loss, 
as automatic TSO system defence measures were acti­
vated with the tripping of pumps and distribution load 
shedding.

===== PAGE 449 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  449 
There was high-voltage violations in Spain during 
the incident that contributed to the trip of generation, 
although they did not meet the time threshold for a 
voltage violation as defined in the ICS methodology. 
Voltage was above 1.1 per unit for 16 seconds, whereas 
the ICS methodology requires a time of greater than 30 
seconds. The subsequent voltage collapse is captured 
under the OB3 (blackout) criteria.
Portugal experienced high voltage and – similarly to 
Spain – the duration did not reach the time thresholds 
specified in the ICS methodology, and therefore there 
were no OV incidents. There was a significant loss of load 
(L2) as pumps and industrial consumers were discon­
nected, as well as the distribution load. There were two 
T0 events with the loss of a transformer and an over­
head line. Additionally, a G2 violation was recorded at 
the time of the blackout, as all generation facilities were 
disconnected.
The highest criteria experienced in France by RTE 
was scale 1 related to OV1. France also had G0 and T0 
violations.
Frequency degradation (F) ICS criteria violation was a 
below scale (BS) violation (FBS). The reason is that the 
frequency deviation magnitude thresholds were met, 
but – similarly to the ICS voltage criteria (OV) – the dura­
tion of the deviations were not sufficiently long to be 
registered at a higher scale. Furthermore, the frequency 
deviations are registered at a synchronous area level, 
even if local anomalies might occur. 
All oscillations that occurred prior to the blackout – as 
detailed in this report – did not cause any ICS criteria 
violations.

9	
CONCLUSION AND 
RECOMMENDATIONS
9.1	
Summary
Overall, the investigation concludes that the blackout 
that affected Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025 was 
the result of multiple interacting factors. The incident 
evolved through a sequence involving a combination of 
voltage fluctuations and oscillatory phenomena, leading 
to widespread generation disconnections in Spain, 
particularly inverter-based resources, followed by a 
cascade of overvoltage disconnections and ­culminating 
in the loss of synchronism of the Iberian system with 
the Continental Europe Synchronous Area. The technical 
analyses indicate that the fast voltage increase was 
driven by a combination of interacting factors identified 
in the Root Cause Tree, which unfolded over very short 
timescales, leaving limited time for effective operational 
response. These include limitations in the availability and 
effectiveness of voltage control resources, the ­reactive 
power behaviour of connected assets, the protection 
settings of connected generators and the behaviour of 
small-embedded generation, compounded by limited 
observability.
The investigation relied on an extensive dataset 
collected from TSOs, DSOs, and SGUs, noting that 
collecting complete, high-quality, and timely data 
proved ­challenging and that some critical data remained 
missing, incomplete, or heterogeneous. 
This experience underlines the importance of robust 
data collection processes, standardisation, and clear 
obligations to ensure that future investigations can 
be conducted with adequate accuracy and complete­
ness. It also underscores the importance of all system 
users consistently fulfilling their obligations under the 
­applicable requirements.
The Expert Panel’s work has focused primarily on 
deriving clear, actionable recommendations to reduce 
the likelihood of similar events and strengthen the 
overall security and resilience of the European grid. 
These recommendations are the central outcome of the 
investigation and are structured into two categories:
(i)	 recommendations directly linked to the identified 
root causes, which are reflected graphically on the 
root cause tree (Figure 9-1); and
(ii)	 recommendations developed based on the investi­
gation results, for which the Expert Panel considers 
that implementation may be beneficial for all 
system actors, but which are not related to the root 
causes of this incident.

Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  453 
The increasing penetration of variable renewable and 
­distributed generation, further market integration, 
broader electrification, and evolving environmental 
and geopolitical risks place the European electricity 
system under increasingly challenging operational 
conditions, requiring higher levels of resilience. The 
recommendations address voltage control and reactive 
power management, oscillatory stability, and generation 
disconnection behaviour. They further aim to enhance 
the effectiveness of system defence mechanisms and the 
robustness and preparedness of restoration processes.
Ultimately, the recommendations outlined in this chapter 
­represent a comprehensive set of measures designed to 
enhance operational robustness, improve cross-stake­
holder information exchange, and help maintain a high 
level of ­security of supply across the European power 
system.
Where the recommendations in this chapter refer to 
“TSOs”, “DSOs”, “SGUs operating power-generating 
facilities”, “the national competent authorities”, etc., it 
is noted that the ­recommendations are targeted at all 
European TSOs, DSOs, SGUs operating power-generating 
facilities, national ­competent authorities, etc., and not 
only at those impacted by the ­investigated incident. 
The monitoring of the implementation of the recom­
mendations provided in this chapter does not fall within 
the mandate or remit of the Expert Panel. While volun­
tary, the ­recommendations are intended to prompt and 
support concrete action to help prevent the recurrence of 
similar events. Any responsibility for the consideration, 
follow-up and ­implementation of the ­recommendations 
lies with each addressee. However, none of the recom­
mendations imposes an obligation on their addressees 
to act or to omit any actions. This is without ­prejudice 
to the requirements applicable to TSOs, in particular, to 
­regularly monitor the appropriateness of the network 
operation tools required to maintain operational 
security and identify and implement improvements, if 
needed, taking into consideration the conclusions and 
recommendations stemming from the investigations 
into ICS incidents. Finally, the recommendations may 
serve as a basis for future regulatory development, 
inviting competent authorities to consider possible 
regulatory or implementation measures within their 
respective mandates, with a view to ensuring that the 
lessons learned from this incident are duly reflected in 
the applicable requirements and establishing a frame­
work aimed at preventing similar incidents in the future.

9.2	
Observations on the Applicable Requirements 
The scope of this investigation and the mandate of the 
Expert Panel do not provide it with any authority or 
­intention to interpret the applicable legislation or to 
determine liabilities for non-compliance with legal 
requirements. During the investigation, within the 
limits of its mandate, the Expert Panel made several 
­observations regarding the applicable requirements. 
These observations are not to be interpreted as 
­recommendations in the final report, and are included 
without prejudice to any inquiries and/or follow-up 
actions carried out by the competent national authorities.
More specifically, the Expert Panel observed certain 
divergences from the applicable requirements and, 
in some instances, a lack of alignment between the 
­applicable legal and regulatory requirements and the 
current technical system needs and market conditions.
Moreover, during the investigation, the Expert Panel 
became aware that some parties had differing 
­interpretations of the applicable requirements, based 
on the legislation in force at the time. This was particu­
larly evident in the case of the definition of the upper 
voltage limits on the 400 kV grid and the voltage control 
obligations in Spain under Operational Procedures 1.4 
and 7.4, where the applicable requirements were inter­
preted differently by two generators, the TSO, and the 
NRA. While acknowledging the differing interpretations 
on the matter, for the purpose of this report, the Expert 
Panel has followed the interpretation of the Spanish 
regulatory authority (CNMC).
Finally, the Expert Panel noted certain uncertainties 
regarding the allocation of decision-making responsi­
bilities among national competent authorities in Spain 
(e. g., the national regulatory authority, the competent 
ministry, etc.), particularly in defining or further devel­
oping the applicable requirements. Such a lack of clarity 
in certain aspects has also been encountered regarding 
the respective roles and responsibilities of the different 
actors, including which party is responsible for which 
actions and in what sequence. 
In general, the Expert Panel notes that the general 
principles of the applicable legislative procedure and 
correctly enforced mechanisms must apply to ensure 
legal clarity, compliance, and the enforceability of any 
applicable legislation. Measures that could contribute to 
that include, among others:
»	Issuing implementation guidance by the 
competent authorities for new legislation 
or for specific rules, either proactively or 
in response to requests for clarification 
submitted through official channels by 
multiple affected parties. This approach is 
consistent with standard administrative law 
practice in the EU regulation. For example, 
the European Commission regularly publishes 
guidance, notices, and communications 
to clarify provisions in EU regulations and 
­directives, thereby providing interpretations 
that increase legal certainty for businesses and 
national authorities.
»	Regular monitoring of the effectiveness of 
the applicable requirements and legislation 
by the competent authorities. The energy 
sector is innovation-intensive, and technical 
rules may become outdated or ineffective over 
time. Such regular and proactive monitoring 
by the competent authorities should involve 
relevant market stakeholders and aim to align 
the applicable requirements with current (and, 
where possible, expected future) technical 
system needs and market conditions. ­Moreover, 
the competent authorities should regularly 
(re)consider whether the attribution of the 
roles and responsibilities is (still) effective 
and relevant in view of the evolving technical 
and market reality. Besides the systematic 
­evaluation of the currently applicable require­
ments, regular monitoring should specifically 
focus on newly applicable legislation and 
its implementation, where the effects may 
be uncertain. Similarly, the relevant stake­
holders should regularly assess whether the 
­contractual framework in place between the 
parties remains fit for purpose and effective.
»		Making appropriate use of the existing/ 
introducing new economic incentives, and 
enforcement mechanisms as appropriate, 
including economic penalties foreseen 
under the applicable law for breaches of the 
requirements. Economic incentives, whether 
positive or negative, should be effective by 
ensuring the desired behaviour. Of course, in 
the design and application of both incentives 
and penalties, it is important to keep in mind 
that, in a system of systems as complex as the 
electrical system, with a multitude of system 
users, each party must perform its functions as 
established in the applicable regulations.

===== PAGE 455 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  455 
»	Consolidating and implementing institu­
tional competencies pertaining to power 
system operation. The competent national 
­authorities should monitor and regularly eval­
uate the roles and responsibilities attributed 
by the regulatory framework to various actors 
and, where appropriate, (re)consider whether 
the attribution of those roles and responsibil­
ities is (still) effective and relevant in view of 
evolving technical and market realities. Such 
an ­evaluation of roles and responsibilities 
should not exclude the competent ­authorities 
­themselves, with changes introduced as 
appropriate. Moreover, the effectiveness of 
the overall governance concerning the system 
operation and design should also be regularly 
assessed and revised as necessary.

Description:
Analysis of the possibility to identify, and if possible, 
the development of a guideline for indicators to detect 
potential reduced voltage stability and risk of rapid 
voltage change.
Justification:
Any indication that the grid is in a weakened state can 
create a sense of urgency to act before any other ­incident 
occurs, and as such this might avoid rapid voltage 
changes, if actions can be taken sufficiently fast before 
the next incident.
Delivery owners:
Various specialists on system (voltage) stability within

Having sufficient MVAr support means will help avoid

456  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
R250428_1 – Voltage control mode 
Description:
a) TSOs and SGUs operating power-generating facil­
ities should ensure that generators use voltage 
control mode whenever possible, in line with the 
­capabilities defined in the applicable requirements, 
e. g., ­Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/631 of 
14 April 2016 establishing a network code on require­
ments for grid connection of generators (RfG).
b) National competent authorities should support this 
objective, e. g. by considering proposals from TSOs 
to extend voltage control requirements to existing 
power-generating facilities connected before the 
applicable requirements were in place (e. g. see 
Art. 4 RfG).
c) TSOs should explore the possibility of a centralised or 
zonal voltage regulation, where voltage or reactive 
power setpoints for generators are automatically 
calculated based on real-time voltage measurements 
in reference nodes.
d) ENTSO-E should provide comprehensive guidance to 
all TSOs, national competent authorities, and ACER 
on approaches to voltage control, encompassing all 
­reactive power assets. For generators, the ­guidance 
should cover technical aspects (control mode), 
control aspects (reaction time, ramping requirements, 
­measurement accuracy, resolution, service ­provision 
point), and implementation aspects (sampling, 
enforcement in the case of obligations or incentives, or 
penalties in the case of a service).
Justification:
Operating a significant capacity of generation resources 
with a fixed power factor control mode in Spain 
presented two issues:
1) for every (fast) active power ramp (e. g., schedule 
change), fixed-power-factor-mode resources also 
injected into the system a proportional fast reactive 
power ramp (and hence a voltage ramp);
2) fixed-power-factor-mode resources provided inade­
quate reactive power support that would compensate 
for voltage fluctuations.
The approach to reactive power control by generators 
in France and Portugal differed from that in Spain in 
several respects, and cross-country sharing of effective 
­implementation practices was limited.
Delivery owners:
TSOs, SGUs operating power-generating facilities, 
national competent authorities, and ENTSO-E.
Priority: High
Linked to Subsection 4.1.2 Reactive power contribu­
tion by various assets.
R250428_2 – Reactive power capability visibility and adequacy
Description:
a) In the medium term (years ahead), TSOs should assess 
the system needs that will appear in real-time and 
technically design the system so that it can operate 
in the face of expected uncertainties through an 
­appropriate combination of static and dynamic 
­reactive power resources.
b) In operational planning processes and in real-time, 
TSOs should account for the occurrence of rapid 
voltage slopes (stemming from fast-changing active 
and reactive power flows) by ensuring sufficient and 
effective margins in dynamic reactive power resources 
and appropriate alarm settings regarding the 
­performance monitoring of reactive power resources.
c) ENTSO-E should develop a guideline to facilitate the 
implementation of this recommendation.
Justification:
The investigation identified recurrent mismatches 
between expected reactive power provision and the 
actual real-time performance of some system users, 
reducing the effectiveness of voltage control during fast 
voltage variations. Such mismatches were not unique to 
28 April but had occurred before in the Spanish system. 
Ensuring sufficient, visible, and effectively usable ­reactive 
power resources is therefore essential to manage rapid 
voltage changes and maintain system stability.
Delivery owners:
TSOs, DSOs, SGUs operating power-generating facilities, 
ENTSO-E, and national competent authorities.
Priority: Medium
Linked to Subsection 4.1.2 Reactive power contribu­
tion by various assets.

===== PAGE 457 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  457 
R250428_3 – Automatic activation of reactive power assets
Description:
TSOs should explore implementing automatic control of 
shunt reactors, as appropriate, using predefined control 
schemes to ensure voltage stability in the system. TSOs 
should consider more flexible devices (variable shunt 
reactors and capacitors, STATCOMs, etc.) when technically 
designing their systems in this regard.
Justification:
The investigation has identified that a substantial reac­
tive power capacity from shunt reactors was available 
but not activated during the voltage rise preceding the 
blackout (mainly due to the low voltages a few minutes 
before and the manual action requiring more lead 
time). Approaches to such situations should be analysed 
in detail, and a common European approach should be 
considered where appropriate.
Delivery owners: TSOs.
Priority: Medium
Linked to Subsection 4.1.2 Reactive power contribu­
tion by various assets.
R250428_4 – Operating voltage range
Description:
TSOs should ensure that the harmonised operating 
voltage range foreseen at the European level is effec­
tively applied across Europe, by avoiding or removing 
deviations that allow operation outside this range.
The harmonised voltage range (i. e., 380 – 420 kV, as 
defined in SO GL) is designed to ensure sufficient safety 
margins between normal operation and voltages where 
disconnections occur.
Furthermore, the harmonised range reduces the wear 
and tear of system components and ensures a level 
playing field.
Justification:
The Spanish Operational Procedure P.O. 1.4 (1998) and 
specific national provisions, together with references 
in European regulations applicable to Spain, enabled 
the Spanish TSO to operate the transmission grid in a 
­transient mode at voltage levels up to 435 kV. 
The decision to operate the system within an allowed 
voltage range of 380 – 435 kV, while generators 
remained connected at 435 kV or 440 kV (depending 
on commissioning date), left the voltage margin low or 
non-existent.
Delivery owners: TSOs, national competent authorities.
Priority: High
Applicable legislation: SO GL
Linked to Subsection 4.1.3 Voltage Management.
R250428_5 – Ensuring appropriate active and reactive power variation behaviour
Description:
Undesired rapid reactive power variations, particularly 
those occurring on time scales comparable to or faster 
than the system’s voltage control response, should 
be avoided. In the case of a fixed power factor, until a 
more appropriate voltage control mode is implemented, 
­reactive power ramps follow active power ramps, 
meaning that reactive power ramps can be temporarily 
addressed by ensuring that changes in active power are 
smoother.
This reduction in the rate of change can be ensured, e. g., 
by connection requirements and/or controller settings, 
and/or by incentivising a more gradual ramp between 
subsequent imbalance settlement periods (e. g., by 
correcting imbalances based on assumed ramping to 
incentivise balance responsible parties to follow that 
ramp).
The issue of reactive power generation on transmission 
lines stemming from rapid active power changes from 
generators should be further studied by TSOs.

===== PAGE 458 =====
458  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
Justification: 
Rapid variations in power injected into the ­transmission/
distribution grid by power plants, storage systems, 
and consumers (e. g., a rapid reduction in photovoltaic 
injection following negative prices) can lead to abrupt 
changes in power flow in the transmission grid. Such 
behaviours increase system stress and can contribute to 
greater TSO imbalances and defence plan activations, 
particularly when power factor is fixed.
Delivery owners:
TSOs, DSOs, market participants and national competent 
authorities.
Priority: Medium
Applicable legislation: SO GL
Linked to Subsection 4.1.2 Reactive power contribu­
tion by various assets.
9.3.2	
Oscillations
R250428_6 – Continental Europe Synchronous Area Framework for inter-area oscillations mitigation
Description:
Establish a framework to improve the damping of inter-
area oscillations in the Continental Europe Synchronous 
Area:
a) CE SA-TSOs should define the required level of damping 
for inter-area oscillations, collect damping measure 
roadmaps from TSOs, ensure their consistency, and 
verify that the combined measures are sufficient to 
meet the targeted minimum damping level.
b) CE SA-TSOs should establish a periodic and structured 
process for sharing validated Dynamic RMS models 
across TSOs, based on standardised CGMES dynamic 
profiles, including clear versioning, ­documentation 
of assumptions, and managed confidentiality 
­arrangements, to support coordinated inter-area 
oscillation studies and post-event analyses.
c) In accordance with the applicable requirements 
(see Art. 38.4 of SO GL), ENTSO-E should conduct a 
­coordinated study to assess the damping of ­inter-area 
modes in Continental Europe Synchronous Area 
regularly, based on a shared dynamic model of the 
Synchronous Area with two objectives:
»		based on the above studies, tuning existing 
damping measures (PSS, POD) and the 
­implementation of new ones will be proposed 
to reach a sufficient damping level;
»	remedial actions for real-time management 
(e. g., topological, generation dispatch, or 
exchange reduction) of low-damping episodes 
will also be proposed if the minimum damping 
level cannot be reached.
d) The analysed damping measures in this report, 
which show a high impact on the damping of 
­critical ­inter-area oscillations, such as POD-P/-Q on 
­inverter-based devices, additional synchronous 
condenser or STATCOMs, should be prioritised in the 
context of system studies and implementation plan­
ning, without prejudice to the applicable regulatory 
frameworks.
Justification:
The analysis highlights that Continental Europe Synchro­
nous Area has a low-damped inter-area mode that 
can directly or indirectly affect its operational security. 
Moreover, the evolution of the Continental Europe 
Synchronous Area (fewer synchronous generators, more 
inverters, extension with new countries’ connections, 
etc.) could lead to new inter-area modes with low 
damping.
Delivery owners:
CE SA-TSOs, national competent authorities and ENTSO-E.
Priority: High
Applicable legislation: SO GL
Linked to Subsection 4.2.3 Validation of the Analytical 
Model.

===== PAGE 459 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  459 
R250428_7 – Enhance dynamic monitoring and operational oscillation detection
Description:
Improve and expand the monitoring and detection 
framework by efficiently using existing PMUs and 
­oscillographs, or, where needed, installing additional 
PMUs, oscillographs, and power quality monitoring 
devices accessible to the TSO, particularly near inter­
faces with power plants, third-party-owned HV network 
sections, DSOs, and HV consumers. TSOs should analyse 
present and future system operations to determine 
the system needs for such measuring devices. Enable 
efficient PMU data exchange between TSOs to enhance 
wide-area ­visibility and coordinated assessment of 
system dynamics.
Implement automatic detection systems and ­effective 
early-warning tools to identify oscillations in a 
timely manner (including both inter-area and forced 
­oscillations), locate their source in case of forced 
­oscillation, and support prompt corrective actions, noting 
that automated corrective actions should be applied 
selectively.
Justification:
High-quality, real-time measurement data is primarily 
needed to reliably detect and localise oscillations and 
to tune, validate, and continuously monitor system-
wide damping controls. Early and reliable detection 
­constitutes the primary prerequisite for any further 
­classification or response to oscillatory phenomena, for 
both inter-area and forced oscillations.
Delivery owners:
TSOs and national competent authorities.
Priority: High
Applicable legislation: SO GL
Linked to Subsection 4.2.3 Validation of the Analytical 
Model.
9.3.3	
Disconnections
R250428_8 – Validated protection settings for generation units and generation evacuation grid 
connected to the TSO and DSO
Description:
TSOs and DSOs should assess the adequacy and consist­
ency of the protection settings for generation units and 
evacuation grid elements (e. g., transformers below 
which several power-generating and storage modules 
are connected, including distribution-connected and 
distributed energy resources). This verification should 
ensure that withstand capabilities (high/low voltage, 
RoCoF) are aligned with the highest capabilities of 
grid users connected downstream, with explicit checks 
on over/undervoltage thresholds, and minimum time 
delays (commensurate with system dynamics and meas­
urement uncertainties, e. g., ≥ 100 ms or even > 1 s where 
applicable). 
Compliance with the minimum timing requirements 
and voltage thresholds established by the applicable 
regulations and ensuring a sufficient margin in the 
adjusted thresholds to prevent potential measurement 
inaccuracies from causing unintended disconnections 
remains critically important. If this is not the case, appro­
priate corrective actions to achieve compliant protection 
settings should be identified and implemented.
If necessary, TSOs should assess, in coordination with 
national competent authorities, the possibility of 
applying the relevant requirements (e. g. Art. 4 RfG), 
where justified by system security needs.
Justification:
The analysis and expert inputs point to sensitivity to local 
protection settings (e. g., overvoltage thresholds meas­
ured away from the point of connection, instantaneous 
trips without delay) that can unnecessarily disconnect 
generation when voltages oscillate or rise transiently. In 
some cases, the protection appears to diverge from the 
applicable requirements.
Delivery owners:
TSOs, DSOs, and national competent authorities.
Priority: Medium
Applicable legislation: SO GL
Linked to Subsection 4.1.3 Voltage Management.
