460  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
R250428_9 – High-voltage ride-through requirement for Type A power-generating modules
53	
GC ESC Website 
54	
SO ESC Website 
Description:
Type A power-generating modules should be capable of 
stable operation without disconnecting from the grid for 
a voltage-versus-time profile. ENTSO-E should evaluate 
and suggest relevant potential improvements to the 
applicable requirements under the RfG.
Justification:
The analysis in this report on small-scale PV generation 
trips, part of it of type A, highlights their sensitivity to 
high-voltage episodes, even when transmission-side 
voltage remains within acceptable limits.
Given the rapid expansion of PV installations across 
Europe in recent years – with a substantial share of 
systems being small-scale  – it is critical to prevent 
­unnecessary disconnection during high-voltage events. 
This is essential to maintain both grid stability and 
reliability.
Delivery owners: ENTSO-E.
Priority: High
Applicable legislation: RfG
Linked to Subsection 4.3.3 Analysis of Relevant Factors 
Influencing the TSO–DSO Flows.
R250428_10 – Regular controls on grid users’ assessment of withstand capabilities 
(high/low voltage, RoCoF)
Description:
TSOs, DSOs, and private grid owners should put regular 
controls in place after any protection trip or unexpected 
disconnection to assess whether the observed behaviour 
of grid users during real events is consistent with the 
applicable withstand capability requirements (high- and 
low-voltage ride-through, RoCoF ride-through).
These assessments should be learning-oriented and 
aim to identify potential inadequacies in protection 
settings, control behaviour, measurement locations, or 
the ­applicability of existing requirements.
Justification:
The blackout analysis demonstrates that at least 10 
disconnections were not in line with the applicable 
requirements. TSOs, DSOs, and private grid owners 
should take every opportunity to address this problem 
during everyday events that do not necessarily lead to 
serious consequences, to detect structural weaknesses 
early and avoid their manifestation during major system 
disturbances.
Delivery owners: TSOs, DSOs, and private grid owners.
Priority: Medium
Applicable legislation: SO GL
Linked to Subsection 4.1.3 Voltage Management.
R250428_11 – Investigation on behaviour of non-observable embedded generators
Description:
TSOs and DSOs, together with the electrical industry, 
should further investigate the disconnection and 
reconnection behaviour of inverters, in particular 
­distribution-connected inverters (including rooftop 
PV systems and other embedded generation < 1 MW). 
For this purpose, the Grid Connection and System 
­Operation European Stakeholder Committees (GC ESC53 
and SO ESC54) should be used as a platform to exchange 
­knowledge and experience.
Justification:
The data the Expert Panel received from PV system 
manufacturers during the investigation showed that 
many inverters tripped due to overvoltage during certain 
periods on 28 April. The Expert Panel also identified an 
important role of the reconnection time of the non-­
observable PV systems in the loss of generation.

===== PAGE 461 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  461 
However, the Expert Panel was unable to conduct an 
in-depth investigation and considers it beneficial to 
continue and intensify the exchange with DSOs and 
inverter manufacturers on this matter at the European 
level to better understand the voltage-related behaviour 
of non-observable embedded generators.
Delivery owners:
GC ESC and SO ESC (chaired by ACER), TSOs and DSOs.
Priority: Medium
Applicable legislation: RfG, SO GL
Linked to Subsection 4.3.3 Analysis of Relevant Factors 
Influencing the TSO–DSO Flows.
9.4	
Recommendations Not Directly Linked to Root Causes
9.4.1	
Voltage Control
R250428_12 – Reactive power support for inverter-connected installations in case of no active power 
transfer 
Description:
TSOs should investigate options to ensure that HVDC 
systems and other comparable transmission-level invert­
er-based installations with voltage-support capability 
continue to provide reactive power support (functioning 
as a STATCOM) at all times, even in the immediate after­
math of a loss of DC connection.
Justification:
Following the blackout and loss of active power transfer 
over the HVDC, reactive power support at both ends was 
lost; however, subject to appropriate converter design 
and control strategies, HVDC converter stations could 
technically continue providing reactive power support.
Delivery owners:
TSOs, SGUs operating HVDC systems or other comparable 
transmission-level inverter-based installations.
Priority: Low
Applicable legislation: NC HVDC
Linked to Subsection 4.1.2 Reactive power contribu­
tion by various assets.
9.4.2	
Oscillations
R250428_13 – Continental Europe Synchronous Area procedure to create snapshots common grid model
Description:
A common procedure should be established to create 
a snapshot common grid model of Continental Europe 
Synchronous Area promptly after a significant event, 
allowing accurate simulations of the system under 
similar conditions to those of the event.
The snapshot refers to a calculable network model 
derived after the event, based on available state-esti­
mator results, topology, operating points, and relevant 
dynamic data. The procedure should define the minimum 
content and timing of the snapshot, while allowing 
TSOs to rely on their existing tools and vendor-specific 
implementations.
Justification:
Since the investigation of system oscillations relied on 
incomplete and non-harmonised post-event data across 
Continental Europe Synchronous Area, some simplifica­
tions had to be made for the simulation. Therefore, a new 
standard procedure for creating consistent post-event 
snapshots for dynamic analyses could be beneficial.
Delivery owners: CE SA-TSOs.
Priority: High
Applicable legislation: SO GL
Linked to Subsection 4.2.2 Construction of Analytical 
Framework for Oscillatory Analysis.

===== PAGE 462 =====
462  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
9.4.3	
Disconnections
R250428_14 – Streamlined cross TSO/DSO/PGM investigation data governance
Description:
Establish a permanent, standardised framework for data 
provision during incident investigations or for broader 
system analyses to improve understanding of overall 
system behaviour. This framework should ensure fast, 
complete and uniform access to all required datasets from 
TSOs, DSOs (including distribution-connected generation 
data available to DSOs), SGUs operating power-gener­
ating facilities, SGUs operating large demand facilities, 
and SGUs operating HVDC or other inverter-based instal­
lations and other parties capable of providing relevant 
data on small-scale generation or storage facilities. The 
framework should be jointly ­developed by TSOs and 
DSOs, coordinated at the ­European level, and subject to 
oversight from the national competent authority. This 
framework should define:
»	the exact data types and formats (event logs, 
dynamic recordings, high-resolution PMU/
SCADA, DER status, protection activations);
»	latency and completeness requirements, 
including defined escalation mechanisms;
»	authorised data-sharing;
»	predefined legal/contractual provisions 
removing the need for ad hoc negotiations.
This process should allow investigations to fully and 
reliably compare oscillation behaviour, ­disconnection 
patterns, and defence plan performance across all 
voltage levels, taking into account applicable SO GL 
Article 40(5) provisions and national RfG banding 
thresholds.
Where relevant for incident investigation purposes, 
the framework should define conditions under which 
selected operational data already available in real-time 
is preserved and made accessible for post-event analysis, 
without introducing additional real-time operational 
obligations.
In addition, regular data-provision readiness ­exercises 
should be conducted to verify and benchmark all 
­partners’ ability to deliver the required datasets 
within the specified timeframes and formats. This 
­recommendation should apply to all installations 
(existing, new, restored or modified), ensuring uniform 
obligations and avoiding gaps in data availability.
This framework is intended to support incident investiga­
tion, system learning and analytical consistency and does 
not replace or modify existing regulatory ­compliance or 
enforcement processes.
Justification:
The investigation faced delays and analytical limitations 
due to gaps in the available data, particularly from 
SGUs operating power-generating facilities and from 
DSOs. This reduced the ability to reconstruct dynamic 
behaviour, identify oscillation sources, quantify DER 
disconnections, and understand protection responses. In 
future events, a structured, pre-agreed data governance 
framework would help ensure timely, consistent data 
provision and thereby enhance both the speed and the 
quality of incident analysis.
Delivery owners:
TSOs, DSOs, SGUs operating generation, demand or HVDC/
inverter-based installations and national competent 
authorities, and other parties capable of providing rele­
vant data on small-scale generation or storage facilities.
Priority: Medium
Applicable legislation: SO GL
Linked to Subsection 1.1.2 Data Collection.

===== PAGE 463 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  463 
9.4.4	
System Defence Plan
R250428_15 – DER-aware dynamic LFDD
Description:
Develop and implement an adaptive LFDD scheme 
that accounts for high DER penetration and maintains 
­effective load shedding at all times. This may include 
reverse-power blocking, feeder selection based on DER 
footprint, and other adaptive methods.
As this change affects the design and effectiveness of a 
regulated system defence measure, the updated defence 
plan should be submitted to the national competent 
authorities for information. Where specific elements 
require regulatory approval under national law, the 
relevant parts should be submitted accordingly.
Justification:
The defence analysis shows that the current LFDD 
often sheds DER < 1 MW along with load due to missing 
reverse-power blocking and insufficient DER awareness. 
A DER-aware, adaptive LFDD directly addresses these 
gaps and improves the effectiveness of defence plans 
under high renewable penetration.
Delivery owners: 
TSOs, DSOs and national competent authorities.
Priority: Low
Applicable legislation: NC ER
Linked to Subsection 4.4.4 System Defence Performance.
R250428_16 – Defence observability and readiness (data and drills)
Description:
Create a unified framework that provides real-time 
­visibility at the feeder level, including power flows, 
directions, DER status, and LFDD activations. It should 
also ensure the delivery of a standardised post-event 
data package within 24 hours, containing LFDD logs, 
­estimated DER losses, reverse-power blocking status, 
and a concise timeline of early actions. In addition, the 
framework must include regular joint drills between 
TSOs, DSOs, and producers to validate operational 
­readiness, response times, and the quality of forensic 
data. This framework should be integrated into the 
defence plan and submitted to the national competent 
authorities for information. Where specific elements 
require regulatory approval under national law, the 
relevant parts should be submitted accordingly.
Justification:
The analysis highlights limited means to quantify 
DER < 1 MW disconnections and evaluate defence 
­performance. Consistent real-time observability guaran­
tees forensic packages, and joint exercises directly close 
these gaps and demonstrate end-to-end readiness.
Delivery owners: 
TSOs, DSOs and national competent authorities.
Priority: Low
Applicable legislation: NC ER
Linked to Subsection 4.4.4 System Defence Performance.
R250428_17 – Modernised system defence plan for fast voltage deviations
Description:
To reflect today’s high RES and DER environment, TSOs 
should modernise the system defence plans to explicitly 
address fast voltage-related phenomena. This includes 
identifying fast-developing operational anomalies, such 
as rapid voltage changes, rapidly changing net positions, 
oscillatory behaviour, or voltage excursions beyond 
normal operating ranges.
The deliverable of this recommendation is a documented 
update of the system defence plan, defining:
»		the scope of fast voltage-driven threats 
covered;
»	the detection criteria and decision logic at the 
defence-level; and
»	the governance for activating defence-level 
responses before existing measures become 
ineffective.
»	The identification and implementation of 
concrete technical measures should be 
addressed through other relevant recom­
mendations and as outcomes of the studies 
supporting this defence plan modernisation.

===== PAGE 464 =====
464  //  Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report
Justification:
The 28 April blackout showed that although current 
system defence plans include voltage-related elements, 
they were not sufficiently equipped to prevent a fast, 
overvoltage-induced cascading collapse. A streamlined, 
modernised defence framework, tailored to promptly 
identify and address operational anomalies under high 
DER conditions, would strengthen system resilience and 
help prevent similar cascading events in the future.
Delivery owners: TSOs.
Priority: Low
Applicable legislation: NC ER
Linked to Subsection 4.4.3 Voltage Stability.
9.4.5	
Restoration
R250428_18 – Black-start and island-mode real tests
Description:
Make realistic black-start tests mandatory and ­periodic, 
preferably every 3 years or after major control or 
protection changes, in accordance with applicable 
requirements, covering power plant-related aspects 
such as auxiliaries, AVR/excitation, governor modes, 
and house load. Introduce a black-start readiness index 
and require TSO validation before certification renewal. 
Where possible, black-start tests should also consider the 
expected static and dynamic behaviour of system users 
during the planned island operation. To closely replicate 
real black-start scenarios while minimising impact on 
consumers, selected demand facilities (such as power-
to-heat), BESS, and hydro pumps should be included in 
the tests.
Justification:
The investigation showed that black-start retries, 
misconfigured modes, and the oscillatory behaviour of 
islands impacted by non-observable RES can significantly 
delay the formation and preservation of sufficiently 
stable islands. Periodic, witnessed testing reduces first 
start failure risk, improves preparedness, and shortens 
restoration paths. Reliability of black-start facilities 
tested during testing should be considered in the design 
of restoration plans.
Delivery owners: 
TSOs, Restoration System Providers (RSPs), DSOs and 
national competent authorities.
Priority: High
Applicable legislation: NC ER
Linked to Subsections 5.2 The restoration sequences in 
the Spanish system and 5.3 The restoration sequences 
in the Portuguese system.
R250428_19 – DER reconnection and DSO visibility
Description:
Define a framework for DER for controlled reconnection 
during restoration. This includes:
»	a staged reconnection governance framework 
ensuring sufficient load before generation to 
integrate DER governance into restoration 
plans;
»		improved real-time or near-real-time control­
lability and visibility for TSOs and DSOs of DER 
in distribution systems relevant for restoration 
operations;
»	avoidance of early energisation of feeders with 
high DER penetration.
In addition, ensure adequate operational visibility for 
DSOs of production and storage facilities involved in 
bottom-up restoration scenarios of distribution systems, 
including connection status, availability for reconnection 
and blocking status during staged restoration.
High-resolution recordings and detailed post-event data 
required for incident analysis are addressed separately in 
Recommendation R14.
This framework should be integrated into restoration 
planning and submitted to the national competent 
authorities for information. Where specific elements 
require regulatory approval under national law, the 
relevant parts should be submitted accordingly.

===== PAGE 465 =====
Grid Incident in Spain and Portugal on 28 April 2025  //  Final Report  //  465 
Justification:
The Spanish experience demonstrates that controlled 
DER reconnection during restoration is feasible and effec­
tive when appropriate visibility and control frameworks 
are in place. However, the investigation also identified 
gaps for small-scale DER and in other systems, justifying 
the need to generalise such approaches.
Delivery owners: 
TSOs, national competent authorities and DSOs.
Priority: Medium
Applicable legislation: NC ER, SO GL
Linked to Subsection 5.8 Behaviour of distributed 
energy resources and load during restoration.
R250428_20 – Enhance restoration common trainings
Description:
Promote common training across multiple involved 
­entities in a restoration scenario (TSO, DSO, relevant SGUs, 
RSPs) at least every 3 years, to ensure that each entity’s 
role and responsibilities are clear and regularly practiced 
by all involved operators. Training should focus at least 
on the following aspects:
»	the role of the frequency master per island, 
with standard frequency control on the first 
black-start unit and with standard speed 
droop settings on additional sources running 
in parallel on the same island;
»	controllable load and ensuring that the load is 
higher than the minimum stable active power 
limit of additional units before synchronising 
them to the same island;
»	resynchronisation between islands;
»		common restoration procedures defining 
agreed roles, decision authority, sequencing 
and time-bound operational steps for critical 
actions (e. g., generator synchronisation, load 
pick-up, island expansion and fallback actions).
Justification:
These trainings remove the main restoration blockers or 
control conflicts, such as overgeneration in small islands, 
reactive power balance fragility with risk of overvoltages, 
weak tie closures, and misunderstandings between TSOs, 
DSOs, relevant SGUs, or RSPs. This will reduce the time to 
first load and resynchronisation while lowering the risk 
of island re-collapse or trips during resynchronisation.
Delivery owners: TSOs, DSOs, relevant SGUs and RSPs.
Priority: Low
Applicable legislation: NC ER
Linked to Subsections 5.2 The restoration sequences in 
the Spanish system and 5.3 The restoration sequences 
in the Portuguese system.
R250428_21 – Ensure at least 24 h blackout-proof communication and critical tools
Description:
Ensure at least 24 h blackout-proof voice communi­
cation systems and critical tools (e. g., telemetry and 
remote-control signals) for DSOs, RSPs, and relevant 
SGUs, independent of public telecom providers.
These arrangements should be integrated into 
­restoration and emergency procedures and submitted to 
national competent authorities for information. Where 
specific elements require regulatory approval under 
national law, the relevant parts should be submitted 
accordingly.
Justification:
During the restoration process, TSOs reported significant 
difficulties in contacting several DSOs and some SGUs 
due to failures in their voice communication systems, 
while TSOs’ own communication systems remained 
operational. Several DSOs experienced issues receiving 
telemetry and remote-control signals at their facilities, 
which led to significant delays in restoring some areas.
Delivery owners: 
TSOs, DSOs, RSPs, relevant SGUs and national competent 
authorities.
Priority: Low
Applicable legislation: NC ER
Linked to Subsection 5.9 Voice communication and 
remote-control problems during restoration.
